UPDATE: DIED after 2 months of use. I'm not a heavy or careless user of this kind of stuff -- this was plugged into a connector on my nightstand that also handled a mini-USB cable for my bluetooth speaker, and wasn't moved around at all. I tested it initially with my iPad Pro and my iPhone, but after the initial testing, it was used ONLY for charging my iPhone 6s usually 3 times per week or so. The first 6 weeks, it worked perfectly, and I was thrilled with it. Unfortunately, it started malfunctioning after 6 weeks (lights flashing randomly); after 8 weeks of use, it no longer worked at all. CANNOT recommend. Sorry.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: I've been living with this for about 10 days and I've had a chance to use it with my new-ish iPad Pro 9.7" and iPhone 6S.

So far, no problems at all. Functions just like the original cable except this one is longer and has some extra features -- aluminum housing on both ends is much more "solid" than the plastic and everything is well secured with no manufacturing defects that I could find.

Probably the best part of this cable is the LED light that tells you where your device is in the charging process. Pulsing red means it's charging; flickering green means it's almost done; solid green means it's 100%. The solid green light stays on for awhile (haven't been able to time it precisely as it seems to vary a little from charge to charge -- I'm thinking maybe a couple of hours or so before it goes off; then it stays off unless something "wakes it up" (a notification, a phone call, etc.). I charge the phone on my nightstand and I've had no problem with brightness, but then I sleep like a rock once I get to sleep and it didn't keep me awake, either. Some folks might have a problem, though, because the light is rather bright.

It fits just fine with my Speck case on the iPhone and the MoKo ultra-light case on the iPad.

I actually like this enough that I'll be ordering another one before I make my annual trip back home for the holidays so I can charge both devices at once. It's a nice cable, well made, great length, and I can tell by looking at it whether my device is finished charging.

title: Super easy to change this tailgate latch out
text:
Super easy to change this tailgate latch out. All in all the swap out took maybe 15 minutes at most (just latch assembly). It was really easy to swap out the key tumbler from the old latch.

The only issue I had and it could be a manufacturing issue or an install issue. I don't think it was install issue as I have installed low voltage wiring for 20 years and know how to run it properly etc. The issue could come from the factory as I have had some new wiring (just out of the package) damage from the factory. It is also possible it could have come from the installation activities. Let me clarify the issue was the included RCA cord and not the camera assembly, the cable was simply bad.

As always test the system before installing it permanently. It was a super easy fix for me, throw away the old wire and grab another RCA cable which I had in my electrical spare parts bin. I did not ask for a replacement from Amazon as it was way to easy for me to grab a new cable. I had the spare parts and the spare cable was a little higher quality (braided shielding and thicker diameter). My experience over the years with how often bad wiring occurs tells me very few people would experience this issue. Since the issue could have been me, the manufacturing of the cable or a combination of all, I have not taken any stars away.

The Camera (image) looks good, well as good as I would want. I installed this into my 2012 F150 work truck The install took 4 1/2 hours total. That total was also including installing an [[ASIN:B000C19DNM Pop & Lock PL8250 Power Tailgate Lock for Ford (For tailgate with OEM lock)]]. Since the wiring for both had to be done to the same areas of the passenger compartment, I elected for the an all at once installation. I am a little more picky than some on running my wiring, again due to my experience over the years. I would estimate most folks could do this within a couple of hours if they are familiar with their vehicle and accustomed to wiring electronics, and have a good set of tools to work with.

Oh this also was a 45+ year old man crawling around on the ground running wiring and so forth. I did not have a lift to facilitate the process which would have greatly sped up the installation process. Plus saved me throwing out several Danny Glover, Lethal Weapon quotes. :P If you have to ask go watch the movie bonus points if your 45+ and can relate once you watch it.

The instruction are lacking if your a novice, regarding the change out of the latch assembly. Its really just 2 bolts and slide the old one out and the new one in. If the new unit seems awkward to get back in slightly pull the handle as if opening the latch when trying to reinstall it.

It took a few minutes of fiddling to get the camera where I wanted it set. (rotation within the latch assembly) and I followed the advise of the instructions to put some silicone on the back of the camera housing between it and the plastic assembly. This secures the camera in the desired rotation and also reinforces the retaining clips ensuring your camera doesn't fall out.

I did notate the handle was slightly harder to pull to release the tailgate. That however was after the electronic lock assembly was installed. In a test fitting prior to that, it performed just as the original did. So IMO this product works perfectly and the harder pull was that of the power locking assembly.

I would 100% buy this product again.

I am super pleased with my purchase and the product in general. I elected this as a more factory looking camera.

title: Portable, Quality Means for Listening to Music
text:
I like listening to music when I spend time in my backyard. I used to rely on my alexa for this purpose, but more often than not, the volume and clarity were not that good. A portable Bluetooth speaker was the answer and I found just what I needed with this Bluetooth, from Tpone.

What you get with this Bluetooth is a portable, chargeable speaker with that offers up to 18 hours of playback on a single charge. Getting it fully charged will take time, but after that, it’s a matter of pairing it with the Bluetooth on your phone. In about two minutes, it will be ready for use.

The sound quality you get with this Bluetooth speaker is quite good. I like the bass, and for my needs, the volume is sufficient. It’s not powerful enough to blast you away, but for what I need, the volume level works. I use it mostly when I sit on my back patio and/or jump in the pool. I don’t need extreme volume, so this works. There is a plus and minus button on the unit that at first seem like volume controls, but they are not. If you push these, the music will either advance forward or backward to the next song on the list. The volume is controlled by your phone or whatever device you have paired.

There are different colored lights on this speaker that react to the music, adding to the visuals. Again, for my needs, I really don’t care about the lights. But I can see how this could certainly add to the coolness factor for some people. The added colors and the way they react to the intensity of the music is a nice addition. Oh, and I like that I can use this to charge my phone. If a phone is paired, it could drain the phone’s power quickly while you play music. You can easily counter this by plugging your phone directly into the unit, helping to keep your phone charged.

Having the means to listen to music is an ongoing need for me. Whether I am listening to music in my backyard or taking a trip to a nearby beach, I need to be able to play my tunes and the easiest way is to use a portable Bluetooth speaker. This Bluetooth from Tpone delivers on most all counts. The easy pairing, the bass, and the overall sound quality make this an easy winner and an excellent Bluetooth choice.

title: Really like it so far
text:
I haven't had this for very long yet, so I can't comment on longevity, but so far I like it. I take it for granted that there will be some sacrifices when using this type of mouse, I just don't expect to get the same flexibility and usability in terms of various buttons and their placements, so I can't really knock it for being a bit worse in that area than some regular, non-ergonomic options. It works very well and the buttons are easy to click and have a nice "click" to them (unlike cheaper ones). Of course, it takes some time to get used to an upright mouse if you haven't used one before, but after a while it becomes easy/natural.

Regarding the wrist angle, I had some wrist pain and in the past I'd used a cheaper upright ergonomic mouse to help. This is not carpal tunnel, I get joint inflammation on the top side of my wrist, so it may be a bit unusual.
When my old ergonomic mouse broke I decided to try a more expensive one in hopes it will last longer. I can't provide any definitive conclusions on whether this particular aspect of my "treatment" really does anything. My ultimate conclusion is that while treating with other things (e.g. braces, compression, cold or hot), using an alternate device sometimes to change the stress points probably doesn't hurt. Sometimes when going back to use my normal mouse, just putting my hand into position seems to cause some strain, so I think this upright position is helping some. But my experience is that if I use anything for too long, I'll find some joint and/or muscle getting stressed. I'm concerned that this upright mouse position may not be as good for my elbow. So my conclusion is mix it up to spread out the strain rather than hammering on a single weak area, and try to be more careful in the future to start treatment sooner, when I see the early warning signs of strain, before it gets bad.

title: So Far, So Good (**Updated 08/11/2017**)
text:
I've bought expensive USB cable. I've bought cheap USB cables. I've had braided nylon USB cables that felt like they were taking your skin off you hand when they rubbed against you. Other than the braided cable every single cable I use to keep my bedroom tablet plugged in with has split, torn or ripped at the point just above the micro-USB plug end where the cable meets the plug (no, I don't, as I've been accused in the past, yank on the cord. I always use a firm grip on the plug.) Some last a month or two. My old white Kindle charging cable started flaking apart the same day I put it in use. I'd probably still be using the braided cable which hasn't failed but won't stay plugged in.
They advertise that this cable lasts 10x longer and has a 5,000 bend lifespan. I've only had it a short while. There just under seventeen months left on the warranty. I'd honestly be ecstatic if it lasts that long. I'm tired of worrying about shorts or what might happen to the tablet if it goes from plugged to unplugged over and over. So, here's to hoping that this cable lasts as advertised.

Update May 2nd 2017 - Well, here we are a little over three months since I purchased this cable and although it has developed a permanent bend just past where it plugs into the tablet it show no cracking, no lightening of the covering which would show stressing. This has literally at just three months has doubled the average lifespan of my USB cables. This device which is plugged in 24/7 (unless I need to charge my eReader) gets used numerous times a day, it just doesn't sit there. I'm extremely happy with the durability of this cable.

Update August 10th 2017 - I am amazed. No other cable has ever lasted as long as this Anker. I've had cables fail the same day, the same week and as I've mentioned it has developed a distinct bend from the way it hangs from my tablet, kept in the pocket of the grab bar on my bed, the cable shows almost imperceptible whitening just above the connector from strain but no cracks, splits or crumbling. It also stays firmly plugged into my Fire tablet and on occasion it's fine with my PaperWhite as well. Will certainly buy this brand again. Very impressive quality.

title: These won me over
text:
Prior to receiving this review sample I was happy with in-ear type phones, but always grabbed headphones when I wanted to listen to music without disturbing others, These phones changed that. For one thing they are super comfortable. For another the sound is incredible. In fact I have been testing various phones - mainly from this brand, but also some Sennheiser models - and this is head and shoulders above the pack.

I'll be honest and disclose that comfort edges out sound when phones sound good enough. I will normally not quibble over a few hundred Hz one way or the other as long as I can wear the phones without noticing them. These are not only unobtrusive, but downright comfortable, which is a major reason why these have now replaced my trusty [[ASIN:B00ENZRS76 Brainwavz HM9 Hi-Fi Noise Isolating Headphones]].

Soundwise the specs do not begin to describe the richness, especially bass. In fact, when I read the 20 Hz to 20 MHz range I thought that the sound would be somewhat generic for phones in this range. I own a pair of IEMs (in-ear monitors) that go as low as 18 Hz at the same 95dB at 1mW sensitivity, yet these sound much deeper than those. I love the balance of sound across the frequency spectrum as though it's on a smooth continuum. Every one of my test albums I played through these phones sounded so good that I decided that it's time to hang up the headphones and go with these.

Part of the reason why I love these from a comfort perspective is the over the ear memory wire. I prefer that style, but not everyone does. They are definitely stiff and take on a shape that will be uniquely yours over time (and a very short time at that!) Also, while this ships with a [[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]] the phones will not fit after you have contoured them to your ear. The case is useful for carrying around the array of adapters and tips that are included. In fact, the final reason I love these phones is the included triple-flange style silicon tips, which block out the rest of the world and allow me to focus solely on music.

If you love music and want to hear every note faithfully reproduced in their natural frequencies these phones are it. I can honestly say that I have not used a better set of phones from any brand in this price range, including some Sennheiser models that have a street price of fifty to seventy-five dollars more than these, so the value is definitely there.

title: What's Lower Than One Star?
text: I ordered this when it appeared on Vine to replace a recalcitrant Buffalo router that we had to buy in a hurry to replace our original router. However, right after we received this My Net AC1300 the Buffalo began working properly again. So the My Net has sat waiting for the day when we needed it. Last night was it. We unpacked the unit, plugged it in according to the drawings in the extremely limited "instruction" booklet, which is done all in images, and followed the steps. In the third step we were supposed to open Network and Sharing Center in Windows. Presumably, when we clicked "Connect to a Network," we were supposed to see a prompt which told us "this is a new router that has not been set up; click OK to start setup." We never received this prompt. The router just sat there with its blue power light flashing and we could never get any further in the setup. We tried all sorts of things, including resetting the router, unplugging it completely, etc., but we never received the prompt to set up that the booklet claimed we were supposed to receive. We tried manually typing the IP address it stated in the next step into a browser, but since we could not follow the previous step it did little good. We finally installed another router my husband had purchased right before this item appeared on Vine and had put away for an emergency.

title: Depends On Your Intended Use- Ours Was To Replace OLD DVD Player
text:
We have an old DVD player in our basement that tries to up convert but it is not always that great. It has some nice features that were great when we got it, but we wanted another one to replace it that did not take up so much room.

WHAT THIS WAS USED TO REPLACE
The DVD machine this replaced was a really old Philips. It played all regions. No fancy settings, except a sleep timer setting that shut it off after so long. The menu was ancient and very clumsy to navigate.

DID THIS PLAY AS WELL AS THE OLDER ONE?
This DVD player played DVDs as well as the older one. So far we have not had any issues with it. It was only hooked up to the HDMI and the used a mini USB to USB cord the plugged into the outlet. We made sure that it was powerful enough to run the player.

PICTURE
The picture was comparable to the old DVD player- perhaps a bit nicer in some cases. I am actually surprised that it has performed as well as it has.

TRAVEL
I have to say that traveling to a cabin we go to occasionally was nice. We are able to bring this DVD player with us to plug into any TV and watch some DVDs if we want to. It is without TV service so DVD is the only way to really have entertainment if we want it.

DOES IT PLAY BLURAY?
This is not designed to play BluRay.

ANY ISSUES?
This is not a top of the line DVD player with super high definition. If you are looking for that, this isn't it. Is it good DVD quality? Yes. I think so. If you have the right set up, it is a great way to take up little room and still be able to play DVDs. I am not sure I would have this as my permanent player in my bedroom or anything. But it is great to use once in a while at home or travel.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Although this is not fancy or super high quality, it plays DVDs as well or better than our old player so we are happy with it. The footprint is small and it is portable.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. This is a decent player and so far has been good in a pinch to use for playing DVDs. I like the small footprint and portability especially when we have to go somewhere for a while. It is nice to be able to tuck it into our luggage/bags to take with us. The remote is a bonus.

title: Fine Camera Strap
text:
I have a camera, a Samsung NX300, that I bought a couple of years ago that I use for everything. I prefer it to my camera phone and I like it better than my older point-and-shoot camera. It is not high-end by any means, but it is better than the average camera and I am pleased with it. It came with a neck strap, but the strap is the weak point of my camera – too short and not well made. I have been looking for a good strap for my camera and I was afforded the opportunity to review this one. So far it has proven to be a nice one and it works well for my purposes.

I have the “Color10” camera strap which is a blue background with a floral pattern. It is a cloth cover sewn to a thin leather backing – not the most heavy construction but just fine for a camera. The ends of the strap are sealed with large leather connectors that attach to the thinner nylon straps that fasten to the camera itself. Looking over the strap, there are no loose threads and the seams seem to be straight and tight. There’s no problem with the workmanship.

I was a little surprised when I looked in the package and there was a little envelope, with two rings and leather cut-outs so that one can attach the strap to a camera that otherwise has no suitable place to attach it. My camera has two small metal eyes that are not anywhere big enough to feel through the nylon ends of the straps but they can handle the rings without issue so there is no problem using this strap with my camera. This is a thoughtful inclusion – other straps I have seen do not come with these, so this one is better suited for more cameras.

The strap seems to be about the right length and it is very comfortable when I wear it around my neck. There’s really not much more I could ask of it – it is well made and it is comfortable.

I really like this camera strap. The manufacturer showed some thought in the design and made this strap workable without requiring additional hardware, and it is made well too. It is slightly more expensive than some other camera straps I have seen but I think the design and the inclusion of the rings and leather cut-outs justify the price. If you have a camera and you need a better strap than what came with it, this one is very much worth some consideration.

Disclosure: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at minimal or no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Perfect for my application; battery life is less than advertised
text:
I use this to illuminate objects that I am photographing (mainly small items that I sell on various sites), but also to provide extra light for smaller rooms when I am making videos of my band at rehearsal and/or on gigs.

The battery life is touted to be 90-110 minutes under maximum illumination power, but I have gotten around 75 minutes. For me, this is still pretty good I especially like the fact that the battery is integrated, so there is no need to purchase extra batteries and chargers like the other lights that I investigated before purchasing this one. Moreover, this will work with the same external batteries that I use for my tablets and phones, as well as the wall chargers and cables for those devices.

Illumination is soft and can go from warm to cold, depending on your shooting environment. Since I am by no means a professional (or even an advanced) photographer, I found this light to be all that I need for easy to shoot videos and stills.

One thing that I am on the fence about is the mount. It is a little shaky in that it tends to not firmly hold the light steady when installed in my camera's hot shoe. I can live with it since I keep my rig stationary, but if you are on the move that mount is going to be the weak spot.

Despite my dislikes I intend to purchase one more of these as both a spare and as a second light source for some shots that will benefit from the added illumination.

title: A very good antenna but highly directional
text:
The trick with this antenna is not getting frustrated with moving it around and pointing it in the right direction. I mounted mine on the hand rail of my apartment balcony, second floor and now receive all local channels 4-68. Channel 68 being about 45 miles away. All are received in full green in windows media center, without using a preamp.

Previously I had it mounted under and bolted to the 3rd floor balcony to try and keep it out of sight. Reception was iffy on 4 favorite channels. I then moved it to its' present location with the idea that the antennas footprint is considerably smaller than all the satellite dishes mounted on balconies throughout the complex. The mounting bracket and pole that come with it, are the same type satellite dishes use, Very strong and versatile. You will need to buy some good bolts, I used 4, 5/16" x 1- 1/2" Galvanized Lag and flat washers, I predrilled 3/16" pilot holes first. I just thought I'd mention that for those not fastener savvy.

I would guess the antenna mount alone is worth 1/3rd of the entire antenna cost. Recommend a good quad shield coaxial cable with the thick, sollid copper wire. A shorter run is better if possible. I only have about 12 feet to my PC/TV.

Once I figured out how to mount this antenna correctly, a month ago, I haven't had to adjust it.

I wish I could give this 3.5 stars. It works, and helps in all the ways I didn't like my old one, so it is worth at least 4 stars. But there are some things about it that could really use improvement.
To explain, I had a nice backup camera that I installed previously which only ended up being about 100 degrees of view. This wasn't as wide as I hoped, and only showed me what was directly behind the car. THIS camera, however, is a full 170 degree wide, which even shows the edges of my bumper in the fisheye effect. I can see the space next to me, cars behind me, everything that I can't see well usually thanks to the cloth convertible rear view window I have. Thankfully they used the same wiring harness as my previous camera so I didn't need to re-run my power and reverse trigger from the rear light, all of that I could keep which made the wiring pretty painless.

But what I didn't like:
1) The camera is VERY noticeable and it sticks out pretty far. I found the license plate holder covered up the state label of my plate and stuck out too far (camera was beyond the frame of my car) so I used the 2nd mount it includes which can attach to the plastic area over my plate. But even that, because of the mounting bracket requiring space above and behind the camera, sticks out like a sore thumb and still sits the camera beyond the bumper. As in, if someone parallel parks and gives my car a "bumper kiss" (as they call it when parking here in NYC), I have no doubt it will damage the camera as it hits there before it touches my bumper. As you can see in the included picture, bumper kisses are common here.
I turned the camera down so it is at least not sticking out past the bumper, but more in line with it now. I still get a good enough view thanks to how wide the camera is, but I wish I could position the camera better with more choice. I'm forced to use it like this or risk damaging the camera.
2) The picture quality is just OK. The older camera I'm replacing may have only been 100 degrees and not wide enough, but the quality of the image was superior. This one looks more like an old cell phone in color reproduction and smoothness. That's ok, it does the job I guess, but the old one was more pleasant to look at, especially at night. This works well enough at night, but my old one spoiled me because I know it could be better.

All in all, its a decent product that honestly gets the job done. But I wish it had better ways to mount it directly to the car in a way that takes up less space / looks sleeker / doesn't protrude, and that the camera image quality was a little bit better, especially in low light. title: good hardware, terrible migration software
text:
The drive delivers on the SSD promise: very fast access times, even on an older computer supporting SATA1 only. The computer boots up so fast it reminds me of old days before operating systems became so bloated. (Yes, I'm talking pre-history.)

However, as others have noted, the software supplied with it for migration is just terrible, it only works if everything is perfect. And the instructions and error messages are completely inadequate (mostly missing, really).

I wanted to do more than complain, however. I figured I'd share some experience and some tips, that might help another user.

My existing disk was a 1TB hard drive that had some bad sectors (hence my desire to replace). I removed enough data from it to reduce the usage down to about 160GB, figuring that was good for a 250MB destination disk. Then I tried the Samsung cloning software. Many times. It kept failing, sometimes early, often after a few hours. With no useful information (unless you count obscure error codes that are not documented to be information). I tried running disk defrag, achieved no useful result, other than a failure after the cloning reported 100% complete. Deeply frustrating.

I couldn't do a system image restore, because Windows (Microsoft is another producer of dumb and unfriendly software) will only do a restore to a disk of the same configuration. (Here the message is simply that it "can't find a suitable disk", you have to hunt to figure out why.) And I wasn't about to buy a 1TB flash drive.

And I wanted to give it one good try before settling for reinstalling from scratch, because I didn't want to spend several more days getting my computer back to where it was.

Solution: I highly recommend using defraggler (from Piriform) to clean up your disk. You might also find it useful to shrink your partition to the minimum possible, using the WIndows disk management tool. Then I highly recommend using the Macrium Reflect Free Edition to do an "intelligent" clone of your OS volume to the SSD.

After I did this, everything worked perfectly, no problems. Wish I'd known about these tools and all the gotchas ahead of time.

Another tip: If you want to set AHCI in the BIOS (yes, now I'm getting to advanced users), you may need to first enable the AHCI drivers, otherwise Windows will not boot up (you'll get a BSOD). Do a search for this, there's a Microsoft KB article.

Good luck!

title: Small and Strong, but Unbalanced
text:
I have worked with a lot of Bluetooth speakers and I have seen a good variety in features and sound quality. I have a set of Monster headphones and they are excellent; I expected the same from this speaker. It’s a good speaker, but it has a weakness in the sound profile.

It pairs and connects quickly and without any issue. I was able to connect it to my computer without any problems and it was ready to go in less than 20 seconds. In terms of connection speed via Bluetooth, this one is slightly faster than most.

I really like the fact that the speaker has a slider switch for power instead of a button you have to hold down. It makes knowing the speaker is on very simple and it also makes it very simple to power off. This is a big plus to me and is one of the best features in my mind.

I tested the sound quality fairly extensively and make a few important observations, most of which were positive but there was one important issue. The speaker has good volume (controlled by the source) and excellent operational range - I went as far as 30’ and there were no cut-outs or crackles, a good sign. The sound profile though is slightly problematic. The bass is strong - very strong - and is enough to dominate the whole sound output. Many speakers and headsets are heavy-handed on the bass, so this is not totally unexpected but is a bit heavy for my tastes. The highs are good and everything is clear and crisp. The midrange is very flat to the point of being practically non-existent, likely because the bass is as high as it is. Because the midrange is so flat, the output has a tendency to be dull and lifeless.

This is not a bad speaker and it is a decent choice if you want a small and strong speaker. But, be aware that the sound profile is unbalanced.

title: Large 21" screen for better drawing experience
text:
I'm not a professional artist nor do I have a lot of experience with digital art, but that is one of the reasons that XP-Pen is a good choice for someone like me. Wacom rules the digital art world but for someone who is only a hobbyist when it comes to digital media, I have a hard time justifying paying the price that they charge. With that in mind, XP-Pen and Huion are the brands that I target for my budget.

Previously, I purchased a Huion Kamvas 13 and it was a great product but with my aging eyes, I needed a larger screen as even the 1080p resolution screen on that 13" screen was a little bit difficult for me to see without reading glasses. So when I had a chance to upgrade to a 21" XP-Pen, I took it.

This puts me in a situation where I am able to compare the two brands with each other. Both brands sport very similar pens and both screens have a matte surface to give the pens some friction for that "paper-like" feel. I'd say it's more like pen on paper feel, whereas I would've preferred to have more friction but it's something I think is worth training myself to get used to.

The XP-Pen drivers are on-par with the Huion drivers. Once the drivers are installed, it will show a preview of the screen layout that you have set up in Windows and it's quite easy to select the correct screen area that the pen should direct its touch to. From there, the pen buttons can be customized to macros that fit your needs and of course you can set up a different macro for each app that you use.

There are no additional macro assignable buttons on the XP-Pen screen, but there are standard OSD menu buttons at the top of the monitor, just like any other monitor you may own.

I'm happy to report that the XP-Pen drivers run alongside the Huion drivers without conflict. I have a Huion macro pad to make up for the buttons that are missing on the XP-Pen monitor.

So not being a professional artist, I do still try to spend as much time as I can to learn digital drawing and painting. In addition, I have interest in video and photo editing, so this pen tablet is great for selecting subjects using the rotoscope tool in video editor or smart select tools in image editors. Then there's 3D modeling. The pressure sensitive pen is great for sculpting in Blender and other 3D modeling programs. This is also something I'm trying to learn as well.

Despite the multitude of uses that I described above, I also don't have the desk space to devote to this 21" beast. It means that I needed a way to safely stow it. I didn't expect that I would find a carrying case for a large monitor, but to my surprise, that's exactly what I found! This [[ASIN:B099ZSDQ6V KISLANE travel carrying case]] fits the XP-Pen perfectly. It is big enough for the monitor, including its adjustable height stand and has plenty of pockets for the power adapter, pen, usb cables and my Huion macro pad. I didn't think there would be a market for people who thought "hey, it'd be great if I could bring my 24-inch iMac on my trip!", but thanks for that! Now I have a case for my 21" pen tablet.

One thing to note: I ran into an issue with inconsistent pressure with the XP-Pen drivers where I would run the pen across the scree and the darkness or width of the line would be very jittery. It was only alleviated by turning off the setting called Microsoft Ink. After my computer upgraded to Windows 11, I haven't seen this issue. So if it happens to you, try turning of that setting.

title: The screws are the worst!
text:
As convenient as this product makes hooking up networking cables, the cheap screws that come with this wall plate make installation a nightmare.

Do yourself a favor, if you have an extra light switch plate laying around, use those screws instead. I've installed two of these ethernet wall plates into two different low voltage mounting brackets. There are no threads in these mounting brackets. You're essentially creating the threads as you go. This necessitates a greater amount of torque and the screw heads are shallow. If using hand tools, this will require immense amounts of force to prevent stripping the heads. Normally, only a small, flat blade screwdriver is all that is required. But this installation works best if you have a powered screwdriver that will provide the necessary torque.

If you can run the screws in and out prior to installation, it may prevent some headaches. I did something similar to the first low voltage mounting bracket I purchased too.

You'll also find that if you have some screws from an existing light switch plate, that they have a deeper slot and are half the length. The provided screws were much longer than necessary. I replaced the screws on the second wall plate I installed after backing out the originals with a set of pliers after the heads were damaged.

To put this into context, I have the right tools and do more DIY than most other people I know.

title: Worth it for the app alone
text:
Kimberly R. Norton's helpful August 3, 2014 review thoroughly covers most aspects of this card. Actually, after spending a lot of time with the review sample that I received, this is a solution more than a mere card.

First, a caveat. This card requires a reboot of a Windows XP system before it's recognized as a removable disk drive. In a real medical emergency this could be an issue. Granted, XP is obsolete, but Murphy's Law would probably go into effect if you were in a time-critical situation. Plus, this is strictly a Windows based solution.

Now for the reasons why I love this. Foremost is the app itself. It leads you through the creation of medical information that is needed if you were being treated while unconscious or unresponsive. The text files can be read by any system, as well as uploaded to your phone. I have labeled my data card to note that the information is also on my smart phone - just in case the card fails for some reason. The heart of this solution is the app that created the medical data and the files that it produces.

The card itself is clever in that an 8GB flash drive is contained in the form factor of a credit card. The USB 2.0 plug slides out of a protected channel that does not appreciably add to the thickness of the card, so it will easily fit in a wallet.

In addition to the medical data this solution provides a scanner guard that you can use to sandwich your credit cards between that and the Medic ID Guard card. What this part does is guard against RFID identity theft, which is a very real problem. It does not take much to thwart thieves - wrapping credit cards in aluminum foil will do the trick - but this solution is much cleaner and is actually a side benefit. Prior to getting this solution I had been using [[ASIN:B00GC4RTKC RFID Blocking Secure Sleeve]]s. This solution, however, is a lot more convenient.

Bottom line: there are some things that I do not like about this solution, but the benefits greatly outweigh them. As I mentioned, the app alone is worth the cost of this solution because it allowed me to create complete medical data in a structured way. I could have never done that on my own without additional hours of research to discover what information is actually relevant.

title: Returned to Canon for repair for out-of-the-box sensor mis-calibration
text:
Tried to write a review of this on DP Review, but their over-the-top, religious zealots banned one post for using the word "gobsmacked" (when describing my experiences with the first 6D) and another post because of the word "pissed," (after calling Canon and finding out I would have to send it to them at my own cost) both banned claiming violation of their "rule 6," for "profanity." So..., I'll make sure my review is somewhere that people can or might see it and be able to use for their determination if this camera is right for them.

For the price, overall, it's NOT a good deal. Uses the same processor as the Rebels (ie; T7i) and the same articulating screen. Also, the focus points are all bunched-up in the center of the sensor, so a FF sensor is kind of meaningless for AF when you only cover 40% of sensor and it's all in the center? Also, the sensor is a step back from the older 6D. It claims more MP's, but really, if it doesn't have the DR of the original camera it's supposed to replace, then I say it's a step back. Yes, it has DPAF, but that's a function of the processor, not the sensor. So it's basically a weather sealed (maybe) FF T7i. Except without the flash...

Honestly, the T7i feels like a toy, but the few weeks I had and tested it, it was rained on, snowed on and I generally beat the camera up. It took the abuse with zero issues and the DPAF worked brilliantly. Photo's rivaled that of this 6D MII.

First day I had the 6D Mark II, something seemed wonky, but an update of the firmware to 1.0.4 fixed the weird switch issue. Nothing could fix the wildly un-calibrated ISO issue though. After talks with Canon repair center, they said to ship it to them. Since it was after the 30-days I have to return something at BB, I had no other choice.

So why did I send it in? The ISO calibration was WAY off from the get go. Orders of magnitude off. The orig 6D had me gobsmacked (oh my..., there's that profanity!) with it's low-noise at very high ISO. That was unbelievable. This camera though couldn't touch a 5D MII, a 70D or the T7i. Same lens, same coverage (making allowance for 1.6CF of the 70D/T7i), same shutter speed, same aperture, the three test subjects were 1200ISO, with the 6D MII, to get the same exposure, I was at 3200 and higher ISO. Kind of the opposite of what you'd expect, especially considering my opposite experiences with the original 6D. Esp from a $1600+ NEW camera/sensor. And sending back to Canon means YOU Pay the shipping to them. And insurance. So roll in $35 more into the price of the camera.

Some will say just a fluke and that these things happen. They do. But with all the issues combined in a camera that is sub-par to a $750 rebel in almost every aspect, well..., I say stay away until the price comes down to a point that it makes sense to buy a FF rebel with (alleged) weather sealing and no flash.

title: Good every day ultrabook
text:
The Asus has a sleek look with its silver brushed metal lid and slightly rounded sides. Between this and it being JUST under 5 lbs, it makes for an easy transport if you want a laptop to carry around.

I noticed immediately the ultra-fast sleep mode. As soon as the lid is closed the laptop goes into immediate hibernation. After opening lid and clicking to un-hibernate, the laptop is back to active within 2-3 seconds.

The touchscreen has a sleek design with a black outline around the active screen that frames the look of the screen nicely. If you put pressure on the top of the laptop lid it does not affect the screen at all which tells of the durability of the laptop casing. The touchscreen has very nice vibrant display graphics that allows it to be seen easily from various angles without too much glare.

The visuals of the screen are great, which make for impressive video viewing. Picture is great and graphics are very crisp whether it is a Powerpoint still picture on display or a movie. The audio is great, too. While not a gaming pc, this is a nice one for video/audio usage.

It is a very thin and elegant design. The DVD multi recorder fits nicely along the side panels along with three USB ports, a microphone jack, SD slot, network slot and HDMI port.

The grooved out design around the touch pad is a small detail that has a nice impact on the overall look of the keyboard and touchpad (the touchpad is a bit of a different design with the 'clicks', but honestly, at this point with various keyboards for various devices, I'm used to things being different and just roll with it. But FYI to buyer). Keyboard is nicely laid out with light/'chiclet' touch keys and touchpad is sensitive without being too touchy. Considering that I also have a Asus Ultrabook S500-CA with a twitchy as heck touchpad OOB, this is a welcome relief.

Battery life appears to be great as well. I had the machine in hibernate for approx. 6 hours after machine was fully charged and the battery was not even down past ½ charge after all that time. And while in use, it does last about 6 hours. Considering the size and weight, that's pretty good.

Now for some negatives (or at least not so greats).
Fan vent is on the bottom which can be seen as a negative to anyone that works with the laptop sitting on their lap. I would imagine that the fan would be blocked in this instance and would not function properly and possibly allow machine to overheat? Gonna need a cooler for this one while using it for any length of time.

No SSD at all?

It barely comes in under 5lbs. As stated, I also have a ASUS Ultrabook S500CA, which is a 15" screen and weighs less. It also doesn't have a DVD drive, so.... You're definitely adding weight here for that and a few other options (and losing USB and other ports).

No full Microsoft Office Suite/software (you'll have to pay to get more than a trial version or use something else). Just making that clear. - edited as before I had stated 'Windows'. Sorry for any confusion.

All in all, this is a responsive laptop with impressive visual and audio that can be useful to an everyday user. It probably has some drawbacks to someone needing serious processing (no SSD), but for a lot of users, this one is good. I like ASUS, I find them to be reliable laptops, their designs tend to be good, and this ultrabook is no exception.

For everyday use, I'd give this 4.5 -5 stars. Anything else, take off a star or two.

title: These Were GREAT To Use For Contractor Husband
text:
My husband has a lot of use for communication on jobs he has to do in the contracting world. We have had some jobs here at the house which required walkie talkie communication. Let's see how these performed.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
HOW ARE THEY BUILT?
These walkie talkies are tough. They come with the batteries outside of the units, so you have to put them in.

HOW TO PUT BATTERIES IN
You will need a very pointed screwdriver or a small Phillips head screw driver to get the battery cover off. When you screw it back in, it is pretty sturdy.

HOW TO TURN IT ON
The on button on the top is large and easy to cold, dirty, or gloved hands to turn on and off. You can also adjust volume.

CASE?
The case snaps on and off of the units. They stay hooked to the clothes pretty well as long as you are not moving around a lot. In that case, we found them most useful to hold the walkies in the pockets with the clip.

CLARITY OF SOUND?
The clarity of sound was superb. We were doing roof work on the top of a third story and they worked great. We also had to do work about 100 ft away from the point of origin of a wiring job, so we needed that for communication to test the connections. Again, they worked great. Very clear and worked very well.

TOUGH?
These have been dropped a few times and worked very well.

RECHARGING?
The recharging unit has a place for both walkies to be charged. The plug is separate from the base that you charge in. Each receptacle has a red light on it to let you know that the walkie is charging. The plug is small so you can use it on a power strip or in the wall outlet without blocking other outlets. Recharging is fast- within the hour- and they seem to last quite a while before needing to be recharged.

CLIPS
The clips have to be removed prior to charging.

CHANNELS
The different channels we used all worked well. We did not have to use them in a very busy area with multiple walkies, however, so we did not get to test it with a lot of walkie talkie traffic happening on a huge job site.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a very sturdy set of walkie talkies which charge up quickly and last a long time, these are fantastic for contract work and any jobs that we have had to do. My husband plans to take them to his jobs as well when needed. They have a decent range to them and are easy to operate even with gloves on.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. We really love these walkie-talkies. They have been fantastic so far for all of the jobs we have had to use them for. I will update if we have anything valuable to add in the future as we continue to use them over time.

title: Groovy GPS when used with Fresh Maps update
text:
I first bought this GPS several months ago when Costco had it on sale but ended up returning it because I was not pleased with the time it took to recognize my location. More specifically, I would be on the Capital Beltway surrounding DC and the stern female voice would repeatedly tell me to make a U-turn. Impossible. I then used a friend's hand-me-down Magellan which would not hold a charge, not recognize the location and simply needed to be retired. Enter Amazon and their great price for the Navigon 2100 max. Since I'd read that the device was improved with the Fresh Maps update, I purchased Fresh Maps and I highly recommend you do the same if you're contemplating this beautifully sleek GPS.

If you have a PC, you are able to upgrade by connecting the GPS directly to your computer. If you have a Mac, then it's a little more complicated but so worth the effort. You need to remove the SD card from the GPS and transfer the downloaded software to the SD card with a card reader/writer and then reinsert the card into the GPS. I kept a backup of the original software on my hard drive just in case, but have had no need since the upgrade immediately worked. Now on to what I really like about this system.

The 4.3 inch screen is easier to view than the 3.5, particularly if you have many of the POI's selected for display. I first chose them all, then realized they obstructed my map because I'm in the DC metro area. Mine connects with a satellite in only a few seconds each time and reroutes immediately if I change my route. Previously, it would announce that it was rerouting, but it no longer does that, just does the work. Three choices for trip planning are fine enough for me, I tend to choose the Optimal Route. I love being able to select different destinations, too, if I'm going to different places. The address book is easy to access and locations are easier to save. Traffic support is a great asset and now comes free with this device -- I've been saved from many a jam and not have to be tuned into the radio for traffic reports on the 8's. I have the screen set to automatically change from day to night and have had no problem viewing the screen at any time. With the new software, you are able to turn off the GPS from the touchscreen in addition to the usual power button at the upper right hand edge. I love the 2D/3D view, especially when I'm approaching a multi-lane area and I'm unsure as to which lane I need to take. Two voice selections are fine for my needs, Dagmar is more pleasant, but the higher pitched Sarah gives the text to speech option (TTS), so that's the one I've selected. She's not very pushy, either, as some voices I've heard on GPS systems. In the pre-update version, her voice sounded more Germanic, I assume from its origin of Germany, but it's not as odd now. For me, this GPS is intuitive to use and I can make any adjustments from the touchscreen very quickly. I've yet to have a freeze of the system and it has always known where I was with one exception when I was off road on a gravel trail.

My only real criticism of this unit is the rigid cord which extends straight out of the bottom of the device, being so inflexible that I sometimes dislodge it when attaching the mount to the windshield. I'm not crazy about the mount either, but am trying to decide how to approach a new mounting system. I do not want the display obstructing my field of vision but am not ready yet to get a sandbag type dashboard mount. I'm thinking of constructing something myself using the little plastic disc which was included with this GPS system. Also included is the USB cord, but no AC power supply.

title: Precise, but has a learning curve
text:
I received a review sample and after I got this up and running there was a slight learning curve before it felt natural. After I did become accustomed to it, going back to a regular mouse was a slight letdown.

While the instructions are a bit terse I am still giving this four stars because it's easy to set up. The subtracted star is for lack of clear explanations in the quick start guide for how to precharge the unit or even for explaining that the retractable USB cable that ships with it is only for charging and will not connect the mouse interface to the host system.

This mouse operates wirelessly via an included dongle. My old ThinkPad running Windows XP immediately recognized the dongle when I plugged it in, and the mouse as soon as I inserted the included battery and charged it up.

Once I became comfortable with the mouse I found that it was a lot more precise for graphics applications and games than a regular mouse. Note that the base is fixed to the pen-style handle. You move it as though it's a pen affixed to a sled. After you become accustomed to the buttons and the wheel placement you will be using this like a pro.

There is a LED on the top of the unit that shows the charging state. Once that light turns green you can disconnect the USB charging cable. I initially did not like this feature, but have grown to love it because the battery is rechargeable. Other wireless mice I have used in the past seemed to have a voracious appetite for batteries, so plus one for the rechargeable feature.

Bottom line: this is an excellent mouse that is less stressful than using a normal one. Set-up is a bit confusing, but if you have issues leave questions in a comment to this review and I will answer them to the best of my ability. If the company redesigns the documentation to make it clear to complete novices this would be a five star product.

title: Well designed and pro-level construction and features for transforming an iPhone 6 into a camera
text:
I received this as a free review sample. When I accepted this for testing and review I was a little skeptical. However, this has turned out to be a high-quality kit that will transform an iPhone 6 or 6s into a decent hand held camera, yet it will not interfere with other iPhone functions. With the case and attachments in place you can still make and receive calls, text, browse the web, etc.

This is actually the foundation for a more sophisticated set of lenses that will accept add-on lenses like the [[ASIN:B018TQUEYI 010 | bitplay Portable Add-on 3X Telephoto Glass Lens Compatible]]. As you can see from the product description this kit already comes with a basic wide angle/telephoto lens combination. It is not plastic junk, but a serious lens with a precision metal body that screws into this case. It has two parts - one lens screws into the other for combined or separate effects - and it is as good in quality and construction as the lenses that I used with a vintage Nikon SLR.

The case itself can be quickly removed to reconfigure your phone back into a ... phone. But while it is in camera configuration mode it feels just like a hand-held with a choice of grips, an integrated tripod adapter and even a leather strap. The case does not interfere with any phone function, and especially the iPhone's camera and flash. More importantly - for me - the case offers excellent protection. The lip that is slightly raised about the iPhone's screen is curved inward and adds protection for that critical area. The body of the case and two of the grips are textured so you can maintain a firm hold on the phone while shooting, even if your hands are wet.

Bottom line: this is not a gimmick or novelty - it is designed for folks who take photography seriously. I could not find a single flaw in the design from a photographer's perspective; nor could I find any faults from a build or design perspective. This is obviously not for casual users, but if photography is your passion and you own an iPhone 6 or 6s, this case merits serious consideration.

title: good replacement psu, but may need sata cable extender
text:
I got this to replace the PSU for a Dell E521 (about 3 years old, psu started making a nasty noise). The power rating for the original is 305W, so this one at 460W is more than adequate. (An online calculator suggested that I needed 365W.)

I would describe myself as relatively inexperienced at doing this sort of thing: I've replaced cards & memory & floppy/cd drives, but this was the first time replacing a PSU.

Removing the old unit and attaching this one inside the box was easy (just needed a philips screwdriver). The connections were mostly easy, but presented two challenges, one minor, one major: (1) The motherboard connector (P1) for the old one was a one piece unit, this one had two pieces, so I had to make sure I was connecting them correctly. (2) There is a single SATA cable, with three connectors, but my cd drive and hard drive were far enough apart in the box that I could not connect them both. Solution I'm going to try is a SATA y-cable (essentially an extender) from monoprice.com. I'll post an update about this once it's done. (BTW, I highly recommend monoprice for anything they carry: ethernet cables/connectors, parts, network adapters, etc. etc.)

Once I had it all in there, I plugged the computer in and started it up: everything worked fine, and the PSU was delightfully quiet. So far so good -- I'll post updates if I run into any problems over the next year.

title: Important to understand this is a mouse cursor mover, not clicker...
text:
I actually needed a mouse clicker, and for some reason I just thought all these "jiggler" products would have that option, but they don't. All they do is jiggle or move your mouse. It is completely plug and play, no software. Your PC should set-up device automatically, when it's done, this is how you operate:

1. Long press the only button on the device. It will turn on to A3 mode. This is the slowest mode. The mouse will move imperceptibly.
2. Short press button again to toggle to get to A1 mode. This is the fastest mode. Your cursor is flying around fast.
3. Short press button again to toggle to A2 mode. This is the medium speed mode.
4. If you want to leave this thing connected, but don't want to use it all the time, then simply long press again to turn jiggler off when not in use.

In every mode, there is a timer that shows you how long it's been moving. If you're looking for a cursor mover, this guy gets the job done. But don't make the assumption that I made. These things do not have an option for clicking. That's not the product's fault, it never claimed that, it was my assumption. So I'll still rate this product 5-Stars for doing exactly what it advertises to do... move your cursor.

title: Great color and affordable DSLR video monitor
text:
As a freelance camera operator, I'm no stranger to these. This is clearly designed for us low budget video shooters using small DSLR style cameras, which is why it uses a Sony camcorder battery plate and designed with a hood for outdoor viewing. It has some pretty great features for the price point, including crop mark overlays, peaking indicators, and individual color channels. That being said, it can be used for all sorts of things, such as a Raspberry Pi monitor, backup camera screen, or even a second monitor for your laptop (that's a fun one!). It even has included sound, something a lot of these monitors do not, more on that later.
This is really designed for video use, and for that it does a pretty great job for the price. It comes with a hotshoe mount adapter to put on top of your camera, and uses standard batteries (most LED lights and other accessories also use these batteries, so you probably have some already if you work in video). The colors are vivid and sharp, more accurate than my Atmost Ninja 2 recorder screen, and nice and big for focus checking.
The hood is a nice touch as well, but it requires the snap on frame to attach, and the frame has a weird problem in which it partially obstructs the HDMI port. Maybe I'm just doing it wrong, but I found I needed to leave that corner off the frame if I wanted to use the HDMI plug.
Speaking of the HDMI plug, it comes with one included which I thought was pretty rad of them, but it isn't the more modern micro HDMI type, but the slightly older MINI one. That's the outdated kind that older devices use (such as 3rd generation Intel laptops or cameras like the GH2), but pretty much everything made in the last few years has been using the newer micro one. So it seems weird that they included this one. Personally, it will come in handy because I DO have a laptop that still uses that plug, but I don't intend to use it with this monitor. All my cameras that use that plug are long gone at this point.
Another couple of things to note: The focus peaking is pretty much useless. It oversharpens the image and thinks high contrast parts of bokeh are "in focus", which is weird. Thankfully my Sony cameras have peaking built in so that isn't much of an issue. Also, the screen is large enough and is HD enough resolution (not full 1080 but more than 720) that you don't really need peaking to tell what's in focus. You can see it with your eyes. Also, if using with a camera that is outputting a 16:9 image, you have to change the screen size setting from the default, which is to maximize the screen. Everything looked a little stretched because the display is a little taller than the output of my camera until I turned that off.
As far as sound, I mentioned earlier that this monitor has a speaker. That's good for when you want to review footage on the monitor, and even better if using with a Raspberry Pi or monitor for other things where it might be your only source of sound. It is also really useful if shooting with a Sony A6000 or similar smaller camera that doesn't have a headphone jack... this offers a headphone jack so you can monitor off the HDMI feed. That's pretty useful right there! But don't forget, when you turn the live view back on, you are going to get major feedback from the mic to the speaker unless you quickly turn the volume all the way DOWN first! Or just leave headphones in if that's how you roll.

It is important to note however that it will not accept a 4k signal. The actual resolution is 1280x800, and it will accept up to 1080p as an input, but more than that fails. At the time I'm reviewing this, it seems that there are similar monitors that can accept a 4k input for around the same price. I'm guessing they are updated versions of the same design, as there are no monitors that actually have that resolution for this price, rather they just accept the feed and down-sample to 1280x800, just like this one. So at the end of the day, it probably won't matter if it accepts 4k or not. Some cameras don't like outputting a different resolution than they are recording, so if you are recording in 4k and outputting 1080p, that might be an issue. Otherwise, this is a solid value.

title: We're not mad, just disappointing. Excellent machine & support, app needs more work
text:
It's hard to hate on this drone when it is flying. Mechanically it performs very well in the air. The camera is great & the camera stabilization works very well. The app has been a frustrating experience that has kept me from fully exploring the capabilities of the drone.

After the last app & firmware update we have experienced freezing of the video feed, disconnects from the phone & disconnects from the radio. The good news is that, in the last case, the drone dutifully returned to its starting spot. I didn't have those issues before the update but I did have others.

I have put in a couple of tech requests & their support is very good. In some cases a confirmation email the same or next day & resolution in another day or so. In one case a very nice young man called me to talk me through a gyro calibration.

We have enjoyed using the camera to fly it around the neighborhood. The camera function is fantastic. The attitude adjustment for the camera is intuitive & handy. I'm still learning to fly by the screen so I like being able to "look" up & down to make sure I'm not about to hit something and figure out the location by looking at landmarks & streets.

On the drone platform, the camera can be set to track a person with just the camera & the drone stationary or have the drone follow the person while tracking. We used that to record my daughter's color guard practice. It also has a "point of interest" feature where it flies circles over a particular spot & the operator can start or stop recording while it it is circling. I'm thinking this will be cool for parties this Summer when we can finally have people over again. For now I have is top quality shots of the top of my camper & green pool.

It camera mode it performs very well as a stable, tracking camera. The camera gimble has a lot of range to track a person moving about & the tracking works well. If the person moves out of the frame it will not re-aquire them though in my experience. The camera can be mounted on a tripod or used as a hand-held "camcorder". On a tripod, it kind of hangs off to the side & down so it will interfere with some tripod setups. It is also a bit bulky to use as a camcorder but the stabilization is so good I forgive that. In either configuration a phone has to be used to stop & start recording or take pictures which I do not like & I hope they put out a bluetooth button for that.

The controller is small compared to the ones I used for model airplanes & it is easy to hold. There is no attachment point for a lanyard. The phone is held on a mount that extends out & up & puts the phone in a good place to see but puts a lot of weight up high. The gimbles have a rubber gasket around that makes them water resistant & doesn't interfere with their operation. The controller charges with a mini-usb (ugh) & connects to the phone with included USBC or Lightning cables. The cord going to the phone could be a little more tidy.

The case is nice, thick foam & will hold everything needed to fly except maybe a second battery. It's sturdy enough to put in checked luggage (with the batteries removed of course).

The beginner mode is seriously slow & a good way to get used to flying especially for someone who is learning nose-in hovering & other basics. It also makes a very stable camera platform.

A couple of observations:
I am not great at sorting out things on the app & would prefer robust instructions. I had no idea that the aforementioned gyro calibration was something I could perform myself or that I should have known where to look for it. It took me several tries to figure out how to turn on the tracking features (it has to be "started" after turning it on).

This is my first serious drone so I can't adequately compare it to other models. I used to fly model airplanes & helicopters decades ago & I tend to try to fly these quadrotors like an airplane in line of sight flight. This model seems to resist that more than others that I have flown & tries to force a flat plane rather than let me bank it & swoop around (I hope that makes sense).

I worked in a hobby shop for several years when I was younger (a long time ago). This is exactly what people who came in dreamed of buying; a small, aircraft that could fly in the backyard or far away that doesn't require a steep learning curve to fly or maintain. The camera adds to the fun & makes it useful.

text:

We like it best when they are at least devoting some of their electronic time to doing things more constructive and/or creative, and this is what convinced me to get my hands on this SOSUN Camcorder.

I had not heard of SOSUN until I got this camcorder, but I had read good things about the brand and decided that such a large percentage of customers must be right about something. One of my girls wanted a camcorder and this one seemed to have what she needed and seemed good for a beginner. The camera is lightweight and easy to hold. It can be used for regular picture taking and for video. The quality of video produced is good, too. There are better camcorders out there that create better videos and have more features, but this one is still good for a beginner like my 13 year old.

title: Amazfit is still the best value!
text:
I've owned and had the opportunity to try out many different brand of fitness tracker watch, from Fossil/Wear OS, to Fitbit, Apple, and many of the cheapo brands too. I've said this before, but generally you get what you pay for, aside from the Amazfit brand watches. These and the Xiaomi Mi band series always impressed me, punching way above their paygrade. This latest edition just continues that legacy.
To be clear- there are some pretty neat features and apps that Wear OS / Apple OS will offer that this won't, but for the money this is the best value and user experience.
For starters, everything about the user experience here feels premium for the money. The battery life on this is killer. I charge it about once a month, maybe 2x a month. Granted I turn off features like lift-to-wake, but my experience with Apple and Wear OS devices needed charging daily in comparison.
The display is beautiful- a very vivid OLED, with very responsive touch screen. The animations are fluid and feel premium, and the display is large enough to easily read notifications and even responses from Alexa! That being said, this model lacks the speaker that the Pro model does, so while I can ask Alexa questions, I have to read her answers. I also can't answer calls since there is no speakerphone, however I can silence the ringer if I don't want to take it.
The sensors are improved over the series 2, however the functionality is mostly the same. In fact, if you have a GTR or GTS2 already, one might argue that this is a lateral move and not necessarily an upgrade, aside from one major new feature: With the new Zepp OS, Amazfit is going to allow mini-apps that can be installed on the watch. THIS is the big thing that is missing compared to other name brand smartwatch devices. So far there are only a handful of mini apps in their "store" and arguably not anything I particularly was looking for, but there is talk of an API being released for third party developers. Who knows, maybe we'll even get some basic games or other nifty features coming soon. I still have my GTS2 which I love as well as this, but I'm holding on to this for the potential app development in the future. Can't wait to see what Amazfit does next!

title: PoE = only one power adapter needed! Almost perfect!
text:
First of all, the signal quality is great over my 300' of CAT5e cable going from my entertainment system in front of my room to my projector around the back (cable goes behind walls and snakes around furnishings to get where it needs to go). It is fast and responsive, and the lag seems minimal if any. I love that it can also be used as a pass through, and that it only requires power on ONE side! My old HDMI extender required a power adapter on both the tx and rx side, but this can actually send power over the network cable (PoE) so that the other side does not need its own adapter. Now THAT's awesome!
This is one of the primary reasons I was interested in this, as there are two times I use such an adapter: When I use my projector instead of my TV for movies, and when moving a camera around at an event that I want to send a live feed back to a screen or streaming box for. Currently I have to supply power at both ends of the network cable, but I imagined ONLY needing power on the receiver, and having THAT power the transmitter. For example, in the case of the camera, I could have the screen receiving the signal send power to the transmitter by the camera using PoE and be somewhat more free of tethered power on that side. Also, when using the projector, I could turn on the outlet controlling the projector via remote and have it power on the transmitter behind the TV as well. Less wires and outlet spaces where already difficult / congested is good! THE PROBLEM, however, is that this thing misses its potential by only sending power from the TRANSMITTER! In other words, I can send power from the tx with PoE to the rx side, but the RECEIVER can't power the transmitter! It only goes the same direction as the HDMI signal. This, to me, was disappointing as that's the side I wanted to save from having more wires to plug in. Not the receiving side. That side is never an issue to supply power.
So I was a little upset about that. But otherwise, it is a solid product that seems to do what it claims to, and so far seems more reliable than my previous setup. If it could send power using EITHER side, it would be perfect! So close this time!

title: Flexible, low-profile, great for MP3 players
text:
I use this to connect my MP3 player to a 3.5mm jack I installed in my car's center console. The low-profile 3.5mm connector was very important to me because I wanted to make the connection as slim as possible to avoid accidentally torquing it, catching things on it, or applying pressure to the jack when moving things in and out of the console.

It works quite well for this purpose. the connector is slim - about as slim as they come, such that it basically clamps right up against the side of the player and the wall of the console. The plug itself feels solid and has a small snap when connecting to things. The cable is soft and almost as flexible as a woven cord, even if it does prefer some orientations to others. Sound quality is typical - which is to say, as good as every other cable I've owned.

The only thing I didn't like about the cable was the colors - it really doesn't go with the car interior and stuck out as a result, a bit distracting. So I used a Sharpie Pro - the big chisel-tip type - to turn it black. It is cotton sheathing, so this is quite viable. I was careful - after inking the entire cable and letting it dry, I washed it in warm water, then dried it and ran a soft, clean rag over it about a hundred times, until it came away basically clean. After the fact, while you could tell the original black bits from the inked threads, it's just different shades of black, rather than looking blotchy. I imagine using something like RIT black dye would be about equally effective, if you heated it and let it soak for a good long while.

So I would recommend it. The braided cable looks premium and is much easier to work with than its equally-thick rubber counterparts. This makes it easy to handle the MP3 player while it is still plugged in.

Amazon 1 Star Rating equals to "I Hate It" ... and I do have hatred for aspects of the Bolt, even though I also have love for it.

I Hate:

TiVo wants a fee of $600 for a lifetime license, after you pay $300 or $400 for your Bolt. This is insanity! I could understand if they were asking for $600 for the lifetime of the person, no matter what TiVo boxes they swap out in the future.

The design of the box is terrible, in my opinion. I really hate it. (And please do not say they did it only to allow air to escape, because air can escape just fine on their Roamios and on other DVR's such as the Moxi.)

Final thing I hate is the difficulty prying the box apart to swap out the hard drive after the screws are removed. TiVo knows one's hard drive will fail eventually after the warranty, and/or that people will wanna upgrade to a larger capacity drive. They could have easily designed this box with a removable cover just under the drive, instead of making it where you have to take the whole cover off in parts.

Love:

Hands down, the TiVo interface and extra features of the Bolt are superior to any other DVR out there as of this writing. Once you have the opportunity to use Commercial Skip, you'll fall in love. Also, the Quick Mode feature is very nice, and it works well. The speed of the Bolt interface is excellent.

The TiVo software is really easy to use. The Bolt is easy to get set up. I like that if you have to swap out your hard drive, the TiVo software will automatically install itself on the bare new drive.

I like the online and mobile interfaces which allow you to set recordings remotely.

There are countless people online who feel that TiVo's $15 per month (or $150 per year) fee is too expensive ... and of course if you are paying it, you will wish the fee was a more reasonable $10 per month/$100 per year.

I am hoping TiVo has heard the endless complaints of folks who hate the Bolt's box design and who want a flat box. It will be interesting to see if they do a redesign of their next DVR model. And I'm hoping they come out with a TiVo Bolt OTA for cable cutters where the lifetime license fee will be far more reasonably priced than the Bolt's astronomical $600.

title: So much better than my Ronin S!
text:
I own a DJI Ronin S which I use with my Sony A7 series cameras (an A7S and A7Rii). It worked well enough, but after trying this Crane 3 Lab, I'm blown away and ready to sell my Ronin for this.
For starters, I love the ergonomics of the extra handle. Being able to hold onto it with 2 hands and shift from the handle to the pistol grip makes using this thing far more stable than trying holding just the pistol with both hands. It also makes it easy to pass and shift to a low angle mode, as well as seamlessly pass it to another person easily for those really impossible looking tracking shots (thought a window, down a staircase, etc). I'm also really impressed with the buttons and controls- if you've got a USB cable controlling your camera, there's a lot more you can easily access right from the gimbal without touching the camera than you can with the DJI Ronin S. With the Sony cameras, unfortunately, you can't control the focus motor of an automatic lens with the follow focus wheel... that's a limitation of the camera since Sony doesn't have that protocol in their USB remote interface. Other features work perfectly, however, and I've been told that other cameras like Canon and Nikon work with the focus control as well (this is something I'm hoping Sony changes in the future, but for now I'll just rely on auto-focus during gimbal shots).
Another HUGE improvement over other stabilizers is the ability to LOCK the axis motors in place. This is a fantastic tool to help when balancing (you can lock the other 2 axis and work on balancing them one by one, rather than holding the other positions in place as you work backwards like on the Ronin), and its also great to lock it in place when you are powered down and carrying it around- I've found that when taking a break with my Ronin, it is always awkward to walk around with it since the camera can flop and swing around as I walk. The Crane 3 doesn't have that problem if you just lock the motors in place with a little red switch.
Honestly, I wish I would have waited just a little bit longer before buying my Ronin S so that I could see how much better this is. The app is honestly just OK, I've heard people say they like the DJI app better and I would probably have to agree with that, but this just does everything else so much better that it I'd still say it is worth it in the end. The crane 2 is easier to balance in my experience, more forgiving (less crazy vibrating when the gimbals shifts out of balance), has better features and ergonomics and overall just seems to do a better job.
I STRONGLY recommend it if you are shopping around between those two options.
