title: Balanced Sound Spectrum
text:
Bose is primarily known for their active noise canceling (ANC) phones though they have for years offered non-ANC phones. This is my first pair of Bose phones that are not in the ANC class of headphones and my impression of them is mostly positive. I do see some room for improvement, though.

First off, these are without question the lightest headphones (aside from ear buds) that I have ever worn. I am a bit odd in that I actually prefer heavier headphones but this is strictly a preference, not a criticism. In spite of the weight, the phones fit very nicely and do not feel like they're about to slip off if you lean down. This is not to say they're tight, but they are tight enough to hold well. They're easy to adjust too, so getting them to fit just right is simple enough. If exceptionally lightweight headphones are your thing, this is what you want.

The cord is a little different than other phones I have used in that the jacks on either end are of different sizes. This is good and bad. It's good in that there's no question of how to attach the cord because it only fits one way. But, it also means that a normal cord that comes with practically any other headphone will not work.

The sound quality is definitely better than average but not perfect (certainly not audiophile-level). The sound spectrum seems to be fairly well balanced. The highs are good and the "edges" are crisp and clean for most tracks. The midrange is ok but slightly hollow. The bass is very good without being overdriven. One of the problems with a lot of headphones is that they tend to overdrive the bass which is fine if you really like your bass, but too much can overpower the rest of the spectrum and give some of us headaches. That these phones do not over-amplify the bass is a pleasant surprise.

Having a pair of Bose QC-15 ANC phones, I can compare the two models' sound profiles and there are some slight differences. Where the QC-15s are great at the highs and overdrive the bass, the midrange is sorely lacking. The SoundTrue get the bass right and have good highs but fall slightly short on the midrange (though still better than the QC-15s). Comparing just the sound profiles and ignoring the ANC function, I prefer the SoundTrue over the QC-15s.

The carrying case is nice and should provide some protection when packed for travel. I would have preferred a slightly harder and more crush-resistant case but that's me being picky. There's not a lot of extra room in the case so storage is not really an option with the case.

The price is a little high ($180 as I write this) and that might be a little steep for some. It comes down to whether a less expensive set of phones delivers the same (or better) sound profile.

My overall impression of the Bose SoundTrue headphones is positive. These are very comfortable and exceptionally lightweight and the sound quality is good though not perfect. These phones are above average and are worth consideration if you want non-ANC headphones or if you're looking for very lightweight headphones.

title: Inexpensive, Basic Lens Protection
text:
A UV filter on a lens can be a cheap and effective way to protect your expensive glass. Some of these filters are better than others, and this one is on the lower end of the scale. That said, it's worth its asking price.

Most digital cameras already have decent UV filtering built in so there's not a lot of sense to getting a UV filter for that purpose. However, these filters do have a very important role - they provide very inexpensive protection for the lens, for both dirt and scratches. An inexpensive filter like this is a lot less expensive to replace than a lens that cost hundreds of dollars.

My complaint with this filter is the same as with other inexpensive filters I have used. It's reflective, and in certain situations I can get reflections between the lens and the filter that can mess up an otherwise good image. A fine example is when photographing trains or oncoming cars that have turned on their headlamps. In those cases, this filter interferes and causes very noticeable reflections when the angle is just right.

The majority of the time, this filter is fine protection for my lens and I shoot with it in place. However, there are times when it is a detriment and I remove it for those cases. A more expensive filter that cuts down reflections is a better choice for those situations. However, those filters cost a lot more in most cases.

This is a decent UV filter for the price. It provides good basic protection for the lens on which it is attached and the price is reasonable. There are cases where it's more of a problem than a help, though, and for those cases it is easy enough to remove.

title: Very good desktop replacement system
text:
I decided to purchase a new laptop after my old laptop was taken over by the family for a variety of tasks. I was mostly happy with the system I had, a nice HP Pavilion system with a decent feature set, but considering that it is 2-3 years old and does not run everything I want to run anymore I wanted to make my upgrade to a new system worthwhile. In researching I found this particular system and I pounced on it, as I found it at a steal of a price. It is not perfect, but there is an awful lot in this notebook.

My very first notebook was a Sony Vaio, so I imagined that this would be familiar territory. I was greatly mistaken, as things have changed dramatically since then, mostly for the better.

First off, this is a fast system with lots of expansion room. This is very important to me because I do a little bit of everything - I do some gaming, I write software, I write short stories, I hang out online. I am not considered a power user in that regard so an AlienWare ultra-high-powered expensive gaming rig is not really what I need, but I don't need an entry-level system that is good for little more than checking email either. My needs are for a well-rounded machine that can do most things well. This notebook fits that need.

I am especially impressed with the bright, large screen. I do occasionally toss a movie DVD into the system and treat myself to a private showing of whatever movie I have chosen, and all of that screen real estate makes for an enjoyable experience.

As for DVDs... With Blu-ray built into this system, watching new media movies is not a concern. That's a very nice plus.

I like the fact that this system has two individual hard drives instead of one large one, as I want to create a dual-boot system and not wipe out the whole thing. I was unaware of this when I purchased the system, thinking I had a unified drive, though that was an oversight - the labeling and documentation are clear.

The system comes with 3 GB RAM, expandable to 4. Up to this point things seem to be comfortable in that amount of room.

My first task was to strip off the trial software I don't want or need, which includes MS Office 2007, Webroot SpySweeper and Norton 360. Some people will appreciate these applications but for me they are in the way and clutter the hard drive with unneeded stuff. If these applications were full-release apps with more than 30-90 days of use, I likely would keep them all but in my case I already have licensed software to use that meet the same needs.

The documentation states that there is a firewire port, a VGA port and an S-Video port, and it took searching the web for a manual with technical diagrams to reveal that these are hidden on the right side, under a cover. Nothing that came with the system says where to find those ports, and the cover that conceals these ports blends in well enough to truly hide them - I did not find them without help.

Even more concerning to me is the number and placement of the USB ports. There is one on the back, and two on the right side close to the front edge. I work with an external mouse but I use the built-in keyboard, and I am right-handed. So, if I plug anything at all into those two front edge USB ports, the cords interfere with my mouse use. The solution, then, is to plug a 4-port hub in the back and then plug everything in there.

The built-in speakers are all right, though nothing special. If you want better speakers plug them in and all is well. That said, the built-ins are quite acceptable for most use. You would not want to use them for listening to symphony music, of course, but they're just fine for gaming and general music.

I am very pleased with the graphics. My litmus test for gaming is Neverwinter Nights 1 & 2, and both of these play quite smoothly. I have not loaded up Unreal Tournament 3 yet - that's next - but it should have no difficulty at all with that game.

I did run into one problem that required a call to Sony technical support. Because Sony does not include recovery media with their systems, it is up to the owner to create them and Sony makes it easy with included utilities. There are two options for creating the media - 1 dual-layer DVD or 2 single-layer DVDs. I chose the single dual-layer and after an hour of writing and grinding, the DVD ejected and the system said the creation failed. Assuming it was the target medium, I tried again with the same result. I called Sony thinking I needed to request the recovery DVDs and the technician told me that the single-layer DVD creation would work but that a glitch with this specific model prevents the dual-layer media creation from working. When I used two single-layer DVDs, everything created without a hitch.

This brings up a good point. Some places provide horrible service with operators that no one can understand. I got through in a reasonable amount of time (it was 5am but I still had a brief wait) and I got a very pleasant fellow who was very easy to understand (he did have and accent, though I could not place it) and was very helpful.

This is my desktop replacement system. It does everything I need it to do, it works well and it has a good feature set. It is certainly not perfect, but even at full price it is a good deal for what you get. It is NOT a top-of-the-line gaming rig but it's not marketed as such. If you want a good well-rounded machine, give this one some consideration.

title: Acer Aspire: Everything We Want in a Computer
text:
Computers are an important part of life. I know, I know- we need to get away from electronics and try to return to the days when more personal interactions were the norm. But regardless of how you feel about the proliferation of electronics in everyday living, there is no denying that most of us need them to one degree or another. We are writers/bloggers in my home and need good machines to carry us through the day. And the Acer Aspire Touch Desktop is one excellent machine for everyday use.

Let’s start with the physical attributes. This Acer computer features a very large flat screen with excellent clarity, making it ideal for watching videos, television shows, etc. The keyboard and mouse are wireless, so there is no issue over wires getting tangled as you work. Best of all, the CPU is part of the monitor. There is no separate tower or other computing unit, and that means this computer is space efficient. All you need is a place wide enough to handle the width of the monitor. The keyboard is certainly different from the one I was using previously and it took some adjusting to get used to. But this is the case with any new keyboard and you know what?- the adjustment period for this keyboard was less than a day. In almost no time at all, my wife and I took to the change and had no further issues.

As for the set up, well, it doesn’t get much better than this. I can remember when it would take several hours and much frustration to set up a new computer. But with Acer Aspire, the set up was complete and the computer was ready to use in less than 10 minutes after removing it from the box! We actually scheduled some time in our day, thinking it was going to require a fair amount of time to complete everything. It was so fast I started to worry that I did something wrong. But that wasn’t the case- everything is pretty much ready to go, straight from the package.

Because of our writing and blogging, we often need to have multiple windows open at any given time. This was an issue with my wife’s laptop and it would often slow her computer to a crawl. With this Acer computer, there is no such problem. She can have ten separate windows open, along with Microsoft Word and Excel, and the speed is still as good as ever. Again, this is a definite plus, as computer speed is a top concern for us and many other computer users.

I always try to find something that needs improvement when I write a product review but with the Acer Aspire, I can think of only one thing, and it relates to the Office Suite. They give you Office Suite for a free trial but once the trial is up, you will have to purchase it yourself. Acer could easily make this improvement and while this type of criticism has really nothing to do with the functionality of the product itself, it is about the only issue I can find. Everything else about this computer is well above average.

Computers are essential to my household. We need our computers for writing, for the classes I teach, and other uses. With the Acer Aspire Touch Desktop, we have found a cutting- edge computing machine that fits our needs perfectly and has everything we desire. It’s an excellent computer that would look really good on your desktop and I recommend it when it comes time for your next pc upgrade.

text: This is a review for the TK-408 switch.  I noticed the reviews seem to show up on several different models.  This model has the round PS/2 type connections for mouse and keyboard, and female connections for VGA. It also has audio connections, so you can use one set of speakers for several different computers. There are no USB connections on it.  All the cables are included.  I use this to switch between PCs; some reviewers mentioned trouble with MACs.  The only real issue I have encountered is that if I power up a computer that is off and I am currently switched to another computer, when I go back to the one that was off (that is now on), the screen resolution has dropped.  If I switch to the turned off computer while it still off and power up and boot up before switching away, there is no issue and then I can switch back and forth all day with everything staying as it should be.  It's just a very minor annoyance.  If the computers you are switching between are always on, it would never be an issue.  The other thing that I found out is that for me the audio was not of much use.  The reason is that I am often listening to music on one computer; when I wanted to switch to another computer to do some work, the sound stopped, obviously because now I was on another computer that didn't have music playing.  I ended up just hooking up 3 sets of speakers for my 3 computers.  A lot of space used up, but a better solution for me.  The sound situation is not a problem with the switch, as it was doing exactly what it should by looking for output from the line out on the computer that you are switched to.  Some reviewers mentioned problems with delay in the hotkey switching.  I haven't noticed this and usually it takes no more than one second to switch.  My switch uses ScrLk twice followed by the port number the computer is on.  I have tried out two more expensive switches that don't have hotkey capability and you have to press a button on the switch.  With Trendnet switches, you can do either - use the keyboard sequence or press the physical key on the switch.  I have had this switch in service for a number of years and the only physical issue I have encountered is that once in a while the master keyboard and mouse connections loosen up and have to be re-seated.  The switch has given me many years of flawless operation and so far has proven to perform better than much more expensive switches.  Very good value for the price and I highly recommend it. title: Disappointing - The Low Price is Justified
text:
This is my first exposure to Panasonic Active Noise Canceling (ANC) headphones. This particular model is very inexpensive relative to most ANC phones on the market, and unfortunately the low price is justified. These phones fall short in a couple of important areas.

First and foremost, these are ANC phones and the ANC function does indeed work. That said, the degree to which it works is in line with the pricing. I have a very specific fan in the house that I use as a benchmark, as most ANC phones are able to nearly completely wipe out the white noise that this fan generates when on the lowest speed setting. The Panasonic phones kill a good bit of the fan noise but allow more noise than almost every other ANC set I have tried. In the office I tried these phones in an area serviced by two large air handlers that generate a lot of noise and these headphones did remarkably well though still not as well as most other phones I have tried in the same environment. Now, when compared to the likes of Bose, Panasonic does a very poor job but then again they cost maybe 15% of what Bose costs. When considering this price differential the Panasonic phones do a decent job with their ANC which should be acceptable by most for traveling.

One area where these phones fail, though, is in build quality. These headphones are extremely lightweight and they feel very flimsy and fragile. These are not the headphones to take when traveling frequently. To add insult to injury, they come with a cloth carry bag which offers absolutely no protection at all beyond serving as a dust cover.

Worse, though, is the miserable sound quality. I don't know if my specific headset is the problem but while I have a decent full range of sound, everything across the spectrum sounds slightly tinny and hollow. I was encouraged that Panasonic does not overdrive the bass as many manufacturers tend to do and instead delivers a fairly balanced spectrum, but this does not make up for the poor quality of sound. As these are inexpensive headphones I would never expect them to be audiophile quality, but the sound should absolutely be much better than it is.

I was encouraged to see that Panasonic includes a 2-prong adapter in the package, but then they omit the 1/4" adapter which is something I actually use.

Panasonic has made a very inexpensive ANC headphone and unfortunately the low cost is justified. While the ANC capabilities are within reason for the price range, the sound quality and build quality are severely lacking. If looking for ANC phones for the purpose of using the ANC function, and keeping costs low is important, then these phones may fill that need acceptably. However, if sound quality is in any way important, these are the wrong phones and will sorely disappoint.

The Gorillapod Video Tripod (Black/Blue) is a good idea on paper but in real life it just doesn't quite measure up.

The pan & tilt head is incredibly stiff which leads to jerky motion and bounce in your video. There also, on mine at least, appears to be a good bit of free play or slack in the vertical movement of the control arm. I've tried to tighten this down to no avail. The mounting screw seems to be a bit long. It wasn't bad mounting my RCA Small Wonder video camera but when I mounted my Kodak still camera the screw bottomed out and left the camera loose on the mount. The mount itself seems quite secure tight and sturdily attached to the tripod.

I like the adjustability of the legs but if you're not using the tripod on a metal surface for the magnetic feet to cling to it tends to just slide around when adjusting the pan or tilt. The magnets do appear to be strong for their size and will hold my RCA Small Wonder video camera fully horizontal on the 'fridge or door of my car. I tried this with my Kodak Z-650 still camera and it was too heavy for the magnets to support.

While on the subject of the magnetic feet I wanted to add a warning that if you're using an older CRT style monitor care should be taken to keep this tripod several feet away from your monitor. Even being more than a foot away from my 19" CRT cause distortion and image warping. There is the potential for damage to CRT monitors.

As a stationary camera mount this is a pretty cute product; easy to carry, lightweight with near infinitely adjustable legs. If you just want to plop down your camera so you don't have to hold it this product works fine. When you bring the flaws of the pan and tilt features into play the enjoyment goes downhill fast.

title: Amazing sound with a few small drawbacks
text:
I've had several sets of Bose Companion speakers over the years, but this was my first experience with a Bose Bluetooth product. Setup was quick and easy, and as you can use the speaker as the battery is charging for the first time (plugged in), I had my speaker powered up and connected within five minutes of unpacking. You can pair the SoundLink III with up to six devices and it will automatically connect to the last known device. With a 30-foot range, you can be several rooms away and still get crystal-clear sound.

The sound quality is fantastic...good bass for a speaker this size. You can also REALLY crank up the volume on this one; sound is still full and balanced at max volume. I love that the unit is portable and holds a charge for quite a while (up to 14 hours; the battery lasts up to two years). Because the battery is not user-replaceable, I tend to keep it plugged in when I am using it for long periods.

The one downside is the fact that there is no remote; it would be nice to at least be able to adjust the volume remotely rather than walking over to my phone and using the volume buttons, or walking over to the speaker and using the buttons on top, which are covered with a rubberized layer, but this is a small issue overall.

title: JBL Balboa Sub10 is a worthy contender
text:
Although the JBL Balboa Sub10 delivers very good performance for a relatively modest price, I would never refer to it as "the little subwoofer that could." That's because it's far from little; this thing is quite big by my standards. However, considering that the function of a subwoofer is to reproduce low-pitched audio frequencies, I'll accept that fact that it's the size it needs to be do its job well.

Because I live in a multi-family building and have neighbors with which I share walls, I have not been able to crank up the volume beyond medium. That being said, I have been quite pleased with the bass sound and have not experienced any distortion with this subwoofer at the volume range that I have used. Audiophiles who do not have cost as an object will no doubt want a more expensive subwoofer than the Sub10. However, for the rest of us who are just looking for a dependable, reasonably priced subwoofer for our sound systems, the JBL Balboa Sub10 is a worthy contender.

• This standing power strip is well made.
• It feels durable and the cord is thick and well protected in rubber.
• The cord works well on our crafting table, as it has 5 plug in outlets and 3 USB ports. We can have multiple items such as a sewing machine, heat press, die cut machine, magnifying lamp, etc all plugged in it at the same. Not to mention you can charge your phone also at the same time.
• It makes it so much easier to unplug and plug in your electronics as you do not have to crawl under your desk or table to find the outlet or fat laying power strip.
• Because you can plug the cord in behind your desk/table, there is not a tripping hazard as with some extension power strips.
• The distance between the outlets is wide enough that you can actually fit three plugs on one side and two on the other. So many times, power strips are made with outlets that are too close together so you only get half use out of them.
• The base is sturdy, and it sits flat on the table/desk. Does not easily tip over.
• It has worked exactly as it is described.
• The quality is worth the price point. Probably exceeds it.
Overall, this is well made functional standing tower power strip. Well worth it’s cost. We will most likely be buying another for our den/office.

title: Buyer beware--lens mechanism problems
text:
This camera was highly recommended from a very trusted source, and the reviews were mostly positive. I expected a lot from it, and for a brief period, (maybe 4 months) it worked well. Then the problems began. Lens errors. Yes, despite Canon's insistence that this sort of thing "never" happens, the mechanical lens error you will read about in other people's reviews (known issue with this camera) of this camera happened to me. I bought it hoping they wouldn't, but alas, I am apparently a sucker. Next time, I shall heed the warnings of my fellow Amazonites. No more Canon products for me....

As time wore on, the lens error became more and more of a problem. After another three months, I called Canon. The (arrogant) tech support guy just said, "Oh, this happens when the batteries are weak."

"Oh really?" I said, unwrapping a new set of Energizer AA's. "Let me just stick these puppies in here and see what happens... Huh. Well, would you look at that. So much for your battery theory pal."

After embarrassing him thusly, his only "solution" was to send the camera in for Canon to look at it (at my expense). This would take a minimum of six weeks, after which there was no guarantee I would not continue to have the same problem with the camera. I mean, come on--a design defect is a design defect, after all. I was certainly not the first person to have this problem with this camera. Not only that, but no camera for SIX WEEKS?? I would not have survived.

Sadly, before I could pack the thing up and send it in, I dropped it from the staggering height of three feet. You guessed it, end of camera. Canon makes cheap crap with poor durability and cheap lens mechanisms.

So guess what I did? Yup, I bought myself a Nikon. I've had three of them with ZERO problems over the years. This is number four. My replacement is working beautifully, and is smaller to boot. Excellent image quality too. I will not buy a Canon again. Fool me once, it's your fault. Fool me twice, it's mine.

Buyer beware.

title: Windows 10 Pro with energy efficient hardware...
text:
We've been grabbing a few of these mini pcs to test them out and see if they're good for Distance Learning. We have a lot of spare pc peripherals including old school 4:3 screens. But for many, an all in one chromebook or cheap laptop is still infinitely more convenient. But if you do have these accessories laying around, and you're curious how this Minix works for Distance Learning, I'm happy to report it's great! I just reviewed a Beelink mini pc that is very capable too.

The 1080p camera, microphone, speakers and monitor connected with no issues. Windows did all the firmware work. The only software we had to fetch was Logitech's unifying receiver for the keyboard and mouse. In California, many k12 schools are using CLASSLINK and GOOGLE CLASS. I went into my child's account, played around with all the apps. Opened and closed browsers, everything was pretty snappy.

It's mind-boggling that Windows 10 Pro is $200 alone. Of course if you're going to pay full price for Windows 10 pro, you wouldn't put it in a low end computer. Nevertheless, it is awesome that it's included here. I recently reviewed the Beelink T4 which has the Z8500 cpu. On paper, that's slightly a faster cpu, but interestingly, the Z8350 in the Minix is a newer cpu. They may have made the Z8350 more efficient or something. In any case, normal human beings won't be able to tell the difference. LOL! The MINIX Z83-4 Plus is a little bigger than the Beelink T4, but comes with a wifi antennae, and a built in micro SD reader.

Basic activities such as web browsing, watching Netlfix, Youtube, kids doing work on ClassLink, etc., this mini pc is very capable.

text: My husband and I bought two sets of these three years ago from Circuit City during their going out of business sale. We both travel quite a bit and were in need of decent headphones for longer flights (let's face it, the ear buds provided by the airlines just don't cut it). My husband accidentally left his set, in their pouch, in the seat back pocket on a flight last year and was in need of a replacement set for our trip to Germany last week. I was amazed by the price when I came onto Amazon to check - $29.99 was a steal compared to the $80 we spent a few years back! This headset is not the top of the line, but it is effective in canceling out the low aircraft drawl while in-flight. (They are also quite nice when you need to drown out the crying child in 23F. ;)) The battery life is remarkable. I have had to change the battery on my set only twice in the three years I've owned it. The only complaint that I have, which results in the four star rating instead of five, is that after wearing the set for a few hours (i.e., Amsterdam to Houston, TX), my ears begin to ache on the outside. It is almost like the headset becomes to tight over longer periods of time. I tend not to wear earrings on airplanes, so I can rule out the possibility of pinching. Other than that slight achy feeling, these are wonderful for the casual traveler and the price simply cannot be beat!

title: Not as versatile as I'd like, but works okay
text:
Most people are raving about this camera because they are using it with their iPhones.

But if you don't have an iPhone, keep looking, there are other kits that will be more to your liking. Because of my lack of an iPhone (oddly, I just got one two days ago, so I may give this another try and then update the review if I like the camera more) I had to use the included link to the executable Windows program. The program is outdated (like from the days of VCR's and answering machines) and has no documentation.

By documentation, I mean there are minimal instructions and no built in help files. I was able to get it to work by running the software with a lot of finagling and figuring it out by means of hunting around through my past experiences hooking up cameras.

All in all, a bit of a disappointment, I was hoping to catch the wankers who keep spraypainting my carport.

Update - Still using this with the PC, just a note, you have to leave the PC software running to report. This camera works through an extension cord but not a surge protector. Not sure of what the range is and at least in our house, it needed to be on the same circuit breaker as the base, but this could just be weird wiring in our house.

A nice feature of the camera is a motion detection feature, so you don't end up with hours of blank unmoving street view for example. For the recording, pretty much continuously, it takes about 2GB per night (this is with camera on from about 9pm to 8am). There is a way to look at the recorded footage in super fast motion, so it takes about five minutes to watch the entire night's events (use VLC);'oh, hello again, curious kitty who keeps hanging out on my porch.'

This is not an outdoor camera, but we are using it outdoors anyways (tried placing it near a window, but glare of light on the window blinded the camera). I don't have any need to record stuff indoors. Because of the camera we caught a strange creepy person coming up to our house while we were out yesterday, they also visited the houses of two of our neighbors. If not for the camera we wouldn't have known about this. There are a lot of strange characters in our neighborhood and there have been a few incidents; nothing major, a crazy woman tried to break in while we were eating dinner, a man with dementia was wandering around our bridge, kids stealing wood from our woodpile, you know, ordinary disturbances, so this person was exactly what we wanted to see while we weren't home.

The software allows for up to nine cameras to be in use, I can't even imagine that, but it might be cool to have another to watch our backyard, we might be able to catch the raccoons or the river otter who we've only gotten fleeting glimpses of.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This sleeve is the perfect bridge between sleeve and case. It has the cushioning in it with soft interior that a sleeve has with padding, but it also has two handles and a curved pocket in the front to slip the recharging cord or other items in so they don't ruin the laptop.

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM?

It is easy to keep handy in the house so I can recharge in it or just leave it protected until I have to use it again. When I want to travel, I slip the entire thing in my carry bag and it fits perfectly.

POCKET AND STRAP
The pocket in the front houses my recharge cord nicely. It also is a nice place to keep the shoulder strap when I am not using it. The strap attaches to the sleeve at two nylon loops at either end of the zipper.

KITTY PRINT
The cat print looks just like our cat. And yes, it is on BOTH SIDES of the sleeve. It is accurate as what is in the photo. I really love this as does everyone in the family.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a really cool looking sleeve that has handles and a zipper pocket, I could not ask for more. It is lightweight and perfect for storage in the home or office, and slips nicely into larger cases for travel.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. Even though I got shipped the wrong item at first, it was corrected and I love this sleeve with the handles and pocket. It is really nice and the print is very realistic.

title: Good HDMI-CEC support; unimportant to most, important to me.
text:
I purchased this Panasonic Soundbar in June of 2013. At the time, my requirements were:
- Good sound (can't afford GREAT sound)
- Wireless Subwoofer
- HDMI input and good HDMI-CEC support
- Bluetooth support

In my search, I tested the [[ASIN:B00811NMMI Toshiba SBX4250]] and the [[ASIN:B00BLX9510 Samsung HW-F450]] from my local Costco. My final choice was the Panasonic.

Sound:
- Acceptable sound -- The front speakers are not a big improvement over the built-ins. With the subwoofer turned off, it is easy to mistake the Panasonic sound bar with the speakers from the Television.
- Good subwoofer -- The sub sounds good even at high volumes and fills out the overall sound from the sound bar.
- The Samsung has clearer mid and high ranges so the Panasonic seems slightly muffled in comparison.
- Overall sound better than the Toshiba.
- Wireless range for the subwoofer is short -- especially if placed behind the sofa (interference from people sitting in front of it). Range is about 15 feet with clear line of sight.

Decoders and Passthrough:
- AC3 and DTS Decoder (Toshiba lacks DTS)
- ARC (Audio Return Channel) -- If you use the Netflix app built in to your TV, audio is generated by your TV. Normally, an "optical out" cable from the TV back to the sound bar is necessary. ARC removes that need.

HDMI-CEC (also Aquos Link, Anynet+, Bravia LinkSync, Regza Link, etc):
This is where the Panasonic beats the Samsung. HDMI-CEC allows Televisions to control a connected device -- no matter the brand; The TV remote should be able to turn on a bluray player and send navigation (up/down/etc) and standard playback buttons without the need for a second remote control.

In the case of a sound bar, through HDMI-CEC:
1. The sound bar should turn on when the TV turns on -- Panasonic does this, Samsung does not.
2. The TV should play all sound through the sound bar and volume buttons on the TV remote should control volume on the sound bar -- Panasonic does this.
3. Turning on a bluray player, the sound bar should turn on and switch to the correct input automatically. The TV should also turn on and switch to the correct input -- Panasonic does this. It's then up to your TV do its part.

In conclusion, I chose the Panasonic because it gave me the ability to eliminate a remote control through HDMI-CEC (which Samsung didn't) and it had both AC3 and DTS decoders (which Toshiba didn't). With the added ability to play music from my phone through bluetooth, I'm still happy with my purchase one year later.

Tip: Unlike the Samsung and Toshiba, the Panasonic has a small "receiver" unit that adds another machine to your entertainment center. For me, I use some velcro strips and attach the "receiver" to the back of my TV. It is only 1 ¾" thick which was thinner than my wall mount.

As with most "upgrades," each version gets a little bit worse in terms of basic functionality. I never upgrade software when I have a choice, but we're not given a choice in this case. title: GREAT flash option for radio wireless setup - beautiful light quality.  iTTL + HSS work great.  Detailed comparison to Shanny:
text:
This past weekend I got to use both the SN600N and the Yongnuo YN568EX with the YN622 triggers. Basically both function completely with the YN622 triggers in both manual and iTTL modes. The only thing that I noticed with the SN600N was that manual power 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 all seem to be about the same output using the YN622 triggers - you have to lower it to 1/8 or less to start seeing lower outputs. Not a huge deal, but I'd like more output options. More on this below:

Here are a few details that a pretty important about these two alternatives to the Nikon SB series:

a) The 568 light is much higher quality - and I really mean the LIGHT quality. It is even, consistent, and clear. On the other hand, the SN600N is very scattered - what I mean by this is there are lines of brightness and darkness from the flash burst. This must be an internal flash "lens" issue - whatever the light is bouncing around and through within the flash is creating texture and light inconsistencies. This is not the case with the 568.

b) Yes, the SN600N is a more powerful flash, but in my opinion, it needs to have more levels of output on the lower end (1/256) because it's TOO bright for some situations. I use grids and modifiers during wedding receptions, and I like balancing the natural light with the flash output. 1/128 with the SN600N is equal to about 1/64 on the 568. I use the 568 at 1/128 quite a bit for details - so this was kinda a bummer to me.

c) The AF beam on the SN600N is better and more centered than the 568 - but they both need to improve designs. The ONLY reason I'm holding onto my Nikon SB900 at this point is the AF beam - which makes accurate AF possible in pitch black - no joke. The AF beam on the Yongnuo is a joke - they need to fix it on the 622 triggers too - it's basically worthless and too bright/annoying to the subject.

d) In my experience using the 568EX, the batteries get warm and stay warm, whether you're using the flash or not. If the flash is on, the batteries will get warm. It also EATS through batteries. I used to be able to photograph 2 weddings without recharging my Nikon SB setup (using SB600 previously) - now I have to recharge between weddings. I've upgraded to 2800mah EBL AA rechargeable (previously using Amazon 2000mah) and it has helped quite a bit.

So this is my current setup: SB900 on camera, 2x 568EX off camera group A+B for reception lighting, and then SN600N as group C for periodic fill. Rather than commit to a single brand, I'm using them all as tools for different situations, because they all work differently. I also am really enjoying the SN600N as on-camera if I don't need the AF beam - the quality of light is bright, crisp and rich - and the SN600N "brain" (basically how it works using iTTL mode) just works really well with Nikon - it's a very consistent flash, sometimes even better than my SB900. I like that it can zoom all the way to 200mm, too. If the SN600N had a better AF beam and better quality of light, I would ditch my SB900 and use it all the time. But I switch between the SB900 and the SN600N for different effects. I actually like the previously mentioned internal lens flash inconsistencies at times - it creates a grittiness that I like.

title: Sleek design, nifty tech, and terrific sound quality...
text:
Replacing my altec lansing speakers from the early 2000's. Honestly, I'm not an audiophile. My altec speakers were pretty good speakers too, and I can't tell the difference. My upgrade is simply cosmetics. This logitech set is black and sleek, looks more modern. My altec speakers were grayish, very early 2000's design.

I like the nifty wireless controller that looks like a little echo dot, but it's smaller. So coming from speakers in the early 2000's, my first question was.. Can this function like old school speakers if I don't care for all the tech? So I simply used the 3.5mm connection method from my dell to the logitech, but there was NO SOUND. So you have to at least power up the wireless controller for the first time. Because under the controller is a button to switch from bluetooth to wired. Press the WIRE option, and you will then get audio. After this, if you remove the batteries and take away the wireless controller, the speakers will continue to work as 3.5mm connected speaker. You just have to turn on the wireless controller on the initial set-up. So this is good. My concern was what if the wireless controller is lost or damaged? If that happens, then you would like the speakers to go on like old school speakers connected simply by 3.5mm. So I'm happy to report, this will function without the wireless controller module. I'm not even sure turning on the wireless controller in the initial set-up is absolutely required. Your PC my pick-up sound the moment you plug in the 3.5mm jack. For me, I had to turn on the wireless controller during the initial set-up.

Another thing I wondered is if I connect a bluetooth device, say my smartphone, to these speakers, then disconnect, will the speakers automatically revert back to wired? The answer is no. To connect to a bluetooth device, you have to press the bluetooth pairing button under the wireless controller, and it will stay in this mode even after you disconnect. You have to press the "wire" button to get back to 3.5mm.

One more thing, the left and right speakers have 2 slots in the back to insert the stand. So you can configure it to stand vertically or horizontally. Conclusion... I love the sound, the sleek design and the technology. 5-Stars.

title: Speedy, Lightweight SSD External Drive
text:
I like tech. I've had a computer since the commodore Vic-20 came out. That being said I'm not into competing with or against other computers and computer users. I don't run testing or speed diagnostics on my hardware. If it works and feels or seems to be working as advertised and expected I'm completely happy. I just don't care to sit here are see how many micro-seconds faster my new drive is than my older ones.
All that being said I use external drives exclusively for maintaining backups of my personal files, photos, documents, music, eBooks, Etc. Everything else I can simply reinstall in a couple hours. I don't have that many things installed. My computing needs are simple. But I have lost files due to a drive crash so I meticulously make weekly backups of my important files. Currently I've been using two USB 3.0 Seagate Backup Plus drives to make my backups every Monday.
This new Samsung solid state drive is remarkably faster at copying files to than my mechanical drives and easily a quarter the size and weight of the Seagate drives. I had a couple hiccups when I first formatted the drive to NTFS (I had no need of proprietary encryption) and started copying my files over to the drive but after one or two false starts I got tens of thousands of files copied over with no more problems and have for several weeks just copied new files to the existing collections in their directories and once again this SSD drive flies through the process much faster than the Seagate drives. Now I have three complete backups of my files and feel that much safer and secure with three copies of my files and I love that there's no moving parts. The cable's long enough, about eighteen inches, to work fine with my laptop though someone with a desktop may want to invest in a longer cable.
I'm knocking one star off for a device this expensive not coming with even a cheap hard shell case or even a rubber plug to protect the USB port from dust. It's the one point of possible entry of foreign matter into the drive and causing damage or failure. For the price they're currently charging it wouldn't have been any real hardship to include a case or plug to protect this device.

title: Affordable SSD that works well as an OS drive
text:
What can a 256gb drive be used for? If one wishes to have storage space, we're talking in Terabytes, not Giga. For portable storage, a micro-sd card or usb pen drive has just as much storage for about the same price. So what niche does a 256gb, M.2 drive fit in?

There are two possibilities that I can think of:
1. A live-usb linux distro install. When combined with a USB 3.1 enclosure, this drive can be used to boot a PC into a linux operating system without affecting the internal drive of the computer. This can be useful for troubleshooting or simply testing out various distros. A drive like this would perform much better than a micro-sd or usb-pen drive.
2. Used as an internal OS drive for a computer. Even with Windows' requirements for space, a 256GB NVME drive will perform better than a traditional Sata drive, meaning faster boot up and faster app launching. It is always good practice to keep your data and OS separate, so for your pictures, videos, and other large files, put them on a separate drive, but use this drive to install your operating system on. This gives you the freedom to refresh your system without fear of losing data.

Specific to this Pioneer 256GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Gen 3x4 Internal Solid State Drive, I currently have it in an external enclosure and am testing Windows 11 (which is only in Insider Preview at the time of this writing). I ran a crystal disk mark against it and posted the picture. I'm happy with this drive and how well Windows runs on it, even through USB.

title: Good Basic Protection for Your Laptop
text:
I have a sleeve for my tablet that works out very well for me. It provides some protection for the screen and provides some limited protection against drops and bumps. This is the first sleeve I have used for a laptop and so far I like it. It is appreciably cheaper than a laptop bag or backpack, but it also has less room for accessories.

The sleeve I have is the 15.6” version and it fits my laptop almost perfectly. There is a small amount of wiggle room in the sleeve so that the laptop can slide a little from side to side and it’s just enough to make slipping the laptop in and taking it back out much easier. There is sufficient padding around the edges to make this sleeve useful for bumps and bangs but it will not protect the laptop within from hard drops on the edge.

The outer material is a tight woolen weave and it does a good job of repelling water (though it is not completely waterproof). When splashed with water, the majority of the water beads up and rolls off, and of what remains most can be simply brushed off. The end result is a very slightly damp surface, nowhere near enough to get the laptop inside even slightly wet. So, when toting the sleeve outside it will effectively protect the laptop inside from rain.

There are two pockets inside this sleeve. One is lined in a fleece-like soft material that gently cushions the laptop and allows it to slide in and out more easily. The other pocket is zippered and it is lined in vinyl; it is a good place to put papers, smaller accessories like a travel mouse and other small items. This pocket is not big enough to handle a lot of extras like a full laptop bag.

I inspected the sleeve closely and I have not been able to find any problems in the way it is made. There are no loose threads, stitching is tight and straight and there are not crooked material patches. The zipper works smoothly and so far does not catch on the material of the sleeve. Overall I am pleased with the materials and assembly.

This is a very nice laptop sleeve and I am pleased with it. It does a good job of providing some protection to the laptop is holds, it is water repellant and it seems to be made very well.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Sturdy Tripod Legs are Superior to Most
text:
The Vanguard Auctus Plus 323CT Professional Tripod for Cameras and Camcorders is even better than I was anticipating and now I must purchase a new tripod head to get the most out of this high quality photographic instrument. To maintain a stable and secure foundation for a camera, this is outstanding -- attractive, easy to assemble, sturdy, and versatile. It arrives in a very nice cardboard box with a handle, so if you're inclined to store it in the box, you have that option. Also included is a black and orange carrying case with a shoulder strap and there is a little zippered compartment near the top of the bag for the hook, included hex key, car key, flash drive, roll of film or whatever you'd like to store. A hand crank raises and lowers the center column and it moves very smoothly, not too easy and not too hard. The tripod can simply be converted for macro shots with low camera placement. For low angle photography using very wide legs, the bottom half of the center column can very easily be removed by simply unscrewing the hook and turning the bottom ring. Very smart and pretty fast, too. Having the option to attach anti slip spiked rubber feet is a great advantage in snow or sand and adds to the stability of the tripod. When the tripod arrives, the large rubber feet are snugly attached and I doubt that they will be lost when removed to use the spikes or standard rubber feet. The three sectioned legs are extremely easy to extend with a slight turn of the amply sized twist locks and each leg has clearly marked segments for perfect measuring. They can be locked at the top, another stability and security advantage, at three angles (25, 50 and 80 degrees). If desired, a camera bag or weight can be hung from the hook on the center column. The rubber foam casing at the top of each leg makes for a very comfortable feel and aid in moving the legs and carrying tripod. Although there's a little bubble level, mine was dry, so customer service is sending me a replacement level. It's small and may be obstructed when a head and large plate or camera are attached, but it's a nice little bonus nevertheless. Changing the camera screw from 1/4" to 3/8" is another simple process that takes seconds. I'm not sure if the orange anti-shock ring really does much, but it can't hurt. This carbon tripod can hold 39 pounds and it weighs around 8 pounds. It has an ample extension and I'm very satisfied with it in all regards for use in the studio as well as in the field.

UPDATE: Vanguard CS is out of this world. When they promised to send a replacement bubble level, I was politely told it would be 2-3 months before they were expected from the manufacturer. Several weeks ago, I received a padded envelope containing a brand new perfect bubble level. It's rare that follow-up isn't necessary in a situation like this, but Vanguard clearly maintained the information to fulfill this promise. If I could award another star in my review, I would!

title: A Disappointing Camera From Samsung {Edited}
text:
My first impression upon unboxing this camera was "Wow, that feels cheap." Everything's made from unattractive plastic. The single dial on the top rear of the camera (oddly blank) feels light, spins too easily and clicking it feels mushy. The other buttons on the camera, power, movie and flash all have the same, cheap, mushy feel. The shutter button has poor tactile feel.

The camera is surprisingly heavy; for me uncomfortably, painfully, so.The back is so taken up by the huge 4.8" LCD screen that the thumb rest is too short, more of an afterthought that cause me quite a bit of discomfort during extended use. The DSLR style handgrip is quite large (perhaps too large for small hands) to accommodate the massive 4360 mAh battery.

On paper the idea of an Android OS with a 4.8" LCD screen and a big APS-C sensor sounds great but I was sadly less than impressed.

Because of the Android OS startup time from fully off to ready to shoot is a very long 23 seconds. In standby mode the camera was ready to shoot in approx. 4 seconds. The camera runs warm, very warm, even just sitting idle on a cool 50 degree day. I would worry about overheating in the summer months.

Image quality was unimpressive especially in low light. Early morning, post sunrise, images with sky and clouds were extremely grainy and noisy. Performance in full light was better but not spectacular. Auto focus was run of the mill, often seeking excessively in low light situations. High ISO performance was exceedingly poor. Past ISO 800 images were rather noisier and grainy. In auto mode the camera seemed to make poor choices for ISO and shutter speeds.

Controls. Almost every setting is accessed via the large LCD screen.

There are over twenty pre-configured shooting modes. I used several of them while checking out this camera. These selections are made from a top to bottom scrolling 'carousel' where you scroll through until you find the option you want. I found it annoying to find and stop on the mode I wanted. You're going to miss shots trying to find the mode you want.

Continuous Shooting: burst mode. Surprisingly fast.
Kids Shot: the camera plays one of three sounds to attract a child's attention and then bursts five photos.
Macro: The Galaxy NX has a surprisingly short minimum focal distance with the kit lens and the macro photos I took were among the best results I was able to get from the camera.
Rich Tone: Samsung's HDR mode. Processing time was excessive.
Panorama: This is a sweep mode, smoothly move the camera (a tripod helps) to capture up to 180°'s of view. Disappointingly the camera reduces the image size significantly in Panorama mode.
Multi Exposure: combines two or more images into one.
Drama: combines several images of a moving subject into a single image. The camera was very picky about detecting moving objects. I encountered at least a 50% fail rate trying this mode. Additionally, as with the Panorama mode the image size is greatly reduced.

The camera can also be used in manual mode. Samsung calls it 'Expert Mode'. This gives you access to the standard PASM controls. The settings are controlled by three half-circle on screen dials that I found frustratingly hard to use. Try to change one and my thick fingers would spin the wrong dial. Using Shutter Priority mode I found the processing time of 30 second exposures was a disappointing additional 30 seconds.

There are some things I did like about this camera. It's not all bad. It can produce decent images and I honestly think the majority of the limitations I experienced were due to the cheap kit lens. The 4.8" LCD is gorgeous, in the right light, I recently went back to a camera with a beautiful 3" screen and it felt small. Some of the included shooting modes are fun to play with. Connectivity via WiFi was rock solid (I wasn't able to test the 3G/4G connectivity) even in parking lots of places that offered free WiFi. There were eleven gigs of free space in internal memory. That was plenty of room for a day's shooting and testing. I never did get around to installing an SD card.

In conclusion...
I'm not really sure who this camera is aimed at. They seem to be trying to attract smart phone users with the ability to access the internet almost anywhere and instantly share you photos. But do you really need an expensive, heavy and complex large-sensor camera to post photos to Facebook and Twitter?
On the flip side I just can't see this camera being attractive to professional photographers or high end photography enthusiasts. While the inclusion of the electronic viewfinder is nice I found the all on-screen controls to be distracting and bothersome and the image quality was for the most part lackluster.

A note about durability. As I was finishing up the testing of this camera I bobbled the camera due to nerve damage and it took a spill. The height was not great, less than three feet, and the initial impact was on soil and grass. The lens came apart into numerous pieces. I was able to put the lens back together but it appears to have suffered internal damage and will not focus either automatically or manually. I accept that I caused this damage but I am very unimpressed with the durability of such an expensive camera.

I really can't recommend this camera. Three stars but barely.

A side note about Samsung's technical support that isn't reflected in my rating of this camera. Calling Samsung's support line was a complete nightmare. Audio quality was atrocious. At the end I was practically screaming to be heard. I spent close to an hour and a half on the phone speaking with seven different people. Each person I spoke to had to be told all my information, the camera's information and the reason for my call. Four times I was transferred to 'the proper department.' In the end I had a supervisor tell me, first that the camera did not exist and then, that it must be a UK version and I'd have to start all over and call their UK support line. I then contacted Samsung through their Facebook support page. It's been almost a week and they still haven't decided what to do about the camera/lens.

{Edit}
It took nearly a month of back and forth and arguing to get Samsung to agree my camera was a US version, it was under warranty and they would issue a repair ticket for it. It was shipped off at their expense, repaired surprisingly quickly and shipped back. The camera's now in working order. Only one thing marred the process. When they returned the camera and lens the put a cap on the rear of the lens (I'd shipped it with the lens attached) but only put a piece of what looked like a Post-It across the body opening. I found it odd they wouldn't properly cap the body to protect the sensor though on the whole the packing job, bubble wrapped and foam peanuts was well done. Kudos to their repair facility but I'm still very put off by the whole experience with their support people.

title: Solid Drive Enclosure; Works with Windows and Linux
text:
Drive carriers and enclosures are a convenient method for converting internally mounted drives to USB connectivity. This particular enclosure is for 2.5" SATA drives and supports USB 3.0 speeds. So far I have gotten excellent results with it and am pleased with it.

This is a tool-free device; no screwdriver or wrench is required to open this enclosure or install a drive in it. The cover slides off with a little pressure to expose the plug for the drive and the drive simply pops in. In the box is a foam pad that attached to drives that are not thick enough for a solid fit when the cover is replaced. Once assembled with a drive, this is a solid and compact enclosure that feels a lot like a Passport drive though it looks a lot nicer and feels a little more substantial.

I plugged the drive into a machine running Windows 8 and the system immediately recognized the drive and the partitions on it. I was able to use the drive without issue.

I tried a couple of different configurations for accessing this drive under Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL). First, I tried to access it under RHEL running in a virtual machine. I was unable to get the hypervisor to expose the drive to the OS which is a configuration issue, not a compatibility issue. To determine this for sure, I plugged the drive into a machine that runs RHEL natively with the GNOME desktop. RHEL immediately recognized the drive and opened a Nautilus window with the filesystems on each partition exposed and I was able to navigate the filesystems without any issues. I could not ask for better results.

I put a 500GB SDD in this enclosure and plugged it into a USB 3.0 port and got insane speeds. I could not be happier.

This is a great drive enclosure for 2.5" drives and it works great under Windows as well as under Linux. For the price, this is a great enclosure that works very well.

Disclaimer: I was provided a sample of this product in exchange for a fair, honest and thorough review. Even though I received this product at no cost I have rated and reviewed this product without bias, based solely on my experience with it.

title: Light duty, and good for hanging banners indoors - not for outside use
text:
I purchased this to hand a band banner behind us on stage. In that respect this is perfect because the dimensions are totally as described in the product description, the product photo is accurate, and I knew up front that this was going to be a lightweight support.

There are some limitations. The first is although you can extend the tripod legs to provide decent stability, this is not for environments where passers by can bump into it. Also, with a banner or backdrop clipped to it, it is not going to work well outdoors unless there is zero breeze. It would not take much to catch a light breeze in the 'sail' area of a backdrop or banner and topple this. However, for me this is a major plus because it's light and easy to carry. If you are a musician you already know the advantage.

The cross-member sections are about an inch in diameter, so you will need large clips. The bag was a surprise. I was expecting some cheap, vinyl bag that was an afterthought. While the bag is lightweight, it is designed specifically with pockets for the two stands and the four cross-member sections.

Assembly and disassembly are fast and easy. I marked the posts with small pieces of tape so I could quickly level it after I initially got it to the correct height and leveled it. I recommend that you do the same because the first time it takes patience and a bubble level (or tape measure) to get it set up correctly.

title: OK Budget Phone, no NFC, bad sound
text:
This phone A10s is basically the worse version of the old Galaxy S7 Edge from seven years ago. Slightly higher battery capacity - 4000 instead of 3600, same screen size, but the quality of the screen is not as good. S7 screen glass is much better quality, it's smoother and it's scratch resistant. A10 touch screen response time is worse than S7. There is some kind of a split second lag which feels strange after using S7.

Unlike S7, A10 doesn't have wireless charging :(

Blue light functionality doesn't work when I flip the blue light button. Button is there but functionality is not. No physical home button anymore.

NFC is not supported, can't pay in the store using this phone. Item specs here says "Connectivity NFC" which is misleading. Old S7 supports NFC.

Sound is HORRIBLE for single built in speaker. Comparing to old S7 playing the same song this phone is missing low frequencies, sound is flat and unimpressive, no Dolby. S7 sound has lots of volume, low and high frequencies and it feels like surround sound, like movie theater experience.

Dolby Atmos is disabled on A10 for built in speaker. Adaptive sound functionality is completely missing, nada. When I plug in earphones, Dolby Atmos gets enabled but doesn't make any difference and left ear piece is much more quiet than the right one. The phone doesn't distribute sound equally between the left and right ear pieces.

Not possible to opt out from sending Samsung all your phone logs info. All preinstalled apps had rights to mess up phones operation system and access everything on the phone and send your private info everywhere. I had to go through every setting to change that. New icons look ugly.

Good features are dual sim and a radio tuner so one can listen to the local FM radio without wi-fi or cell service. It still has a jack for wired ear phones, the wire is used as an antenna for the radio tuner. Fresh battery holds charge better than a seven years old Galaxy S7 Edge. It was easy to set up and install applications from Google Play. Phone is unlocked and can be used overseas.

It's an OK unlocked budget phone for everyday use that works with certain carriers only. But lack of NFC, no wireless charging, and bad sound is a big No.

text:
First design review: For the price, it seems like a great tripod, but..., it was falling apart in the new bags it came in, so expect to locktite all screws, including the one holding the QD head to the ball section. And speaking of, the ball was way too tight for anyone to move without tools and that's with the tightening knob totally unscrewed. Sigh..

EDIT: So Ravelli customer care gladly returned the original one and sent me one of the latest designs. Night and day difference. And this one comes completely assembled (unlike the first one I reviewed). This design is VERY reminiscent of the Sirui in design and function. The ball on this is smooth and very effective. I was impressed, was like night and day compared to the first one (of the same model #, so not sure how to order and actually get one of the new designs). Just when I thought they finally had a hit, well, the padded bag has a zipper that comes pre-stripped to save you the years of wear in order to accomplish a popped-zipper. And the way this is sewn-in, there's not a good way to get it back together. So while the tripod (new design) is an exceptional design, the bag..., well..., this one's unusable now and I just took the thing out of the box for the first time to review it. Nice otherwise though, so it might be worth the $20 or so to have someone sew in a sturdy YKK zipper or something like that. Bottom line though, this new tripod (APGL5) is a hit (but I haven't used it yet, will edit again if issues come up) and a keeper for sure.

title: The folks at Roxant have thought of everything!
text:
The folks at Roxant have thought of everything! I wanted a monocular because I only have sight in one eye. I wanted a lightweight scope I could hold and focus with the same hand. I love the focus wheel and the hand strap. When the strap is tight, I don’t even need to grip the scope, just lift it and hold it against my eye.

The size is very workable, and the weight is ideal. The overall quality is great. It feels very solidly built, the lens caps are sturdy and thick and I love that they attach to the scope so that I don’t have to worry about misplacing them.

I also love that it came with accessories that I would have had to buy aftermarket. The case is sized right, the phone attachment in particular is very solid. The tripod is a bit flimsy, but probably stable enough for light use. In any case, it doesn’t take any space in the case and doesn’t add any weight, so I pack it in with the scope. Sometimes I use it as a handle for the scope and it works well.

But here’s the best part: the optics are great! I have an Eagle Solo which just isn’t stable enough against my eye for me to enjoy, and is a pain to focus. The Roxant Falcon gives me just as good vision and magnification as the Eagle. At a fraction of the price, especially when considering the accessories!

I hesitated to order this, since I had a good quality monocular already, but it had so many features I wanted from a monocular (focus wheel, strap, accessories), for the price I figured I’d give it a try. It vastly exceeded my expectations. It will now be my go-to scope for everything.

Thanks Roxant!!!

title: Great Tablet, A Few Idiosyncrasies But Still Like It
text:
I have been using Wacom tablets for so long, I can not begin to tell you. Perhaps it would make a difference to say that my first tablet I got was before Painter hit the market when it was developed by Fractal Design.

My most recent tablet was a workhorse- the ArtZII Tablet which was a pro version graphics tablet. I never had trouble with it and it worked with everything, including most games, believe it or not.

Unfortunately, the drivers began to malfunction so much with WinXP that I was forced to get a new tablet. If I could have gotten a serial to USB conversion adapter, I probably would still be using it if I had a driver to use with it.

The Intuos5 Touch Medium Pen Tablet is a wonderful tablet. Thanks to the previous reviewers, I did not even attempt to use it until I got the clear plastic cover for the pad to keep my pen from wearing down the nibs. I am SO glad I did. Now I feel like I am at home like I did with the ArtZII pad.

WHAT I USE THIS WITH

I like to use this pad with handwriting added to documents to sign things.
I use this for Corel Painter
I use this for Corel Graphics Suite X5.
I use this for general mouse uses when I don't need to use a lot of words on a keyboard.

WHAT I LIKE

The touch feature is helpful when I want to turn a page in Painter just like I would in real life
I like the responsiveness of the pen
I like that the screen can be made larger or smaller with my fingers.
I like that the light goes on in the screen to remind me that it is on.
Auto keyboard that pops out allows me to do minimal typing and not have to grab my keyboard

WHAT I DON'T LIKE

Silly, probably, but the round programming spots on the left side drive me nuts. They are not marked, and I just can not get into them yet.
I don't like that every time I grab the tablet near the round rubber area, it sends the screen coming in- but it does go away okay
The screen changing from one direction to another does not always work smoothly. Sometimes it gets stuck

A FEW MORE COMMENTS

I have not really tried programming this pad at this point as I have had not had the opportunity to do so as of yet. I usually am in such a hurry to do some photo work or graphics or sign something that I grab, do what I need and move on. I hope to study it more in depth in the future and use it even more than I do now.

The programming in Corel Painter X3 seems to work beautifully with this pad which I very much appreciate. The touch levels are fantastic and I feel the closest that I have ever been to using natural media on a computer than I have ever been in the years I have worked on computers with natural media programming- as I said, that is quite some time now.

The pen stand is kind of annoying, I am not sure why they set it up that way, but it is something I can live with. The pen itself is comfortable enough to work with and relatively easy to operate without too much thinking or reading of directions.

I will update this review as I learn more about this system and let you know how I like it. So far, I am quite happy with it, and have had no crashes or lockups while using it. The drivers load up well and I don't seem to have any difficulties.

I am using Windows 7 on a system I recently built so am just getting to know it better.

title: Command for copying audiobook folders properly
text:
One tip for folks who want to fix the "playing out of order" bug when copying files in an audiobook folder over, on MacOS you can use the following command to ensure that a folder's contents are copied to the xtrainerz in alphabetical order:

rsync -rv --ignore-existing <source_dir> <xtrainer_dir>

Then, the files will play in the correct order on the device. This command will skip/ignore existing files if they already exist for whatever reason.

title: Amazing light!
text:
I ordered this 'D&O Lighting 180W Pro LED Panel Series V-Mount (120º Beam Angle)' for review.

Let me start off by making clear that I am not a professional photographer or videographer by any means. I am however aspiring to be both. My passion really is photography but I am learning more about video and someday I hope to turn my hobby into something where I can make money at it. With that said, I had the opportunity to order and review this incredible 180W LED light by D&O and I have to say that this is the best LED light I have ever used. I Truly never thought I would own such an incredible professional grade light. It's super bright and adjustable from 3200 - 5600K so you really have some good range of color there. The light comes with a nice padded case and also includes the AC power cord as well as a remote control which gives you all the functions that is available on the back of the light itself. The light is of incredible quality and everything packs nicely and is well protected in the included case. I had had zero issues with this kit but if I were to complain about anything it would be that it did not come with a C-Stand or anything to mount it to. I had to order a C-Stand just to be able use it, as it will not mount to a tripod. Another thing that I might mention is that the mounting adapter is made of plastic and does not mount very solid to the C-Stand Baby Pin. I worry that over time this plastic mount bracket may break. Since I have never owned anything like this before, I am not sure if this is how all lights of this type are, but I really would have thought that if this was made to mount onto a C-Stand with a "metal" Baby Pin, that the mounting bracket itself would also be metal and made to fit tight and secure to this pin. I have had several times where this light would spin while mounted and I was afraid it was going to break off as the light is pretty heavy. This may be my fault as I am still learning how it works and I have gotten better at getting it tight and secure. Plastic vs metal and metal is always going to win right? Overall however, I am super happy to own such an incredible light and I hope to take my photography to the next level. I do feel that for what you get, it's a bit pricey, but not being familiar with what other kits like this cost, I honestly don't know for sure. I just know for myself, I would have a hard time justifying the price until I was making more money from my "hobby". I hope that this was helpful.

title: I'm quite impressed!
text:
I ordered the Acer Chromebook 15, Intel Celeron N3350, 15.6" Full HD Touch, 4GB LPDDR4, 32GB Storage, Google Chrome, Pure Silver, CB515-1HT-C2AE, 15-15.99 inches so that I might have a lightweight portable travel laptop to enjoy and use for travel and at home. I have had some time with the new Chromebook and I would like to share a few thoughts and experiences with this particular model.

The first thing that I noticed with this Acer Chromebook was how thin and lightweight it was. It reminded me of a Macbook, though I have never owned one. I love the silver metal look and the keyboard is very enjoyable and comfortable to use. The speakers on either side of the keyboard are nice and sound amazing considering the size and the fact that they are housed in a very thin and compact space.

Initially I did experience some issues with the screen where it would not turn on despite the fact that there was power. It was very random but about 80% of the time the display would not turn on. I was able to contact Acer and they did resolve the issue within a reasonable amount of time. I had to send it back to Acer and they replaced the mainboard which I assume was the culprit. As I type up this review I am doing so on the repaired Chromebook and I have to say that though I had that initial experience, Acer made it right and I absolutely love this product! I’m not real savvy with the Chromebook OS but it really is simple and I appreciate the fact that this model comes with a Micro SD slot for my 128gb card which will come in handy to use for loading some movies and or music for on-the-go. Also it will come in handy for loading a few photos to edit with my favorite mobile photo editing app using the excellent touch screen which I quite enjoy.

Speaking of movies I have played a bit with Netflix, Google Movies and Hulu and the video quality is quite amazing with the 1080p screen resolution and, as I mentioned earlier, the sound is surprisingly loud and clear.

Battery life has been pretty impressive and lasts much better than I expected. As I stated before, this has been my first Chromebook experience so the only thing I have to compare battery life with is my much larger gaming laptop which I can't even get a few hours of use before I need to plug in.

Overall this Acer Chromebook 15 has been quite enjoyable, and because of Acer’s great support, I would highly recommend this Chromebook if you are looking for an inexpensive well rounded mobile “Laptop” experience.

title: Good features and powered by mains.
text:
While solar-powered cameras are convenient, I've found that they have too many compromises when it comes to functionality. In order to save on battery power, the software usually shuts down the camera when there is no activity. Usually, that means nothing gets recorded until the motion detector is set off. In addition, a couple of my solar cameras actually had firmware updates that made them almost unusable because the app can no longer wake the cameras up. This means that the only time I'm actually able to view the cameras are when there is actually motion to set it off.

This Reolink camera doesn't have those problems. It can be powered by a power adapter or power over ethernet. While this makes installing the camera more troublesome, it is worth it because I don't have problems like what I mentioned above.

In addition to solving this basic issue for me, I found that the Reolink camera is much more well-built than the solar cameras that I had previously. The camera mount is made of metal and the camera swivel mechanism is made of high-quality plastic.

The camera is pretty annoying during setup because it has a loud speaker that talks and talks until you finally pair it with your phone app but once done, the app runs like any other app that you might have used. It has controls for the pan, tilt, and zoom functions and it will show both of the built in cameras simultaneously.

Pop in a memory card and you have local recording capabilities with a nice timeline to control playback.

This is a high-quality camera that justifies its price.
