title: All plastic, no 1080P recording, and read my advice regarding micro sd card insertion...
text:
I used to have a cheaper one where you connect it to your smartphone, so when I saw this I grabbed it. I read two reviews where one said you cannot record 1080p, but the other said that you could. You know there are cheap cameras everywhere recording 1080p. For $90, I'm disappointed to confirm the reviewer who said this only records videos in VGA and snap pictures at 720p. 1080p is only for onscreen viewing. This won't be a big deal for me since I'm not in a profession that uses this daily. I figure it's nifty to have in the toolbox, and perhaps know my way around my walls. For example, last month I drilled a hole into my wall, thinking I can drop some cables down, but the cables hit a horizontal beam. I think in construction this is called a fire stop. Hopefully this will help me learn the paths I could take in my walls.

For a professional who will use this daily, who perhaps would like to bring back a picture or a video and blow it up on his monitor for a more detailed view, 1980's VGA quality is a big thumbs down! The build quality is also not substantial either. Everything is plastic. The whole unit is about 13.5 ounces.

I do like all the provided accessories, especially the hook. I can see how that will come in handy. To view something in the wall or pipe and to pry it out with the hook. The cable is stiff and bendable allowing you to position your lens just the way you want it.

IMPORTANT ADVICE REGARDING MICRO SD CARD!!!
------------------------------------------------------------
Be very careful when removing and inserting the sd card. You have to be sure to look at the slot, and be sure you slide the card in completely horizontal. If you slide it in at an angle, it will actually still go in, completely in! I made this mistake and the card was rattling around behind the LCD screen. LOL! Luckily, the screen was easy to take apart. Just 5 screws in the back and I was able to pry it in half and retrieve my card. When inserting the card, remember the orientation... with the LCD screen facing the ceiling, the card's gold contact side should also be facing the ceiling.

This is a 5 star product for hobbyist like me. I don't see myself recording much, if at all. For a professional, I think the shortcomings make it a 3 star product. So I'm rating this a 4.

My SB-700 can shoot 4-5 frames in a row without skipping a beat.

That said, it's a wonderful flash for off-camera, since I mostly shoot at around 1/64 and 1/32 settings in manual - and for that function it recycles fast enough. The reason I'm keeping it for the off-camera is because I don't have to charge AA batteries with this flash, and I really appreciate the magnetic modifiers. At 16GB and a 512GB SSD, the specs are starting to look closer to my work laptop than a cheap media center box. This box also has the usual perks of a mini PC like a SATA port for an add-on drive, although with 512GB of storage you won't be needing it as often as those 128GB storage cheap boxes. The Amazon Basics 67-Inch Monopod is basically (pardon the pun) everything you need in a monopod. It extends to a nice height and even at full extension it feels reasonably sturdy. The monopod also includes a wrist strap held in place on the head of the mount by a split ring.

A carry bag is supplied. It's enough to protect the monopod though it's not padded and the shoulder strap is short enough to be more of a carry strap.

The rubber foot of this monopod can be retracted on its threaded mount to expose a metal spike foot for use in outdoor.

The only negatives I've found with this monopod are:
The wrist strap is rather small and I cannot fit it over my hand. For reference I wear a size large glove. For me this is more of a palm strap.

The soft foot has very little rubber extending past the end of the metal spike. I measured this at just slightly over 1mm. Moderate wear will surely leave the metal foot expose and potentially damage flooring.

All in all though this is an affordable and well built monopod and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.

title: It charges alkaline...  but mostly, it's an excellent Ni-MH charger.
text:
More than anyone, I really wanted alkaline charging to work like other rechargeable batteries but the sad reality is that they're just not made for it.

The reality of alkaline charging:
- Duracells seem to leak more than cheapo "Kirkland" brand from Costco.
- Energizers do not hold charge very well.
- All brands leak eventually.
- Takes a long time to charge.
- Unreliable even if successfully recharged -- usually, batteries are connected in series, which means that if one fails, the device will not work.
- Battery leak can happen while charging or while being used in the device, resulting in a very messy charger and messy device.

So after some dumpster diving (or at least, I raided the battery recycling bins at work), I came home with batteries of various brands. For a while, I really did use recharged alkaline batteries exclusively and kept my Ni-MH batteries in the drawer. What I found was that I needed to change the batteries a lot more often and I couldn't be sure that the battery would have a charge when I took it out of the drawer.

Leaking is a big problem. My charger now has one charging port that is stuck because the liquid got in to the spring mechanism and dried. I also have a couple of remotes and devices that had to be cleaned out because the batteries leaked.

In the end, I had to give up on the idea of recharging cheap alkaline batteries because of how long it takes to recharge and that it can leak at any time, potentially ruining your device (mostly, it's just oily and you need to clean it out with a tissue). I just couldn't trust those batteries.

So why did I still give this charger 5 stars? Although alkaline charging was a failed experiment for me, the charger is still a better-than-average Ni-MH battery charger. It has separate intelligent charging and LCD display for each battery and will trickle charge a battery even after the lights turn green. Other chargers that have the same features cost more -- and without the Alkaline charging capability. You really can't go wrong with this charger.

title: Stable and Versatile
text:
I selected this clamp for working with my mirrorless camera. There are times when clamping to a surface or a pole is more practical than setting up a tripod or monopod, so this kind of solution is useful in those cases. It's a decent clamp system and it works well, though it does require some messing with it to get used to it if you've only worked with a tripod in the past.

This idea is simple here. This is a clamp system that includes a couple of adapters for attaching cameras and accessories so that the camera can be held steady without having to set up a big, bulky tripod or having to hold the camera by hand. It comes with two clamps that can be connected via the ball joint adapter so that the system can convert to an anchor support for a pole as well (not the intended use, but practical nonetheless).

Included in the kit is a 1/4" adapter that connects to a standard camera mount (like my mirrorless), and an adapter for connecting a GoPro. It can be used directly with a cell phone, but it is not ideal for that and does require being creative with the clamps (not recommended); better is using the clamp to hold a selfie stick which in turn holds the camera.

The clamps hold tight as do the ball joints. It takes a little bit of fiddling but getting this set up exactly as desired is possible so that you can get the perfect angle. Further, the system can hold a little weight and has no trouble at all holding my mirrorless camera steady.

It seems to be made well and so far I have not had any issues with loose screws, stripped components, wobbly connectors (when properly tightened) or slipping grips. It's still early on in working with this system but so far I see no red flags.

I am happy with this clamp set-up and I will get some good use out of it. It's a practical solution when a tripod or other mount is not workable. It's not particularly expensive, either.

title: Outstanding Flat Cat7 Cable
text:
I have used and tested more Ethernet cables than I can remember and there is no question, all Ethernet cables are not created equally. Every one of the AmazonBasics branded items I’ve tested has been excellent and this cable is no exception.

Typically any device requiring an Ethernet cable will come with one in the packaging - it will work (usually). A good comparison is those cables are much like an old car - it should get you there, whereas this cable is like a high end sports car - it will get you there lightning fast, without fail.

This Cat7 is designed to be thin, but don’t let that fool you into thinking that it lacks capacity - within the thin PVC package contains aluminum shielding and 100% bare copper wires for super fast transfer speeds. The connector bases are reinforced at each end of the wire which really help hold all of the wires in place even if you have to bend and twist it to fit it within the plug. The plugs have a protective rubber boot guard that protects the clip on the plug - this becomes very important when snaking the cable through walls and tight spaces. Prior to doing this I wrap the boot and plug with a small piece of electrical tape to make sure I don’t unintentionally snag anything.

I love the white PVC shielding on this cable - not only is it durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it can be run along a wall and then painted to match the wall color.

I used this 100 foot cable to run between my router to a PoE switch that branches to several power and transmit data to and from one zone of my security cameras - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

This has proven to be an outstanding, dependable Ethernet Cable - this is really a top of the line cable that you’ll love. This is a purchase that you’ll never regret.

title: It works, but odd design. Why front mic?
text:
The good news is that it DOES work, and sounds pretty decent for a cheap no-name brand. If you've installed a double din stereo before, it should be pretty familiar and straight forward.
But let's just jump right into the odd design. Why is there an "external mic" option that is RIGHT NEXT to the internal mic? Usually an external mic is supposed to be mounted somewhere closer to the driver's mouth (up by the visor or mirror, or over the dash by the steering wheel, etc). The purpose is to get better sound, and either having the internal one as a backup if you don't want to mount one, or using it to pick up ambient background noise for NR filtering. Having an external nub right next to the internal one makes ZERO sense at all! Why even have one?! If anything, making it lower than the internal one seems like it would get WORSE sound, and if the position were so good, why not make THAT where the internal one is? Not to mention it looks weird as heck.
The features seem to be functional at least, but it has a pretty noticeable lag to the user interface. If you're expecting an OEM style menu experience, you might be disappointed. This feels like an old-school web browser loading pages when you open up a feature. Compared to modern units like, for example an Atoto F7, this feels like something a generation older at least.
I want to give this at least 3 stars for functional purposes, but the truth is I know that you get a much better unit for not a lot of money more. I can't really recommend it unless it is on an extreme sale.

title: Studio-Grade Headphones
text:
The majority of the headphones I use on a regular basis are active noise canceling (ANC) headphones. These come with the advantage of eliminating low-frequency noise so that the listener does not need to crank the volume to hear, but the disadvantage is that the phones twiddle the sound in subtle ways (usually in the bass range to boost volume but they also tend to flatten the highs) such that dedicated audiophiles can really tell the difference. The Munitio PRO40 headphones are my first higher-quality non-ANC headphones. Though I have not had them very long, I already can say I am pleased with them.

These are very lightweight phones and are very well constructed. They are sturdy yet very light relative to their size. Other headphones of their approximate size can get a little heavy over longer periods of time but so far I have not had that problem with these phones. I will say that when I first put them on they were a little tight and they felt a little uncomfortable. It does not take long to adjust to these phones, though, and after only a few minutes I found them to be very comfortable. The pads are soft enough to make wearing for long periods possible.

For headphones in this price range, sound is absolutely the most important consideration. There is no point in spending this kind of money if the sound quality is flat or hollow. These phones have very good sound and are worth their asking price in that regard. The bass is definitely there (and Munitio makes it a point to tout their bass response) and is deep and rich. The midrange is also very strong which is important - many headphones I have used get the highs and lows right but the midrange tends to be flat and lifeless. The highs are bright and clear. Unlike ANC phones, the sound is untouched and is an accurate reproduction from the source. Overall, the sound is very full and rich across the spectrum.

I chose a set of music tracks for testing that I believed would put these phones through a fairly comprehensive listening test, selecting some club tracks, some hard metal, bluegrass and even some choral accapella. As I listened to these tracks, I was startled by just how much more music is there; these phones definitely bring out more detail in the individual tracks, to the point that a few of the tracks sounded like new versions of old favorites. Individual instruments were more distinct to such a degree that I could hear subtle ticks and plucks that I never before heard in these tracks. Music is definitely more spacial as well.

These phones are fine for listening to music through a device like an MP3 player but this is not where they shine most. These are studio-grade phones and are perfect for using with a sound mixing board. I plugged these phones into a mixer used for live recording and was very, very pleased with the sound reaching my ears - what comes through the cans is untouched via internal electronics and is a fairly accurate representation of the sound as it is meant to be heard. Precision is important when recording live and these phones do a great job of reproducing the sound accurately. From here forward, these are the headphones I will used with the sound board.

I cranked up the volume and was unable to get these phones to distort. I did get my ears to ring, though...

I was a little surprised to find that there are no adapters in the package at all - no 1/4" jack and no airplane jack. Considering that the best use of these phones is paired with a mixing board and these almost always require a 1/4" plug, this is an unfortunate omission. An adapter is only a couple of dollars, though, so this is not a big deal in the grand scheme of things.

The storage case for these phones is great - period. It is very crush-resistant, roomy and should provide excellent protection for the phones under normal to heavy use.

These are studio-grade headphones and are far and away better than most headphones I have used. The price is definitely high, but these phones are worth the asking price and will please all but the most critical music lover. For someone working in a studio or with higher-end audio equipment, these are absolutely worth a close look.

title: Really PREMIUM sound!
text:
I've heard a lot of wonderful things about the Sony noise cancelling sets like these, and let me tell you: it isn't just hype. The sound quality is excellent, and the noise cancelling is eerily amazing. I put it on my wife and kids with the noise cancelling off and then turned it on to demonstrate, and you can see each them suddenly smile like "whoa". Like my Sony studio headphones I use professionally for work, the actual fidelity of the sound it reproduces is excellent, and the microphone for calls is excellent despite being up by my ears and so far from my mouth (other bluetooth headphones I've tried were good for music only, the mic being up by my ears wasn't good enough to isolate my voice from ambient sound, but this definitely does a great job).
The app gives a ton of control beyond what I expected to really customize the experience. For example, I have mine set to auto-pause if the headphones are removed, and to turn off noise cancelling when it detects me speaking to someone, and then resume playback when the headphones are removed/replaced. These features are all customizable, as well as many more. But you need the app. And this is where the cons come in:
1) You really need the app to get the most out of this. I was thinking about pairing this with my desktop and/or TV, but without the app you have far less control, and to be honest I couldn't even get it to pair with my phone using just Bluetooth alone. There seems to be a way according to the instructions, but I couldn't figure it out without using the app installed.
2) For a set that costs this much, I'm surprised at how scuffed up it got after one fall from about 3 feet next to my car. Including pictures. This happened the day I got it. I'm not sure if there's anything that can be done about that, pavement is hard to recover from if anything is dropped, but it's something to keep in mind if you're spending this much money on a gadget. My studio headphones have been roughed around for years and held up fine.

All in all, I'd give it 5 stars if it weren't so reliant on the app to get the features going and/or more resilient to being dropped. Feels like I should deduct one for that. But as far as features and sound quality go, this is a solid 5 out of 5.

title: Official SONY UHS-II
text:
I currently own 3 Sony Alpha cameras, and regularly record in 4K for work. Having a high quality fast card is important if you rely on your footage. That's why I generally only trust my paying jobs to Sony and Sandisk media. This is a real UHS-II card, as you can see in the picture attached. You can tell by the extra pins on the card, which are used for the UHS-II standard to boost the read/write speeds.
Of course, you can still read/write with a regular SD card reader, but you'll only get the benefits of the speed boost with a proper SD card port that supports the extra pins for UHS-II. Unfortunately, my desktop does not support this so I was unable to run benchmarks on the card to show you (it runs as a regular UHS-I with average speeds), but the camera is where it will make the most real-world difference, and most modern Sony cameras will have the support for this standard. If you write a lot of high bitrate 4K, especially with a Sony camera, this is the card for you!

title: The good ol' 3.5mm jack!
text:
I'm a fan of Panasonic's electronics, and have been since I first used their GH camera line for work, and the DVX prosumer cameras before that. I was excited for a chance to replace my working headphones with ones from Panasonic, however I found it interesting that the plug type was NOT MENTIONED on this listing! The last pair of headphones + mic that I ordered came with a USB plug. It worked fine on my laptop, but not on my phone or tablet, obviously. I want a regular headphone jack, as in 1/8" or 3.5mm (whatever you want to call it!) to be compatible with all my things, and not rely on the limitations of bluetooth.
I was a little bit nervous about buying this one since it doesn't say anywhere that it is, in fact, a standard TRRS headphone-jack sized plug, but I'm happy to report that it IS! And the sound quality is what I expected from Panasonic, a good value for the price. One thing to note, however, is that this requires both sides have a wire going to the plug. This is a seriously old-school design that I almost forgot existed. Modern headphones have a single point of cable that splits to the other side in the band, however this is more like earbuds in that there's a wire going to each side.
It's not a deal breaker, it works fine and some people may actually prefer that look, but personally I'm worried about it being another point of contact that could get snagged/rip/break/go wrong, and actually prefer the more modern single-side cable style. But this is still a great pair of traditional tried-and-true headphones!

title: I *LOVE* this camera!
text:
I'm just an amateur when it comes to photography. All I really want is an easy-to-use point-and-shoot camera that I can take on vacations to snap shots of places I find interesting, to use around the house to take photos of valuables for insurance purposes, etc. In other words, my expectations are pretty minimal.
That said, I'm extremely happy with the Kodak DC3400. This is my second Kodak digital (my first was a DC240), so obviously I'm pleased with the Kodak product line.
After unpacking the DC3400, I spent about 10 minutes getting it set up, and proceeded to take a few pictures. Another 10 minutes or so, and I had the photo software loaded on my laptop. Connect the USB cable, and I was able to load the photos onto the laptop immediately. The camera shows up as an icon, like a disk drive, which you can double-click to open and transfer the pictures to a folder on your hard drive -- piece of cake!
The quality of the pictures is amazing. I use the Ofoto service, and had some prints of some of my digital photos sent to my mother. According to her, you could not tell the difference between the digital images and those taken with a 35mm film camera. The colors were vivid, the images sharp -- just what you'd expect from the Kodak name.
I'll agree with most everyone else and say that batteries might be the only downside to this camera. It's definitely worth the investment to get the Kodak NiMh rechargables and the charger. The ONLY time I use NiCads is when I'm my NiMh set is in the recharger, and I need to snap a few pictures.
For the money, I don't think you can top this camera in terms of features, quality, and ease of use.

title: Quite Surprising Sound For This Price Range Of Headphones With A Few Disappointments
text:
I was looking for some replacement headphones for two sets in my family when I had the opportunity to try out some of the new Carlos Santana line of headphones. Let's see what happened.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These headphones come in a great box which will appeal to fans of Carlose. It is well decorated and presentation is done so well, it would make a great gift. These are the black ones, and there is also another set available in white under a different listing.

ARE THESE REAL LEATHER?
According to the case,t these are leather padded ear cups and the lower half of the headband. I am still not sure about this. It is possibly bonded leather. Bonded leather is made from leather scraps chopped up and blended with binders. Sheets made of this mixture are printed with leather look imprinting. Technically it can be called leather, but it really is not leather as I define it..

EAR CUSHIONS AND HEADBAND
These black headphones are comfortable. I can wear these headphones longer than many others I have used. My daughter who ended up with these, uses them constantly and raves about them. These can be worn for several hours without a problem. She has sweaty ears and these are not nearly as frustrating for her as many others.

CORD FOR CORDED LISTENING
This comes with a cord which is only 38 inches long. That is a bit short for me. I find it is annoying and not quite as long as I would prefer, but my daughter does not use it so I guess it is not a problem for her or if you are like her, you won't mind either.

HOW DO THESE SOUND?
We are all surprised at how really good these sound. The bass is well defined and clear/strong, and the mids and highs are definitely clear and not muddy. The bass is not overwhelming either, which is a problem with some headphones.

HEADPHONE CONTROLS
The controls can be a bit difficult to read, but once you know where they are, you can figure it out pretty quickly. The +/- and play/pause buttons are separated by the noise cancellation button which is good.

HOW ARE THESE ADJUSTABLE?
These adapt to all sorts of comfortable positions.. They go longer, tilt in and out and rotate from side to side.

ARE THESE ABLE TO FOLD TO BE COMPACT?
These do fold flat and compact if you need to travel with them or store them in a smaller storage area.

CASE?
This did not come with a case.

SOUND CANCELLATION PERFORMANCE
The noise cancellation is awful. It hardly works. When noise cancellation is turned on, the sound gets pretty compromised. It becomes almost muffled in a way and the base definitely goes down.

OTHER FEATURES WITH THESE HEADPHONES
The ability to know how much power is left on the headphones while using the phone is nice, but it does not help if you are using these some other bluetooth device and not a phone. During phone calls, people hear just fine and we can hear them too (several of us tried this feature with our phones)

THE BOTTOM LINE
At this price point, these headphones are a step up from what I usually get when getting headphones for this price range. The sound is well defined and well balanced. Compactness for storage is great, and the comfort is also very good. The only disappointments are noise cancellation, short cord for corded listening, and buttons being a bit difficult to read.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. With better performance from noise cancellation, these would be really really good. As they are, they are still pretty great. They are a great gift to yourself or someone else and are some of the nicer headphones I have used in my journey through headphones of all sorts as well as those the family has obtained. They are not B&O or Turtle Beach, but they still are pretty good.

title: CAUTION:  Does NOT work with Surface Pro
text: This may be an eminently useful connector when used with the Surface RT - I simply don't know - however, I can attest that it does not work with the Surface Pro.  For reasons which elude logic, the two tablets require signficantly different connectors: the Surface RT's looks like a mini USB and has an angled connection base; the Surface Pro's is apparently a much larger, proprietary design.  Don't be misled by the photographs of the two products on Microsoft's own website which make it appear that the two are identical.  They're most definitely not, which Microsoft customer support acknowledges with an apology for being so vague on this point.  The front of Microsoft's packaging of both units states simply "SURFACE - VGA Adaptor."  Only on the back cover will you find in 6pt type that it's for an RT (or presumably for a Pro).  The major retailers selling the Surface Pro (Staples, Best Buy) both seem confused--though as nearly as I can tell their websites only stock the RT version adaptors.  Pro owners proceed with great caution - it may well be for the moment that the Microsoft Store is the only sure source of the right adaptor. title: A Bit Frustrating To Set Up At Times, But Nice Light
text:
I have been trying to get a decent set up for taking photos of jewelry and pottery for a business I am trying to get going. The smaller lights that I had were just not doing the trick. I got this one to help.

HOW THIS COMES
This comes with the tripod base separately packed in a box. The rest of the pieces come jammed in a foam tray. You have to put the cord together with the two pieces and the transformer box.

CONTROLS
This works great when it comes to changing the light brightness or the temperature. I have to say that the different lights respond very well.

CORD
The cord seems plenty long enough, but in some locations, you might need an extension cord.

ARMS
The arms and swivels are a bit frustrating at times to figure out. They can easily get turned too far one way and you have to undo them to get them to work right. It is not that big of a deal if you get the hang of it. It is handy to have the lights in one direction or two different ones too.

PERFORMANCE
The light is great for taking photos. I have tried it in many directions with different temperatures. I have to say this is one of the nicest lights I have used so far. It really gives precise lighting if you need it in a variety of directions.

STURDY
This tripod is very sturdy. It stands up well and does not wobble or seem unsteady at all. I am very happy with this.

HEAVY
This is a heavy light, no doubt.

CASE?

Sound isolation

I watch a lot of cartoons and strange independent dramas. I also listen to ancient heavy metal, along with a smattering of other unlikely musical genres. Few people want to hear that combination of things spewing from my headphones. Now I can enjoy watching things like the Rectify (Especially the Drip Drip episode) without having to explain later to others in the next room.

Roku and Smart Phone use.
The 518 has a 1/4 plug, and the 439 has 1/8. I like to use the headphones with my Roku 3 remote a lot, and having a 1/4 to 1/8 adapter in my pocket with the Roku remote adds a lot of bulk. title: Perfect for critical listening
text:
Since there are some incredibly detailed and helpful reviews already I will focus on where these phones are best suited. I received mine as a review sample and have been using them for nearly a week to make sure I thoroughly test them.

For me these are best for critical listening, and especially raw mixes if you do recording. Of course they are not limited to that. The fact that these phones are fairly neutral across the entire frequency spectrum makes them ideal for listening to unmixed recordings, as well as music that you are studying or transcribing. The reproduction is so balanced that listening to albums with these compared to other phones - including some other Brainwavz models - is like night and day.

If you are listening to music that is heavily biased towards bass and drums these may not be the best phones for you. If you listen to acoustic music these are near perfect because you can easily hear every note. I tested it on a few jazz albums that I own as well as a broadcast of two friends from a local station that had been recorded directly from the sound board and it was wonderful to hear what was actually recorded versus what a biased pair of phones normally reproduce.

A few notes about comfort: these are light, do a great job of isolating ambient noise without totally eliminating it, and are easy to wear. I am not an IEM (in ear monitor) type of person, but these presented no problems even when I wore them for three to four hours straight. A big plus is this set comes with different sized foam ear pieces and a nice case (the [[ASIN:B00HPPL1M4 Brainwavz Hard Earphone Case]]).

While these phones may not be for everybody, they are perfect for those of us who spend a lot of time critically listening to music and/or transcribing it. If you fall into that category you will probably love them.

title: This Tablet Does What I Need It To
text:
As an old, retired guy, I find technology still significantly impacting my daily life in two ways. The first is that I spend a lot of time every day online - either gaming in my favorite MMO or binge watching the various streaming services. The second way is that I keep in touch with my far-flung network of family and friends via social media. Now, my desktop pc handles the first of those two very nicely. The problem is that I can get immersed for hours in gaming or in a good streaming show. Social media notifications break that immersion, causing me to move away from whatever I was doing to see what the latest notice was about. If I don't, it could be quite a while before I get around to checking my social media and responding to the messages there.

This is where a tablet comes in. I figured it would be nice to have a tablet that quietly beeped new notifications and allowed me to just glance over at the latest notice to see if it needed a quick response or not. Little did I know how hard it would be to find a low end tablet capable of that simple task. This is the fourth tablet I've tried and the first one which could do that one simple thing for me. The other low end tablets quickly crashed and burned for a variety of reasons. This is the first that actually continued to work after the first few days, giving me the notifications I wanted and that I could check out at a glance.

There are some issues with this tablet that folks should be aware of. The sound is tinny enough that I wouldn't listen to music or audiobooks on this thing. The visual quality is sufficient for modern movies and tv shows but vintage ones do look a bit fuzzy. The charge doesn't last quite as long as I'd like it to. The tablet needs to be charged twice a day, even when it's just sitting there beeping when a text message or email comes in. Charging once a day would be nicer but it is what it is. Still, this is the first low end tablet of four I've tried that actually does the simple task I want it to do. So for that, I have to give it a solid 4 star rating.

title: Great performance
text:
EVGA ftw3 version runs super quiet. Can barely hear it run. At highest settings @ 6880 x 1440 resolution, it never runs hotter than 65c. As to whether 2080ti is worth it in general:

Increase in FPS performance- Too many people judge the 2080ti's merit on raw FPS numbers, saying its only x amount of percent greater in performance than the 1080ti. so its not worth it. But what they completely miss is that its not just about the raw numbers. Its about how those numbers translate into the EXPERIENCE of adding/using that component. The performance of the 2080ti is so much smoother, more effortless and frustration free, than the previous generation, that it was worth it for me to make the change.

Alernative Sli option- I tried 1080ti sli for about a month, it didnt affect the quality of my experience in a meaningful way. The presentation is still jittery and stuttering , making for a distracting experience. Support for SLI is inconsistent and it demands more power and space, creates alot more heat and noise. You can clearly see the poor quality of performance in side by side comparisons on youtube. Judge for yourself. Again, its not all about the FPS. A perfect analogy would be to cars- most high end races cars have respectable 0-60 mph speeds, but the experience and qualty of performance arent the same.

Price argument: Just because its expensive and someone cant afford it doesnt mean its a 1 star product. Check the quality, time and effort the reviewer put into the review and judge for yourself. It takes money, time and expensive R&D to make products such as these. Im not going to argue that its not expensive. It is. But consider that it beats two 1080ti SLI in quality of performance, then you realize it isnt. If you are salty that you cant afford it, try skipping some meals and dropping some vices and prioritize things differently. Seems everyone wants free things these days. I wonder if they would work without compensation.

Conclusion: Sure its expensive, but if you can afford it and you want quality performance, not just eye popping FPS numbers, which can be meaningless, get the 2080ti. Some just cant see the difference and thats fine. But for those who can afford it and have more discerning eyes, the upgrade is a must. My only complaint? It cant make poorly coded, inefficient games like Kingdom Come run better at the highest settings on a 6880 x 1440 setup. (Runs nearly every other game at the highest setting flawlessly at these high resolutions) Might have to wait for the next generation for that. Because of that and the "high" price it doesn't get a top recommendation but a very high recommendation.

Now for a nominal fee to netflix or Amazon (Pandora is, I think totally free), I have a wide assortment of home entertainment on demand. That is worth the 169.00 I paid for the unit. title: Lots to like, but somewhat flaky
text:
Been using for a few months now. Initially seemed like an excellent upgrade over an inexpensive single wifi router, but I've seen enough issues that I'm not sure I'd buy again. The worst failure was when I switched from Verizon Fios coax to ethernet and tried to use this as my main router. It worked... for about a week. At first, I just had trouble connecting to corp sites, so I thought it might be my corp network. Later that day, I saw issues with personal devices. Connecting to the router web page was super sluggish and the cpu was pegged. The next day, I went back to using the verizon router as the wired backbone and only using this set for wifi---much better. But, I still see occasional flakiness. Yesterday, one of the units wouldn't connect. I brought it closer to the other units---no dice. I rebooted. I connected it to the network via an ethernet cable. Finally, I rebooted the main/router unit and things went back to normal. Every 2-4 weeks one of the units has issues. Sometimes rebooting that unit is enough. Occasionally I have to reboot the main unit. One of the extender units connects via both wifi and powerline. The other extender unit only connects via powerline (it's too far to use wifi). The powerline-only unit is the one that tends to have issues. But, that was the point of buying this system.

So, the system seems good as long as you don't mind doing a ~weekly reboot. I see about 30Mbps over the powerline-only unit---not fast, but generally reliable.

I've started using MoCA (ethernet over coax) and will likely use that as my backbone in the near future---it's faster (I've seen ~300Mbps for a local transfer over MoCA/ethernet/wifi) and seems to be more reliable than this tp-link set over powerline.

Edit: I ditched this in favor of an EdgeRouter X and Ubiquity access points and am happier now. The Deco system was okay, but far from ideal.

These sometimes leave residue behind, so I was interested in trying this electric duster to see if it would cut down on residue and save money in the long run. I will confess that I was not very optimistic and thought it would be underpowered. However, it has proven to be as effective as a canned duster in cleaning keyboards and other equipment, without leaving any residue and without losing power like canned dusters tend to do as they get cold.

This device is smaller than a tea kettle and relatively light. It requires an AC outlet so it does need to be plugged in when you want to use it. I was hopeful I had missed something on the description and that there was a rechargeable battery but unfortunately this is not the case. This was me being hopeful, not a confusing write-up.

It comes with a few attachments to help direct the air flow over the surface of what you’re trying to clean. The most helpful attachment, to me, is the round nozzle, but all of them have their uses.

I took it to my office where we have an abundance of dirty keyboards that need to be cleaned, and I set to work. I was expecting it to do a mediocre cleaning job, but it gave me a very pleasant surprise and blew air with plenty of force to clean out the clumps of dust that collect under the keys. More importantly, though, the power didn’t diminish like what tends to happen with canned dusters as they get cold, and there was no problem with frost buildup either.

So far, this is proving to be a useful and helpful tool. It produces enough force to get the job done without losing power, and it leaves no residue behind.

title: Steps lively for multi-tasking, responsive touchscreen, DVD RW drive, awesome battery ** APRIL 2016 UPDATE ***
text:
I've been using a 2009 17.9" Gateway Windows 7 laptop happily all these years until just recently when it began to cough and sputter and generally show signs of wanting to die. I nursed it for several months while shopping for a replacement and suddenly this Toshiba L55T-C/5388 appeared from Vine. Serendipity. I am writing my review from the Toshiba actually rather than my tablet which what I've had to resort to for the past few months - that's a nice change actually. My initial impressions after a week of daily use are pretty good overall with some niggling design complaints for the physical hardware.First - for the record ... I'm not a gamer - just a regular person using my laptop to write articles for the local newspaper now and then, do a lot of email, a lot of online shopping, some social media stuff, watch some videos now and then, sort and store serious quantities of photos and average net surfing. If I want to listen to music, I tend to use Alexa (the Echo) for that rather than my computer and we watch movies on the big television around here - though sometimes I'll use my laptop instead of my tablet for tv shows etc when I'm traveling.

This Toshiba has a very nice high definition screen and I haven't noticed any fuzziness or blurred screen edges etc. The HD video I downloaded from Amazon as a test sample looked as crisp and bright on the laptop as it did on our Samsung 1080p television. The sound clarity is very good for dialogue and background music - the full speaker running across the length of the front of the machine is really good and the volume is quite loud.
Additionally, the touchscreen is responsive, but not so sensitive that just brushing it will mess your page up or close an open tab. I did run into a couple of sessions where the screen would go to black as I was scrolling rapidly by touch - this seems to be a Windows 10 issue when using the new Edge browser and not a laptop physical issue. I haven't had a repeat of this in the Chrome Browser in a week. (It could also have been a fluke)

The battery life on this computer is freaking amazing! I've been using it for almost 3 hours now for a variety of things and it's currently sitting at 74% with an estimated 6 hours and 35 minutes run time left. By three hours of use, my Gateway would have already been at 10% and that's before it started having problems. Thus far, I have used this laptop for a five hour straight run - writing, with email refreshing in the background and music playing as a test at the same time and the battery barely hit 52% when I was finished working.

Uploading and transferring files from both the cloud and my old computer hasn't been as big a hassle as I expected. The USB 2.0 thumb drive I had handy worked just fine and everything came over intact. The cloud transfer was a bit stickier just because Windows 10 now wants to make unzipping files more complicated than before. (Thanks Microsoft) Additionally, the DVD RW drive works fine and I have had no problems at all uploading the software for my 3D printer and downloading files from the net for it. For those that are interested, unlike other reviewers, I had zero problems uploading and am now using Google Chrome as my browser etc. I've included a photo of my basic screen - the Chrome icon is right there. You just have download Chrome and then unzip it manually.

My one star deduction is for physical comfort. This is a light computer compared to my previous one and I appreciate that. However, the edges are not rounded off. They are sharp, square and pointy. This means that as you are typing - doesn't matter if it's on your lap or a desk - after awhile, these pointy bits will dig into your wrists or arms and this HURTS. My five hour marathon the other day left a little indention on my right wrist. That is just ridiculous. The second design flaw is the touch pad. It is very large and sits perfectly flush with the base of the laptop. This is pretty, but you tend to brush over it as you are actually typing and that can make the cursor jump - now you're typing in an entirely new location. These two issues are obnoxious enough that I am now looking for a way to create a little rubber bumper for the front edge of the computer and a wireless mouse.

In general, this is a nice replacement for my old workhorse Gateway - I've grown used to the smaller screen because Toshiba has made it very easy to enlarge the font and any image on this screen. The 8 gig of ram makes multi tasking and switching from things prompt and thus far, I haven't experienced any lagginess. There is some bloatware pre-installed (like with any computer), but it is easy to get rid of. WIndows 10 requires a learning curve of course, but that's not the laptop's fault. Four solid stars after almost ten days and if that changes, I'll update.

*********SIX MONTH UPDATE April 29, 2016 ********

After a little over six full months of regular, almost daily use, I have had no problems at all with this laptop. It just does its job with no drama. It streams movies, music and uploads photos and files to the cloud. It handles my word processing needs and email and all the regular stuff anyone does on a computer. It also handles my software for my 3-D printer with grace. I am still very pleased with the battery life and it has had no trouble connecting via blue tooth to my external speakers when needed. I still don't like the slightly sharp edges on the corners, but it's not the end of the world. All in all, this is a nice machine and I'm still using it and pleased with it in general.

title: ARLO Q: Setup is  easy. No direct/local interface or web-page directly over your home network.  Horrible/useless motion sensors.
text:
These ARLO Q (no base, wired version) cameras get IP addresses from your home network and have their own MAC addresses, and yet, you can't use common software that you can use to view most other IP cameras.

According to their technical support, that's because these IP & MAC address wielding cameras, aren't IP cameras.

You basically don't interact with the cameras, AT ALL. Cameras call their servers, you setup an account on Netgear's servers, and you view what the camera sees Netgear's servers from a website and configure everything on Netgear's website, not the camera's website or interface.

Because of this back and forth ALL "LIVE" VIDEO IS A GOOD 10 SECONDS LAGGING!!!

My roommate, for example, was standing in front of me, before the live feed showed her walking up to the door, getting her keys, and unlocking the door and coming in. And I have 160kbps uploads with Comcast!

What's worse is the motion detection (attached video). Both from front porch or backyard get some leaf shadow at SOME point of the day. And that sets these cameras off constantly. Set at MINIMUM motion detection sensitivity. So I basically can't use them for Motion Detection at ALL since they have dozens of false alarms every single day. Worse yet? At nights, the headlights from every car passing by, sets off the motion detection. AT MINIMUM setting. On both cameras.

A couple of days before I bought these, I also ordered a FOSCAM R4 from Amazon for half the price of one of these cameras. It has tilt, pan, and four times the resolution. You can talk to the camera. You can configure the camera on it's own site. You can interface to it using common IP camera software, OR you can treat them like these, have them call home to their servers, and do everything there. The option is super nice.

Also the FOSCAM's motion detection does not get set off with all the false positives mentioned above.

Their tech support is your generic out of the country, going through unrelated scripts of steps rather than someone knowledgable.

2021-02-05 Edit: But thanks to the good people at ACE (yes, it is the place) a new set screw was obtained and with my new 2.5mm Wiha 96325 Precision Hex Metric Screwdriver, 2.5 x 60mm $7.45 on Amazon, it was, well, set. Securing the ball (of ball-and-socket) against the thumb screw which together lock the camera mount at the desired angle. So all is good. That I had to put in a bit of time and money for the fix is in the nature of life: What can go wrong will go wrong. So: No hard feelings.

title: Something to consider
text:
Not a criticism of the particular product but of the grounding mechanism.

Beware of grounding mats. Long term use may cause discomfort, pain and even damage. It should be okay to use briefly, but not for any extended period of time.

This is due to the way energy circulates through the body. Extended use causes the gathering and accumulation of energy in certain areas. This is rarely discussed and relatively unknown to most people.

Another thing to consider- you are plugging yourself into your house's electrical grounding system. You have to make sure your house is properly grounded. Youd be surprised that some may not be. If you are in a building its even worse. Also, all sorts of pollutants travel through the grounding path. It doesnt travel just one way.

Grounding is more complicated than it appears so be aware. There are other ways to do it but its not as easy as just plugging yourself in I suppose. Hence the allure of these mats

title: Even works on my ancient Windows XP machine
text:
I received this as a free review sample. I immediately plugged it into one of the USB 2.0 ports on my ThinkPad T61 running Windows XP and was up and running. No drivers, no fuss.

Since I do not have any laptops with USB 3.0 I could not test that speed, but a directory containing 19.4GB transferred via my USB 2.0 port in a little over twenty minutes. Blazing fast? The real reason why I rated this so highly is the cost. I recall purchasing a 64GB SD card a year ago that was vastly more expensive (at the time) than this half terabyte drive. Of course the SD card was miniscule, but this drive will fit in a shirt pocket. For me this is a convenient way to not only back up my two laptops, but also my phone and two tablets. Those are backed up via a hard connection to my laptop because they require FAT32 while this drive out of the box is NTFS. I would have reformatted it, but it worked so well with my laptop that I left it as is.

If you are planning to use this with an Apple IOS or Android device only, you will need to reformat it via those operating systems.

This comes with a cable that is USB A on the end that connects to your laptop or OTG connector, and USB 3.0 for the end that attaches to the drive itself. The 3.0 end is a little tight in tolerance, but once it's perfectly aligned it slips in and holds firmly.

Bottom line: this is inexpensive mass storage that is great for backing up files and documents, storing large media such as movies and music, or transporting files to and from work.

title: This Frustrated Me TERRIBLY  Let Me Tell You Why
text:
I am pretty good at making things work with computers. Peripherals often need some kind of coaxing or tweaking to make them work well. This, however, was beyond help. Let me explain..

WHAT IS THIS KEYBOARD LIKE?
LAYOUT
This keyboard is what I thought I had been waiting for for years. I have been using my third PC Concepts Ergonomic keyboard that I have used since the early 1990s. I used them because they are set up far better than any of the Microsoft ones. The problem is that they are not USB so I have to have an adapter to use it in USB slots.

TOUCHPAD
This keyboard is set up almost exactly like the other keyboard I have been using. The only difference is the touchpad is in the middle of the keyboard instead of on the right side like it is on mine.

SETTING UP
I was VERY excited to try this. I put my hands on it and was so excited- the spring in the keys and the way that they worked in typing was fast and effective. I could not wait to plug it in! Surely this was worth the VERY long wait for a keyboard like this.

HOW DID THIS WORK?
The box claims that this is plug and play. I plugged it in and ..nothing. WHAT? First the system claimed that there was nothing there. Okay, so I changed USB ports. The mouse signed in haltingly, but no keyboard. I removed all drivers, and then re-installed them. Nope. Nothing. First the touchpad would stagger and no keyboard. Then the keyboard would work but no touchpad. It was very erratic and no matter where I tested it, it would not work correctly.

I tried everything to troubleshoot this thing. Finally I figured out that somehow it appears that thistouchpad/ mouse driver shares the other mouse driver that is in the system. That means that my Wacom pad was no longer working as well as usual. It seemed to be fighting.

Finally I got the keyboard to load up. I began typing. I even considered keeping the keyboard and not hooking up the mouse (probably not possible). Then it happened. I began to type the word "keyboard"

Here is what came out..
keybooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooard.

Did the key stick? Nope. It sprang back. I tried again. Typed fine. Suddenly it happened again. oooooooooooooooo

WHY DIDN'T I JUST GET THE KEYBOARD WITHOUT THE TOUCHPAD?
I got this because due to a wrist issue, I have NEVER been able to use a mouse. Touchpad is all I can use. I also do not have the room on my desk for a mouse pad due to my Wacom tablet. Using the Wacom tablet is not convenient most of the time for regular touchpad use (non-graphic) or I would use that. When I want to do productive work, I want the touchpad in my keyboard.

BACK IT GOES
I tried EVERYTHING to get this to work correctly. I was really hesitant to try another one because at THAT price it should not be this difficult to use. I even tested it on another machine. It worked but had occasional hiccups too.

THE BOTTOM LINE
I wanted this to work SO BADLY. There are just too many issues that made it frustrating. The touchpad not working (seeming to share the regular mouse driver causing other devices to lag along with touchpad not working) , the key repeating, this should not be happening for a keyboard that costs this much. When I put my old keyboard back, the Wacom and touchpad in the old keyboard worked beautifully.

MY RATING
ONE STAR This was very upsetting and try as I might I could not get this to work. I had to send it back. I want so badly to have a keyboard like this that actually WORKS before my remaining keyboard stops working It is really old.

title: Excellent Camera
text:
I have been shooting Olympus cameras since 1978. I have always loved the lenses. With over 2,000,000 shots on my Olympus E-500 camera, I decided it was time to invest in a new camera.

I was reluctant at first to try the EM-1 for three reasons:
- The format is Micro-Four Thirds, not Four Thirds. I take 99% of my photos in the telephoto range, and that is what Four Thirds was optimized to use. Micro-Four Thirds is geared more towards wide angle lenses.
- The camera is mirrorless and uses an electronic Viewfinder (EVF).
- I have to use a converter to mount my existing Four Thirds lenses, and converters have a very bad history.

Out of the box:
The first thing that you notice when you pull the body out is that it is SOLID. The thing feels like it is built like a tank. I have not tried the "splashproof" and other claims, but just holding this body I can believe them. The camera fits well in my hand. My hands are a little large, and my pinky occasionally slides off the bottom. I may buy the grip/extra battery holder later if this proves to be a problem. YMMV.

Using Four Thirds lenses:
I have no Micro Four Thirds lenses and a lot invested in Four Thirds lenses, so using them was a key issue. Olympus has 1/17 or 1 MP of the sensor dedicated to phase detection auto focus, the only type of auto focus that will work with these lenses. I find that the system works very well. Focusing is fast and accurate.

Mounting the converter is easy, as expected. Once mounted, you use a button on the side to release the lens. This is a learning issue since I still normally hit the lens release button on the camera body. I anticipate little real problems with this since as soon as I try to put the cover on the back of the lens I realize my error.

Balance with the 12-60 mm Four Thirds lens is excellent. Holding the lens by the zoom collar, the weight is only slightly behind my left hand. I only have to support the body lightly with my right hand. I personally like that balance. Longer lenses like the 70-300 are also well balanced.

EVF:
I have used a mirrored SLR since 1978 and a rangefinder 35 mm camera and 126 film P&S cameras before that. As you might guess, I favor a direct view to see what I am shooting. EVF have issues with resolution and lag when moving to a different point of interest or following a subject, especially in low light.

The EVF has turned out to be great. I really like Olympus' implementation. There is some lag, but it is generally minimal. The "What You See Is What You Get" is a big plus in my book. Adjust the exposure compensation or manual exposure settings, and the view in the EVF changes to reflect what the image will look like. It is not perfect, but it gets 95%+ of what you will actually get. The display of settings is bright, clear, crisp, large, and surprisingly unobtrusive.

The EVF also allows a lot of changes in camera settings to be done without removing the camera from your eye. Use the two dials, and you can see where the focus points that you are using are. Hit the OK button on the back, and you can use the dials to adjust just about every setting while watching the selections you are making in the EVF. Ditto with the other buttons like HDR and auto exposure mode.

HDR:
I had the opportunity to use in-camera HDR while on a recent trip. The day was cloudy, and there was a lot of shadow against bright grey clouds. The in-camera HDR used a series of shots at different exposures and combined them in the camera. The results were better than HDR Pro in Photoshop CS5.5 IMO. I was much, much happier with the dynamic range and overall look of the images. the 10 fps shooting mode was also great for minimizing camera movement, ghosts and other problems associated with HDR.

Image stabilization:
The EM-1 has a five axis image stabilization system for the sensor. That means any lens becomes can be used. The fourth and fifth axes are for rotations. One compensates for the slight turn of the camera that often occurs when you press the shutter button. I had good success using IS in low light with my 70-300 mm lens set at 300 mm.

Scenes:
the EM-1 has many useful scene modes. I used landscape and panorama with great success. The artistic filters and story modes may also interest you. I prefer to do those types of things in post-processing.

ISO:
The camera has an almost insane 25600 maximum ISO. Yes, you get image quality degradation and noise at that ISO, but the in-camera JPEG processor can actually give you some relief from the problems at higher ISOs. I so far have found shooting up to ISO 1600 produces no discerned degradation. I tried ISO 6400 and found minimal issues.

For those who started with film and were in love with the "high ISO" 1000 film for low light shooting, this is a major and welcome advancement. For those newer to photography that have been using higher ISO cameras for a while, the speed may not be much of a gain, but the image quality should be.

The low end ISO is 200, which is the new normal. I do not find it to be a problem. I would rather shoot at a faster shutter speed than have an ISO 100 setting in most cases. There is an ISO LOW setting, but I do not plan to use it. If you regularly shoot in bright light and want lower f-stops, invest in a neutral density filter.

Back display:
The back display is slightly disappointing. It can only tilt up and down, not rotate so that you can see your composition when you are getting into the shot. It works well for shooting over crowds or getting a low angle shot.

On the plus side, the display is clear, bright and a touchscreen that can be used to select a point of interest for focusing and can be used to take the shot in live view mode. You can also use it to select settings to change. The next generation should be even better, and hopefully it will have a screen that rotates.

SD card:
One change from the E-500 that I do not like is the use of SD rather than CF cards. CF cards are nearly indestructible, and a good Sansdisk Extreme card works virtually anywhere, anytime and is virtually impossible to physically break. The xD card slot disappearing is no loss, but not having a second card slot is somewhat surprising given the high-end prosumer/professional positioning of this camera.

Controls and customization:
The controls are pretty well placed for me with the exception of the auto exposure lock button. That is right beside the viewfinder and too far to the left for my liking. You can do a lot of customization with the control buttons and dials, but there are limits. I have not made any changes yet because I am still learning the camera. Overall the defaults seem logical and useful.

This camera has two dials, one on the front and one on the back. The E-500 only had a back dial, so I am learning to use the two dial system. They work well for adjusting and selecting options. I think the second dial was a good addition. Both are conveniently located for my fingers.

Image quality:
All of this is meaningless if the image you get out is bad. The EM-1 does not disappoint. I know that there are people who insist that they need 48 MP or some other ridiculously large number. The reality is that 16 MP is a great size for printing full-size 300 dpi images on your printer or using a commercial photo printing service. If all you do is screen displays, it is about eight times more pixels than you need for a typical 2 MP monitor.

The quality of the EM-1 pixels is very high, and you get excellent out-of-the-camera RAW and JPEG images. I have no problems seeing fine detail at 100% and higher magnifications.

Summary:
This camera is a winner, and it works with my existing Four Thirds lenses so I do not have to invest another $3000+ in lenses to use it. I have a lot to learn, and it will take some time to get the most out of the camera, but out-of-the-box, using my E-500 techniques, it is already doing great work.

title: At these prices, get the 128!
text:
- I have tried so many different SD cards from various manufacturers, at various price points, in the name of trying to save a few bucks. It was really important to me back when a 128GB card cost $50 or more. They all do the same thing, so what’s the difference, really?
What I've found is that it can be extremely aggravating to put up with when the card does not perform well or does not perform at all. I have heard warning stories about cards that are advertised as one size and actually are another size, causing data loss. With that in mind, I have never tried using the very cheapest card or too-goo-to-be-true card deals. But I have purchased cards on sale at the drugstore or even tried some strange brands. What I have come back to is that it’s just not worth the trouble now that prices have dropped so low. When I am trusting 128 GB of data to a single card, it’s just not worth my time and aggravation to have a card that won’t perform. Furthermore, SanDisk cards like this one are all FAST ENOUGH. I’m not a pro photographer, and I don’t have time to figure out whether a card is Class 1 or Class 3 or whatever. I just want it to be good enough that it can keep up with my devices.

I have now purchased several SanDisk cards, and each and everyone of them has arrived in perfect condition and works perfectly every time. They are faster than any other card that I use and I've never suffered data loss. I am putting this card into my Fiio X5ii Digital Audio Player, and it works just fine. During the initial data transfer I have already noticed that the speed is adequate, and I never experience skipping when playing uncompressed high-resolution audio files. I have the same card for my Nintendo Switch, and it works perfectly.

The prices on these are so good now you have no excuse but to buy good name brand like SanDisk. Just buy it and don't worry about it.

title: Excellent Sound, Frustrating At Times For Certain Devices
text:
Some of my devices lack really nice speakers, so I like to have a speaker handy so that I can listen to music or presentations as I go about my day. Let's take a look at this one.

HOW THIS COMES
This speaker comes in a foam liner inside a sturdy gift appropriate box. It has an audio 3.5 cord as well as a Type C charging cord with USB at the other end. It has a carry handle on it too. There is a basic instruction manual in a variety of languages.

BLUETOOTH
The connections are usually pretty stable, but once in a while depending on the device, we have to remove the speaker and reboot the device and speaker to get it to line up again even if it has already been connected previously with no issues.

SOUND
The sound of this speaker is surprisingly fantastic. It depends on the source recording, of course, but in most cases, I have to say that the sound of this little guy is really great. The top however, does move in and out so you can not block it or put anything on top of it or it can break the speaker.

MICRO SD CARD SLOT
I have to be honest here. I can not get the Micro SD slot to work correctly. I have tried many times to get it to play, but it won't. The directions say that you can hit the mode button and it will get to the micro SD card mode but it just sits and goes back to blutooth mode again. I am not sure why this is happening. The same card plays on other devices just fine so I know it is not the card.

AUDIO
I have also not been able to get my audio cord to work but I think that is because my old MP3 player I was testing it with was not working correctly and that is the only device I would use with that feature of this speaker.

CALLS
I don't use this with my phone so I don't answer calls with it.

CHARGE
A charge generally lasts me about 10 hours or so, depending on usage periods and how spread out they are. It takes between 1 and 2 hours to recharge.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is a great small speaker. It is waterproof (I did not test that aspect at this point) and sounds great. The MicroSD slot has not worked for me yet, but otherwise it is a good speaker.

MY RATING
FOUR STARS. I like this but wish that the other features worked a bit more easily. I will update if I find solutions to the issues I have been having.

title: This is the best e-reader I've ever seen
text:
It's just plain spectacular how good the Kindle Voyage is.

I'm kind of a gadget junkie. Whenever a new Kindle reader comes out, I pass on the old one and buy the new. So I'm coming from a place that has used everything from the old Kindle Keyboard through to this, my newest Kindle, the Kindle Voyage 3G.

First, screen quality. I knew it had 300 v. 221 PPI I had on my PW2, but until I saw it, couldn't believe how much of a difference it made. Now, the PW2 screen is great, but this beats it soundly. For regular reading, I don't see any reason to switch from a PW2 to a Voyage, but I'd imagine that with illustrations and such, it would make a really big difference. I can actually read at one size smaller font than I could on the PW2.

The light: Nice light, no weird shadings. My device is smoothly lit from bottom to top.

Size/Weight: It's smaller, definitely (not the screen though). Couldn't really see any difference in weight between this and the PW2, but honestly, what's an ounce either way, especially once you start sticking covers on it? It's not something I particularly care about.

Storage/Memory: I wish it were a bit bigger. Not that I have any desire to have 2,000 on my Kindle at any given time, but once you get into using about half the memory, these devices always slow down and get ornery.

Wishes/Dreams for the next e-reader: That they'd include text to voice. I doubt this will happen, but I wish it would.

title: Works Better than Expected for the Price; Needs a Heavier Weighted Base
text:
I have a teenage son who likes gaming on the PC and he has been wanting a new microphone for a while since his headset failed. I was given the opportunity to check this one out, and so far it has worked well. I do have complaint with it, though it’s not a deal breaker.

This is a USB-based microphone so it does not take up the audio jack when plugged in. This is good as it does not preempt a standard headphone set when it’s plugged in. Windows 10 detects it and it is immediately available as an audio input device. No special set-up and no driver downloads are required – it’s plug and play.

In use the sound quality has been good considering the price. In a two-way chat, those who have been on the other end of the discussion have told us that they can hear what is being said more clearly and there is less static than the previous microphone we were using, one that was quite a bit more expensive but still not high-end. That’s really all we could ask.

The one issue I have with it is that the base is not weighted well at all and it is very easy to tip it over or knock the microphone from where it sits on the desk. It’s easy enough to fix by either attaching it to a heavier base, using double-sided tape or even Velcro to secure it to the desk, or some other rigging to anchor the microphone assembly to the workspace. In the grand scheme of things, this is a minor issue; that said, I would rather spend slightly more and have a weighted base that isn’t as easily toppled.

For the price this is a good microphone that works better than could be reasonably expected. There is some room for improvement that would increase the cost slightly, but it would make the difference between being a good product and being a great one.

title: Useful for Business, School, and Travel
text:
As much as we travel in my household, we need an assortment of luggage, backpacks, and other user- friendly containers. We have several different pieces and that’s great because it means there is always an appropriate bag for the trip at hand. But one area my household lacks a little is with smaller bags and that is what convinced me to add the Solo Gramercy Rolling Case Laptop Bag to my collection.

First and probably foremost, this bag is made to hold a laptop computer and it has a separate compartment for it. I like that the laptop compartment is quickly accessible because it means that, if you take this to an airport, you can quickly remove the laptop, as you are required to do. But this is much more than a place to store your laptop computer. It is also good for carrying books, brochures, and other paper items, with large and small compartments to keep everything organized.

I sometimes take very short trips that don’t require much clothing or grooming items and I was concerned at first that this bag wasn’t designed correctly to hold such items. But in fact, it is, provided that you don’t have much. As a man, I normally don’t need to take much with me anyway and I have found that I can fit what I need for a day’s change in clothing, plus my personal grooming items, plus my laptop, all within the confines of this bag. It won’t hold much more than that, so don’t think of using this as your sole piece of luggage for a multi- day trip. There isn’t sufficient storage space in that instance, but you can get away with using it for a one or two day trip.

To help maneuver, this laptop bag has four spinner- style wheels and a telescopic handle. This makes it ideal to drag along when you’re at an airport, but I should also point out that this bag is useful even if you have no need or limited need to use it during air travel. It’s also very useful when you need to carry your laptop and school or business books and documents from place to place. It’s better than a traditional briefcase because it has more ways to organize your items.

We like and need an assortment of bags in my household because we never know where we will travel next and what we will need. The Solo Gramercy Rolling Case Laptop Bag is a useful storage bag for airport or other uses and it has made an excellent addition to our collection thus far, as it has come in handy for both travel and business uses.

title: Honestly, VGA?
text:
This usb type-c dock is very, very nice, but it isn't quite perfect.

First, a clarification for those who aren't versed on USB Type-C ports: There is a wide range of features that a Type-C port will support -- it's all up to the manufacturer. Just because you have a Type-C port, it doesn't mean you will be able to use all of the features that this dock provides. Unfortunately, you will need to dig into the online documentation or forums for your device to find out what you will actually get.

Windows PC -- Almost all Windows PC's will be able to use the SD/MicroSD reader, the Ethernet port, and the additional USB 3.0 and USB 2.0 ports. On my minisforum u700, this dock provides two HDMI ports and I didn't bother testing the VGA port. So on my PC and my laptop, I'm able to take full advantage of this hub.

LG V40 -- I'm on the T-Mobile service running their Android 10 rom. In this ROM, LG provided a little-know desktop mode similar to Samsung Dex that makes the phone work almost as well as a desktop PC. In this mode, the phone takes advantage of the SD/MicroSD card reader to transfer pictures and files, connect to your network through the ethernet port, and provide a large-screen experience through the HDMI port. Connect a mouse and keyboard and you have a great desktop experience. Plex and Netflix works extremely well in this mode.

Nintendo Switch support -- NO

My gripes about this dock: Being an 11-in-1 dock, this really should have a 3.5mm headphone jack, instead, they provided a VGA port. If your computer has a type-c port, would you really NOT have an HDMI monitor/tv to plug it in? Also, the lack of support for Switch means that I'd still need a separate Switch dock when travelling instead of having one dock that supports all of my devices.

title: Wrong instructions and wobbly, but still fun to use.
text:
Before ordering this telescope, I researched the difference between reflector and refractor telescopes. The last telescope I had was a hand-me-down (I forget which brand) refractor telescopes. I've developed a strong passion for everything beyond earth, so I looked forward to using this telescope--my first reflector telescope.

Because the telescope requires assembly, I pulled out the instructions...and became very confused. While some of the parts looked similar to what was in the box, I quickly realized the instructions were for a completely different model. Even if these were the right instructions, the photographs provided were taken by a camera and not the clearest quality; good assembly instructions usually have computer-generated images or diagrams, not photographs taken by a camera. The rest of the instruction manual was a general guide on using telescopes, though a much better quick-start guide can be found easily online.

So, with some trial and error, and a lot more time than I anticipated building the telescope, I finally got it assembled. And just in time too, because the moon had just crossed the window of the room I build the telescope in, and the moon was in great view. The opportunity also let me play around with the features of the telescope. It's not very easy to use because the stand is *very* wobbly. The counterweights are too much for the tripod, and the tripod should have used a better, more sturdy material. The dials and weights are easy to use, but the tripod makes everything longer to set up because the view won't always stay while moving.

Despite all that, it's super fun to use. It comes with decent eyepieces to play around with; I didn't know how much of a difference eyepieces can make. With this telescope, I was able to view details of the moon for the first time. It really is just a big ball of rock spinning around.

title: Stainless Steel vs Aluminum.
text:
This is my fourth Apple watch. I’ve purchased the series 0, series 1, 2, two series 4. One stainless, one aluminum. The 4 is such a great watch, I never felt the need to upgrade. I recently paid Apple $ 79 to replace my battery. They actually replaced the watch. I’ve never had a problem with any Apple watch. I purchased the 7, because of a great Amazon price.

Stainless steel vs aluminum. Both are great. I put one bad scratch on my aluminum crystal. It doesn’t affect function, and it only shows when the watch is dark. It happened when my watch hit the rough edge of our granite countertop. My SS has never scratched.

Why spend the extra money to get the stainless? If you want a GPS only model, the SS is $ 300 more than the aluminum. If you want cellular capability, the difference drops to $ 200. Due to health issues, my wife convinced me to get the cellular capability. In an emergency, these will call 911, even when your phone is not around, and even when you don’t subscribe for service. That’s important.

The series 7 has a blood oxygen measurement feature. During Covid, we purchased two different fingertip devices to measure blood oxygen. We were disappointed with both. The watch oxygen measurement works seamlessly. We consider it worth buying for that feature alone.

Summary.

If you want cellular capability, spend the extra $ 200 for SS. If you don’t, buy the aluminum model and save $ 300.
Both are great watches.
