title: Great Choice, Excellent Price
text:
Update: After less than 60 days of owning the TV, the ENTIRE audio panel died. None of the external audio ports work anymore for no reason whatsoever. Worked fine, then boom just stopped working. Thought it was my soundbar, so I bought a new soundbar, but nope, soundbar works just fine when connected to the cable box. Amazon Prime was awesome in helping me return it, and I'll be picking up a more reliable brand. When it came time to purchase a new TV we approached it the same way we approached buying a house. We made a list of the features we wanted (a SmartTV with Wifi, streaming channels, Amazon Prime, 40” and affordable at around the $250 mark). After looking at our options in terms of price and convenience, we decided that it made the most sense to purchase it through Amazon Prime.

After much research, we decided that the TCL TV’s offered the best value, met our budget requirements, and our decision to purchase the TV through Amazon enabled us to purchase the TV with interest free financing over 6 months.
Appearance.
The TV came in a large box with the stand hardware: remote, power cable and batteries plus simple instructions that were in separate bags. You do not get a HDMI or any other cables. The TV has a simple non-fussy design with approximately half inch bezel all around. The stand that comes with it is simple and screws on with two screws at each side. The stand footprint requires about 8.5 inches of depth to stand on. I like that the stand is low profile raising the screen about 2” above the surface it is standing on.

Setup

The old analog phono inputs are on the back and quite hard to reach once the TV is up on the mantle and they protrude straight out the back which would require more space between the wall and the TV if you use them. The power cable plugs into a recessed area low down on the left side and doesn’t interfere with the location of the tv. All the modern input and output sockets are behind the screen on the right side about 8 inches back. We don’t use any subscription TV service; just a double bowtie antenna mounted on one of the gutter pipes at the back of the house. The coaxial input for the antenna along with three HDMI ports, an optical input, 3.5mm jack and USB socket are all here. We use two of the HDMI sockets one for the 1TB Media hub and the other for our notebook.

Once everything is plugged in and turned on. The TV introduces you to the basic setup process. It takes less than five minutes to find your way around. The remote is minimalist with the most basic controls on the front (Volume Up/Down toggle and mute buttons on the side). It’s small, unfussy and easy to use. The UI for the TV is not flashy but functional and easy to navigate. Setting up WIFI, registering your TV and introducing you to streaming channels and how to add them to your desktop are covered quickly and then you are left to your own devices.

Since we are just using an antenna we were initially a little apprehensive. Wondering how well that would work, or even if the TV had a tuner since everyone seems to use dish or cable these days. It has a tuner that works flawlessly. We managed to pick up almost 3 dozen channels many of them HD. A quick look online showed us a map of where the broadcast towers are and helped us aim our antenna for best reception.

In use.

The TV has a really nice clean picture and since it is an LED TV where a grid array of LED's light the screen uniformly rather than a couple of fluorescent lamps there is practically no limit to the viewing angle. The screen is not high gloss and prevents reflection and most glare from bright light sources. When turned on a non invasive 3” horizontal strip of illuminated plastic at the bottom shows you the TV is powered on. It flashes during startup and goes out when the screen is illuminated.

Image

Image quality is excellent BUT on initial setup it is on a bright echo setting. Which is very high contrast and overly saturated. I guess it is a power saving mode (claimed 16 watts) but it is a bit stark and overwhelming and shows some dithering on smooth color transitions as though it is running at a lower bitrate with fewer colors. When turned to theater mode the quality of the picture is MUCH better with very smooth transitions on subtle colour gradients.

Sound

Sound is similar. Like most LCD style TV’s this one comes with tiny speakers. Again the default sound setting seems to be very flat. Probably to conserve energy. There are about four presets and again we went with theater which gives the broadest range and warm midtones without overdoing the bass. It doesn’t sound too bad and is not thin and reedy like the default setting.

Smart TV functionality.

We originally wanted WIFI because as Amazon Prime members we get a lot of free on demand media. This is similar to Netflix where you can watch a huge catalog of TV and movies for free, buy or rent them for a small fee. The same goes with music. This worked perfectly.

What we weren’t expecting was the sheer volume of streaming media available for free via WIFI. There are hundreds of channels, many of them free to choose from, many mainstream ones that let you view their current episodes of popular shows on demand when you want to watch them. You can also sign up for pay for view services like HBO and showtime individually.

One nice thing is that the TV has a global search option. You can search for anything by title, director, actors name, character, keywords and the TV will find everything relating to your search and list what is available by channel. So you can easily pick out what you want to see.

Mobile devices and streaming from those devices

There are apps for Android and iOS as well as Windows. I was able to control the TV from all our devices. In many ways it is more responsive, especially if you need to type in text. If you have media on your PC there are Apps for the TV that will let you stream from your phone, notebook, desktop computer etc.

Streaming from those devices tends to work ok. I did find that the TV’s built-in media player was a little limited in supported data formats. Setting up our digital media hub with its own channel was very easy and luckily our Western Digital media hub has far more extensive support for many of the more exotic file formats like FLAC lossless digital audio. And other formats are more often limited to computers. The TV does support the more mainstream formats like mp3, mpg, jpg etc.

Conclusion

For us, this TV proved to be a very good and affordable purchase. Especially when you factor in the 6 months interest fee financing Amazon offers prime members. We did sign up for a free month of Netflix too. The remote has a dedicated Netflix and Amazon streaming button. But we were not that impressed with Netflix when our Amazon Prime membership offered all the same features and more thanks to the addition of Amazon Prime music.

When you combine all this TV’s features with our media hub and Amazon Prime we are a bit overwhelmed with the sheer amount of stuff out there to watch. Even if we had no antenna and just a WIFI internet connection. The vast number of free streaming HD channels is extensive making the need for TV subscription plans pretty much obsolete unless you have a very specific need.

We really like this TV and highly recommend it.

title: Easy peasy back up!
text:
I read some of the reviews and concerns. Many are saying you need the original power adapter. My testing says that is NOT true. I plugged this cube into two separate charging hubs, not apple brand, and both scenarios worked.

You need a micro SD card (not included). Some of the questions in the Q&A shows that shoppers don't realize this. There is no built in hard drive in this cube, you provide the storage.

Turning off auto-sleep/auto-lock may get you through thousands of pictures in one shot. This is what I mean... I'm no stranger to trying out different back-up programs. The current program we use is from Plex. When the iphone is backing up to my plex server, the iphone doesn't know that plex is working, so it goes to sleep after about 50 pictures. When it goes to sleep, plex stops backing up. So I always turn off auto-sleep prior to backing up. With the Qubii, the iphone KNEW that it was working, so it "almost" never went to sleep. I said almost because after 4000 files, for some reason, the phone went to sleep. Still, this is much, much, better than the plex app. When I started Qubii again, it picked up where it left off and backed the remaining 1000+ files. But I did the test one more time to make sure! I cleared the micro sd card, and I reset the Qubii count. This time I turned off auto-sleep/auto-sleep on the iphone, and it backed-up the entire camera roll of over 5000 photos and videos in one shot! More trials need to be done to conclusively say this thing can't get through 5000 files without the auto-sleep disabled.

After backing up everything, you should remove your SD card from the Qubii and transfer them to a larger permanent hard drive where you store your collection. The next time you charge your phone, the Qubii will remember the photos it already backed-up even if those photos are no longer on the SD card. So you can always clear your SD card. For whatever reason, if you need the Qubii to back-up the same photos again, like I did when I was testing things out, all you have to do is RESET the Qubii count, which you can do in the Back Up Settings in the app.

Below are the two pictures showing you the scenarios in which I tested this Qubii. Both scenarios used third party charging hubs, but I believe I had the original apple cable. As with all products dependent on apps.. one Apple update can ruin everything. LOL! So these types of app products depend on the company to stick around, so that if Apple breaks anything, they can fix it with a new firmware update. Qubii was on Kickstarter, but only time will tell. As is, this is an amazing product.

Or, you flip the keyboard so that the back of that keypad rests against your tablet screen and it is still only secured by the outer elastic strap. Both methods require that you ensure you keep this tablet case upright so that the keyboard does not slip out of this elastic band as time and use deteriorate the elastic and its tension. So, in essence, this is a case that has been around and works well for Kindle Fire and probably this tablet. but, this case was NOT designed to include a keyboard. this was a vendor added item with an existing product. When you pay $200 for a tablet you want to ensure you do not scratch the screen or damage the tablet. And if you like the use of a keyboard, note that a mouse will also be required and that it may be best to look for alternative cases to accommodate your needs in one neat package
Update: July 2016: well after very limited use the key board is no loner functioning. It's not the charge it is a dead key board. I am a senior and disabled Vietnam veteran appreciate each dollar of my disability pay and do not have that luxury of repeat purchases. title: Decent components, poor execution
text:
Slept two nights with these headphones in their stock configuration and decided I could create something far superior.
For several years I’ve owned and extensively used a pair of the original wired SleepPhones. They are extremely comfortable. The drivers are only 2-3mm thick and sandwiched between two layers of felt. The fleece headband stayed in place without feeling constrictive. It was also easy to wash - open the hook and loop closure on the back, pulled out the speakers and wires, wash, dry, re-install.
By contrast, MusiCozy uses thicker drivers (granted, the frequency response is better than the SleepPhone drivers) then adds a rubber cover, then covers that with a thin jersey fabric. The headband was painfully tight, and I don’t have a big head (22.5”). After the first night, I stretched the headband over a small throw pillow for a day and that helped a bit. But the second night, the thick drivers hurt my ears so bad I took the whole thing off. I mostly sleep on my side and stomach. It’s also tricky to charge because the port is only accessible if you line up the slit in the jersey fabric just right. Some simple product testing would have identified these issues. But for $20, I couldn’t be happier….. why?
SleepPhoness wants $100 for their bluetooth units. I’m sure they are top-notch but I didn’t want to spend that much. Here’s my solutions: The entire MuziCozy headband was disassembled….all two components. The bluetooth receiver / battery compartment and speakers come out easily enough. The fake ‘control panel’ on the front isn’t needed. The speakers have a rubber cover that is not needed. Once that is removed, the speakers are only 3-4mm thick, which is good. I disassembled the wired SleepPhones as well. The felt driver covers were re-used with the MuziCozy drivers, then the whole thing was re-installed into the SleepPhone headband.
This is the best setup - the headband is comfortable, I can still use it to cover my eyes, the sound quality is improved, and the MuziCozy charge port is easier to access thanks to the large velcro opening on the back of the headband.
My girlfriend, by contrast, likes absolute silence while sleeping so she uses the MuziCozy headband to make sure her earplugs don’t fall out and to cover her eyes.
So the entire unit has gone to good use, just not in the way it was delivered. I’m happy with the results but the original product need some redesign.

Perhaps if you are normally heavy-handed when you type on a keyboard, you wouldn't face this issue.

Something that I wish this keyboard had is a touch pad. If this device can be both a keyboard and mouse, it would be much more useful.

Overall, the Samsers Wireless Portable Folding Keyboard is a good device but ultimately, it has a couple of shortcomings that keep it from being great.

title: A Really Nice Backpack With Electronics Perks
text:
First a caveat: I am not of the generation who grew up carrying backpacks to school and I do not have a lot of shoulder/upper arm strength; in addition I have arthritis in my neck, so to me any backpack seems a bit strange, stiff, and awkward. Frankly, I think if I'd had to carry around all the books I did in junior high school in a backpack (none of my classes were near my homeroom locker, so there was none of this dropping books off routine--we only had three minutes to get between classes), I'd have severe back problems right now, remembering the thick English, math, science, Italian, and history textbooks, plus a full size ring binder. Oy.

Now to our backpack: I like this. We have less expensive backpacks in our home, to use as a "bug out" bag in case of emergency. This is much nicer: padding, quality of material, and lots of nice pockets (I am a pockets-type person). I particularly like the "hidden pocket" that faces your back, which would be useful for money or any other valuables if you were backpacking or traveling. I have preliminarily tested this by putting my laptop and my 10-inch tablet in the space provided and walking around for a bit. My laptop is six years old and weighs a ton. However, the padded shoulder straps and the sternum strap were helpful in keeping this balanced well on my back. I went up and down stairs a few times and did not feel unbalanced or "top heavy." (I do now, however, understand why people like Airbooks.)

In addition to the laptop pocket with the inner sleeve for the tablet, this has a central compartment with two pockets, one zipped, and an outside compartment with all sorts of slots for pens, memory cards, CDs, whatever. A small pocket on the top of the back could hold a cell phone or perhaps your printout of a boarding pass, parking ticket receipt, whatever, and there are two small pockets, one on each side, one with an opening so you could put an .mp3 player in the pocket and have your earbuds come out through it. This is all in addition to the "hidden pocket." There is a strong handle at either end of the backpack as well as a handle.

My goal is to give this a better workout at Dragoncon, where I can carry lunch and snacks and juice boxes in the central compartment, carry my tablet in the laptop compartment, and also carry my camera, instead of slinging a lunchbox and my camera case over my shoulder. It seems like a much better option. I also see it being useful on the occasional weekend trip. If it works out for me, it's possible my husband might enjoy one as well.

[September: This was really, really good at Dragoncon; I will be using a backpack again next year. Much better than carrying the lunchbox and the camera separately and wearing a pouch. I put my tablet in the laptop pocket, my lunch things (juice boxes, sandwiches, snacks, fruit) in the middle pocket, and the camera in the outermost pocket. The little pocket at the top held my spare cell phone batteries, and my wallet was in the hidden pocket. This backpack needs a strap at the bottom, and, instead of an iPod holder, a water bottle holder. That's the only thing I can see wrong with it. Yeah, I could have put a water bottle inside with my lunch.]

title: Prints Anything and Everything From Galaxy Phone; Easy to Set Up
text:
I really like this HP ENVY 6055 WIRELESS ALL-IN-ONE PRINTER (5SE16A). Finally I’m able to print anything and everything from my Samsung Galaxy S10 cell phone! To set it up with an Android phone, you need two apps from Google Play: HPSmart, and HP Print Service Plugin.

SETUP. Once you have HPSmart, you turn on the printer, open the app, and follow the prompts. The app finds the printer, helps you connect it to your home network, and takes you through the process of loading paper, installing two ink cartridges, and aligning the copier. From time to time, a prompt will tell you to press a lighted or flashing button on the printer in order to proceed.

The setup process isn’t difficult, but you should start it when you have maybe 20-30 minutes to devote to it. There are enough steps that you don’t want to get interrupted in the middle.

HPSMART APP. Something that I really love about the printer, is that I can use my phone to make it scan a document and send the document to an email address. The phone can control all of the printer functions through the HPSmart display--it just takes a tap on a virtual button. I asked the printer to print a photo from my phone’s Gallery, and it came out beautifully. The photo that I took outside my home with the phone’s camera and immediately sent to the printer also came out beautifully.

MANUAL CONTROLS. You can also control the printer manually, at least for copying. When you open the printer cover, the buttons for the number of copies and copying light up. However, this printer is easiest to control with the HPSmart app. (I need to visit the HP web site and download the full manual--the closest now is the Envy 6400 all-in-one printer manual--because the lighted buttons aren’t quite intuitive.) Other mobile devices on my home network (e.g., my iPad Air) are able to find the printer and use it like any other printer on my network.

SPEED; COPY QUALITY; INK The printer is quite fast, and the quality of the printing is excellent. The ink colors are bright and the printing is extremely crisp and clear (even with fine print). The printer uses HP 67 ink cartridges--which are definitely NOT discontinued (as another reviewer reported). My local Staples store has the ink in stock right now (July 2020).

INSTANT INK PROGRAM. If you like, you can sign up for the optional HP Instant Ink program, and the printer will automatically order ink for you. I chose the “Moderate” program, which assumes printing about 100 pages per month, for $4.99 a month (after the first 2 months’ free trial). If you don’t print that many pages, you can carry over the unused pages to a later month (up to a set number of pages). You can cancel the Instant Ink program at any time.

APPEARANCE. The printer has a sleek, low profile. It’s white, which means it will blend in with the decor of any room.

title: Easy to install, consistent signal, fairly good sound quality
text:
Context: I have have an '05 Subaru Outback Limited, which has a 6-CD changer but no cassette deck or AUX-in. I have a decent amount of experience in audio, low-voltage electric, and soldering.

ASIN of other parts I purchased:

RCA-3.5mm cable: B00LM2Y2U4
3.5mm panel-mount jack: B00OGLCR3W
Antenna adapters for Subaru: B000K53QBA
3.5mm braided, right-angle cable: B01K3WYKW8

I installed this in my Outback after thinking about doing so for years. I've never used the sound system in my car and it felt like a bit of a waste, and I would like to listen to audiobooks and music on my commute or long trips. Previously I considered tying the audio into the wiring harness for the CD player in order to attain maximum quality, but it was sufficiently unapproachable that I put it off for years. I ended up going with the iSimple instead of a generic FM transmitter because I wanted to get the maximum possible quality at the maximum power, hopefully improving the battery life of my MP3 player (a Sandisk Sansa Clip+).

As for installation: I watched a video on Youtube by a guy named Dirtcheapdaily (How to add an auxiliary port to any car | Ep.81) which made the process very simple. It took me about three hours total from start to finish, and required that I remove the center console from the car and make some modifications on the workbench. However, I wanted my car to look stock, with everything hidden away - if you don't care about any of that, you could literally do this in 20m.

However, the steps I took were: remove some panels from center console and radio - pull antenna wires out from behind head unit- connect iSimple model to antenna wires via adapters to check length of wires - remove center console and bring to workbench - add velcro and attach iSimple to space inside center console where it won't interfere with anything - drill holes in wall of center console storage compartment - cut switch wires, feed through holes, resolder w/ heatshrink - feed audio wire through hole, solder to 3.5mm jack, seat in hole - trim, then solder power wires to back of cigarette lighter (only has power when ACC is on) - tie all wires down so they don't wander - return center console to car and temporarily reconnect to adjust gain and switch to best radio station, and make sure parking brake doesn't interfere with modules or wires - reassemble car and test one last time.

Regarding quality: after adjustment, I'd say the audio quality is pretty good. When the switch is on, there is no interference whatsoever from other stations. It is not as good as a true line in, but I don't see that as being very important as I frequently have the windows down, hear road noise, or have the car vents running, so for me fairly good is good enough. It is better than many external FM transmitters I've heard, and much more consistent.

I do wish the gain on the unit was a bit stronger, I have it maxed out an still have to crank my volume up to 50% if I have my MP3 player on ~50% volume, which isn't an issue it itself but at 20 the other radio stations are truly deafening. It is possible that the gain is limited by FCC regs, though. For now, I just set all my presets to the radio station I have selected on the unit to avoid accidentally shifting to a different one. This way I can run the MP3 on 50% and the battery will hold out longer than otherwise.

So, as for recommendations - I would say that if you want the best quality in the most unobtrusive form factor, this is a good investment so long as installing it into your car isn't -too- much of a hassle. I found the process educational myself but for some it might just be frustrating. If you just want audio and you aren't too attached to how you get it, I would order an external plug-in FM transmitter first and only upgrade if you feel it would be necessary.

title: Excellent use of storage space, great construction and innovative features (but one shortcoming)
text:
I received this as a free review sample. The reason why I docked it a star is the active tablet window needs improvement (and that could have been one of the stand-out features if properly designed.) Here is the problem: it's the perfect size for an iPad Air 2, but could not accommodate my Tab 2 10.1 inch tablet. It did hold my Samsung Tab Pro 8.4 (even in an Otterbox Defender case). The vinyl window wrinkles and also reduces sensitivity when you interact with your tablet.

If the active tablet window is unimportant to you, then the rest of this backpack is a winner. Pairing my phone to the bluetooth speakers was as simple as flipping a switch and scanning for it on my phone's settings. And the speakers are loud with better than expected sound quality. I was pleased with that - some thought went into the speakers.

The padding is more than ample for protecting electronics, and there are sufficient pockets for the geekiest geek. What I like, though, is the storage areas are not overly complex. I own a Booq bag that is a storage dream come true, but almost requires a photographic memory to remember were all of the pockets are. This one is designed much simpler, but still efficient and effective.

Construction (except for the active tablet window) is first rate. The tablet window is marred by a difficult zipper, whereas all of the other zippers on this bag are sturdier and smooth. The outer fabric seems tough (I have not had it long enough to make any claims beyond that), and all of the seams are reinforced, straight and tight.

It's very comfortable and can be adjusted to evenly distribute the weight of a fully loaded pack. Considering that the bag itself is somewhat heavy this is a major plus for me.

I do want to note one thing about the backup battery: it is rated at (and stores) the full 4000mAh. However, like all batteries using this one's technology it's only 70% efficient, so expect about 2800mAh of usable capacity. That is not a flaw in this bag, but a reality that I wanted to point out so your expectations are properly set.

Overall, this is a well made bag with some innovative features (battery back-up and bluetooth speakers). If the active tablet window is not an important feature it's definitely worth considering. This one will be replacing my Booq because the storage is there without the complexity.

title: How to look like a pro (even if you're not)
text:
This Targus notebook case is a great way to carry around all your stuff and still look cool, professional and ready for action.

The good stuff:

1. It can fit notebooks up to 17" securely and safely. There's a strap to hold your equipment in place, it's nicely padded and has an adjustable inner wall for extra snugness. It even opens like a briefcase for easy packing.
2. The same compartment has three pockets with Velcro closures, a zippered mesh pocket and some slots for letters, warranty cards or other documentation. There's ample space for a mouse (optical, cordless, furry with tail), flash drives, cds and dvds, cords, headphones, bells and whistles.
3. The zipper for the notebook section can be locked with a padlock.
4. The front flap has an easy fastener, and also has a zip pocket, right at the front of the bag, perfect for passport and tickets when traveling
5. Lift the flap for another compartment, and more pockets, with slots for pens, glasses, keys, and whatever else you like to carry around.
6. The back has a padded Velcro-closing pocket for newspapers, magazines or other reading matter.
7. Yet another zippered compartment has two slots for important documents and not so important documents.
8. The handle is tough rubber, defying you to mess with it, and the bottom and sides are protected with a corrugated rubber strip. You can set this one down on the floor - it can take it.
9. Even if you aren't carrying around a laptop all the time, this case works fine as a large briefcase for work or travel, with lots of room for a change of clothes, product samples, toiletries (make sure they adhere to airline safety regulations), files, manuals, snacks, extra undies and more.

The other stuff:
1. If you have a 17" laptop, there's not enough space in the padded section to hold your power cord, but there are so many other compartments and pockets that this shouldn't pose a major problem - other than remembering where you put it. (There's plenty of space for a bottle of Ginkgo Biloba)
2. It's pretty durn heavy to lug around, especially for those already having to contend with a full handbag, cup of coffee and high heeled shoes
3. The generous number of compartments encourages you to carry around more stuff than you need - just in case of emergencies. (And then of course you can't remember where you packed them in the first place)
4. It tends to fall over if you don't put it down carefully or lean it against something.
5. The strap looks a little cheap compared to the rest of the case, and keeps spinning around, so you always have to check that the padded piece is on the inside, but it's easier to carry it by the handle anyway.

Sturdy, roomy, comfy and a tad bit clunky, but overall a good case for larger notebooks, work or travel.

Amanda Richards, September 22, 2007

title: Decent Slider, but Room for Improvement
text:
I am primarily a stills shooter. That said, I do have an excellent camera that is very capable of shooting video and I do need it for such on occasion. I was interested in this camera slider as a way to get smooth shots and to reduce reliance on lens-based stabilization which is not included in my camera body. This has been a learning experience and while I like this slider there is definitely room for improvement.

I will start with the basics. This is a large and fairly heavy animal, which is to be expected. It is roughly 3' long and in it’s most basic configuration rests on a flat surface with no issues. It does have some adjustments that can be made to the individual feet on the frame so it can be adjusted slightly for uneven but mostly level surfaces without using any other equipment. To get much more versatility out of it, though, it can be mounted on tripods on either end to raise it higher or to set up angular shots.

The motor on the frame is controlled by a remote which comes with a battery pack. The remote is not wireless and has to be connected to the motor via the provided cabling. This is all right, but wireless functionality would make it much more versatile. It should be noted that the remote controls the slider, not the camera. I had some concern about this in the very beginning, thinking that the remote would be incompatible with my camera and that this unit would not work for me.

I encountered some issues that bother me. First, when powered on and running the motor runs the slider down the track until it is either stopped or a stop point is set. If one is not set, it bumps into the end and keeps trying to go beyond, making an awful noise that will surely mess up any video that requires sound. In my mind, the motor should detect when it hits the end and stop, even if start and stop points are not set.

When the motor is running and it is not near a stop point, it runs at constant speed and it is very smooth. When manually paused, it stops quickly but it doesn’t jerk to an abrupt stop like it hit something. But, if one of the end points are set and is reached, the motor slows down, then jerks to a stop, enough to notice in video footage. This is most obvious when the remote is set up to film in a loop as the issue can be observed repeatedly.

The motor is not silent, though it is quiet. It is not loud enough to ruin a shot unless absolute quiet is needed, and the motor produces a low-volume, low-frequency hum that slightly resembles the sound of an electric trolling motor on a bass boat, but quieter. The point is that it is by no means silent, but it should be good enough in the majority of cases. This is out the window if the motor is allowed to reach the end of the track before it is stopped, in which case the noise is likely to be a serious issue.

This is a decent slider and if used with some thought will serve nicely. There are definitely some places where it could be improved, particularly in the way it fails to handle reaching the end of tracks.

text:
I bought this camera to replace one of those cheap $20 cameras with the LEDs on the front. While the old cheap camera will prove if a car pulled out in front of you or if the light was green when you drove through the intersection, it couldn't give you more detail than that.

This DVR has crystal clear true 1080p video that puts the cheap camera to shame. This may have cost 3x what I paid for the cheap camera, but the image is 10x better. This camera has great low light image quality. Some will say that the image is noisy, but that is what you get with any digital camera that costs under $1,000. My cheap one was worthless in the dark. The 8GB micro SD card that was included was made by Samsung and so far holds about 1 1/2 hours before being written over. (Recording at 1080p, 3 minute files and using Wide Dynamic Range) The camera was ready to go right out of the box. All I had to do was change the date and time. The manual was well written and easy to understand. The suction mount holds tight and the ball head can be articulated to any position you need. The power cord was plenty long enough to hide it and run it in the overhead, down the passenger side and back to the 12v power supply in the middle console.

As with anything in life, you get what you pay for and you have to balance what you want with what you can afford. As I said before, a $20 camera will tell you if a blurry car pulled out in front of you during the day. But this camera will show you if they were on the phone.

Answers to common questions;

Q: Is this camera HD?
A: Yes the camera records in 1080p

Q: Does the camera turn itself on and off automatically?
A: Yes the camera turns on when the car starts and turns back off 10-15 seconds after the car shuts down. As long as you have it plugged into a 12v outlet that is only powered when the car is on. If the outlet is always on even when the car is off, the camera will not shut down unless you turn it off or remove the plug.

Q: How long can it record, what happens when it runs out of memory?
A: At 1080p, the highest setting the included 8GB card will hold between 1 1/2 hours worth of video. Once it reaches capacity, the oldest video file will be deleted to make room for the new file.

Q: How can I view/save files on my computer?
A: Remove the Micro SD card from the side of the camera and insert it into the included USB micro SD card adapter and insert it into your computer. Or if you want you can always take down the entire camera and plug it in to your computer using a mini USB cable.

Q: Can you read license plates?
A: Yes, but only until the cars reach about 20' away. Since the camera is a wide angle lens, it becomes hard to read. All Car DVRs suffer from this because they have wide angle lenses. I can read plates of cars that pass me too.

title: Packs a punch for the size.
text:
I ordered the iHome Alexa Built-in Bluetooth Speaker Portable Wireless Waterproof Rechargeable Lights Up to Music, with Speakerphone, Passive Subwoofer, Carry Strap, Durable Shockproof Floatable Design (IBT158) to replace an old sub par portable speaker that I’ve had for years. The iHome is quite the upgrade with the built in Alexa, better sound and being waterproof. I’ve had this product now for several weeks and would like to share my thoughts.

I must say that the sound is pretty good and packs a punch in such a small size. It’s much better than the much smaller and several years old portable wireless speaker that I have been using. In fact there really is no comparison at all. Let’s just say that it is the best sounding portable wireless speaker that I personally have ever owned. My daughter who “borrowed” the older speaker some time ago (and she never gave it back) keeps asking to "borrow" the new iHome as she says, “it’s louder and sounds WAY better”. I absolutely agree with her. Plus the lights on this thing are a nice touch, and there are options (via a button on top) to cycle through and change the color options or turn them off.

Setting up the iHome for Bluetooth and Alexa was easy and very straight forward, and there has been no issues whatsoever. We are mainly an Android household however my oldest daughter uses an iPhone and everyone has had the same great experience. So far my only complaint is that the Bluetooth connectivity distance isn’t the greatest but with that said, none of my Bluetooth devices really have much range in our home so I am not going to knock points off for that. The sound out of this little guy makes up for the Bluetooth short comings and the bonus of Alexa being packed into this as well as the waterproof features make this a great value for the selling price.

One thing worth mentioning is that to use Alexa, you can’t just say “Alexa” to activate her. You do have to physically press a button on the iHome speaker to access her, which isn’t a huge deal breaker, but because of this, you can’t use other Alexa devices to make an announcement and have it broadcast to the iHome speaker. Being fairly new to the Alexa and smart home world, I am not going to hold this shortcoming against the iHome device. It actually makes sense that with this being portable, you wouldn’t want to have Alexa always listening and drain the battery while on the go. Speaking of Battery life, it's decent but not spectacular by any means. This is pretty subjective however as usually when I use the iHome, I'm listening to it at a pretty high volume ;)

Another observation is that this uses micro USB to charge, and I really would like to see more devices using the newer and better USB C charging capabilities.

As far as the “waterproof” capabilities go, I must report that I have yet to float the device in a pool or let the kids play with it outside while running through the sprinklers. I know that it says it’s waterproof and it absolutely looks like it would hold up to getting wet as it is very well built, rugged and quite solid, but I don't want to risk ruining this new toy that the whole family has been enjoying so much.

This Bose portable speaker can support two Bluetooth-connected devices at once, so you can switch between two devices (e.g., an iPad and a Kindle Fire) without repeating the pairing process every time. The speaker's voice prompts help you with pairing, and tell you which two devices are currently paired. The voice prompts can be disabled, if you wish.

This Bose speaker is definitely an improvement over the speakers built into my old Sony Bravia TV. Voices are much clearer--including the dialogue from British TV shows--and the sound is far richer. Of course, using this speaker instead of a TV sound bar is only a temporary solution, because the speaker needs regular recharging. When fully charged, it delivers sound for many hours (up to 8) and outlasts the charge on the [[ASIN:B004B8GF7Y TaoTronics® Bluetooth Transmitter]] that I added to my non-Bluetooth-enabled TV.

Whether the TaoTronics transmitter was connected to the TV's headphone jack or to the TV's AV ouputs, this speaker paired instantly. However, when the TV transmitter was connected to the AV outputs, the speaker produced some static unless it was positioned close to the TV. When the TV transmitter was connected to the headphone jack, the speaker produced no static at all, no matter where it was positioned (within the Bluetooth range).

This Bose speaker charges quickly with the included AC adapter and USB cable. Pressing the speaker's power button produces a battery indicator that glows red, amber, or green to indicate the current level of charge. The speaker is lightweight enough to carry around in a backpack or tote bag. There is a case available (see [[ASIN:B00NJGRKG4 Bose SoundLink Color carry case]]), but I don't think a case is needed, because the speaker seems to be sturdily constructed.

title: Delivers Adequate Power to Charge Four Devices; Features Small Tabletop Footprint
text:
What I really like about the CHIL POWERSHARE 5.1 AMP REACTOR is the small tabletop footprint. This charging station consists of a white 4-port USB charger (reactor) inserted into a black silicone stand (tower). The silicone is stiff enough to support the charger, but still flexible enough to allow removal of the charger if you don't want the stand. However, the tower stand is what makes this charging station fit so conveniently into a small space. And because the stand holds the charger with the ports facing up, the charger ports are highly accessible and it's fairly easy to coil and manage the USB cables that are plugged into the ports (and into your mobile devices).

The charger has three 1.0 amp ports (each suitable for charging power banks, Kindles, small tablets, and smartphones), and one 2.1 amp port (suitable for charging iPads, iPods, and large tablets). Thus the ports deliver a total of 5.1 amps. These particular four ports are adequate to keep all of my family's daily-use mobile devices charged, because we rarely need to charge two devices that require 2.1 amps at the same time.

To test this Chil Powershare Reactor, I plugged in an iPad (2.1 amp), a Kindle Paperwhite (1.0 amp), a Motorola Droid Razr smartphone (1.0 amp), and a Qi wireless charging pad (1.0 amp).

---My devices to be charged began with varying amounts of charge: iPad (77%); Kindle Paperwhite (nearly empty); Motorola smartphone (86%); and Qi-enabled Samsung Galaxy SIII smartphone (45%).

---After 55 minutes, the charges had increased: iPad (97%); Kindle Paperwhite (about 50%); Motorola smartphone (100%); Samsung smartphone (82%). This was much better than I expected; definitely as good as or better than other charging stations that I've used. Qi wireless charging is generally slower than direct charging, so the Samsung smartphone was charging as expected. At this point I unplugged the iPad and the Motorola smartphone, as both were almost completely charged.

---After 85 minutes, the remaining two devices had added to their charge: Kindle Paperwhite (about 75%); Samsung Qi-enabled smartphone (95%).

I'm completely satisfied with these results. Any 1.0 amp port and a Kindle USB cable will charge any of my Kindles (Fire 8.9" tablet, Keyboard, Paperwhite); any 1.0 amp port will power my Qi-charging pad for the Samsung smartphone and other devices; and any 1.0 amp port plus an appropriate cable will charge my power banks and Motorola smartphone. The charging occurs rapidly enough for my needs.

If you're concerned, as I once was, about plugging an older USB device into a USB port that delivers more power than the device really needs, you needn't worry. The device will NOT blow up--what's likely to happen is that the device will charge a little faster, although some older USB devices won't charge at all. (For a clear explanation of this, look online for the enlightening ExtremeTech article, "How USB Charging Works, or How to Avoid Blowing Up Your Smartphone".)

The Chil Powershare Reactor has an ordinary wall-outlet plug (no extra grounding prong--just two prongs, one wide, one narrow). It has a moderately short power cord (about 45"), but the cord can be coiled inside the silicone tower or around the reactor for portability and "cable management".

The packaging materials state that this charger "limits 'vampire drain' when inactive", but give no further details about this presumably energy-saving feature. The charger does NOT have an on/off switch, so it's always on when plugged in.

This 3M EASY-ON PRIVACY FILTER FOR IPAD2 offers fairly decent privacy, but it doesn't black out your screen for someone standing behind you (looking over your shoulder) or black out the screen completely for someone sitting beside you and leaning in. It offers privacy for the vertical (portrait) iPad position only--which is actually a nice feature, since you can hold your iPad up in the horizontal (landscape) position to share with anyone and everyone nearby without removing the filter.

Installation is extremely simple. You stick small adhesive patches on each of the four corners of the stiff plastic filter, then gently stick the filter onto your iPad. (Check to make sure you have an iPad 2 or 3rd/4th generation iPad, because the cutouts for the home screen button and front-facing camera must match up.) The filter goes on bubble-free, without any need for a cardboard "squeegee".

The privacy filter is easy to remove. The kit includes a heavy plastic sleeve for storing the filter after you've added the corner stickers, and also includes four extra corner stickers for when the first set of stickers wears out. You need to use some care when removing the filter: on my first attempt, three of the sticky corners stayed on the iPad. Probably that was because I applied the filter on top of existing screen protector film and pressed the corners down firmly. On my second application, I pressed the corners down quite gently, and the stickers stayed on the filter when I removed it for the second time.

Because the privacy filter doesn't completely black out the screen when someone is sitting close by you, I rate it at 4 stars ("I like it" on the official Amazon scale).

title: Near-Perfect  Faux Crocodile Cover With Intriguing Stand Design
text:
I love the look and feel of this VERSO "DARWIN" CROCCO standing cover for the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" tablet. Red is my favorite color, and the faux crocodile texture is really fun.

This cover holds the tablet firmly with silicone-enhanced elastic corner bands (patent pending). The bands have a rubbery material on the underside of the elastic that grips the surface beneath it, so the tablet does not slide around inside the cover or want to fall out. (I have screen protector film on my tablet, which seems like a good idea when a tablet is held in place by elastic bands rather than a hard plastic shell. This [[ASIN:B009NHU556 3-Pack Ultra-Clear Screen Protector)]] is easy to apply, and you get three chances to get it on right.)

The cover's built-in stands are quite intriguing. There are two of them attached to the inside of the front cover. One stand supports the tablet at a low angle for typing; the other supports it more or less upright for watching movies. Both provide comfortable viewing angles. The stands themselves are flat, microfiber-covered pieces that match the rest of the cover's interior. You pick the stand angle you want, and open out the appropriate stand. The stand is connected to the cover on top and also with a ribbon underneath, so that the stand converts into a triangular support for your tablet. This design is very clever, and I would consider it perfect if I hadn't already tried the [[ASIN:B009X0167Y Marware Vibe Standing Case]], which is a little easier to set up and offers more viewing angles.

This Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover has an elastic band that holds it tightly closed inside a book or tote bag, as well as an automatic magnetic wake/sleep feature. For the wake/sleep feature to work, you must insert your tablet with the camera at the left and the charging port at the right. This I don't like, because the charging port ends up at the tablet's bottom edge when you use the stands. This means you are limited to using the low-angle stand whenever your tablet is plugged in, because the plug contacts the table top. (With the Marware Vibe cover, the charging port ends up at the tablet's top edge, so you can use the tablet at any angle when it's plugged in.)

According to the accompanying retail literature, this Verso "Darwin" Crocco cover is "compatible" with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9", the Nook HD+, "and more". Because the cover holds the tablet with elastic bands, it should fit any tablet near in size to the large Fire or the large Nook. However, it is definitely too small for an iPad 2.

For me, it's difficult to choose between the Marware Vibe cover and the Verso "Darwin" cover. But in the end, as usually happens, good looks win out. My 8.9" Kindle Fire HD tablet is going to stay in the red faux-crocodile-skin cover, which is eye-catching, looks and feels luxurious, and is extremely well made.

title: Possibly the worst tablet ever made
text:
I've been a professional software developer for more than twenty years, and in that time I've used a very large variety of computing devices for both personal and professional use. I don't think I've ever hated a computing device more than I hate this abomination. Actually, I can't remember actually hating any device prior to this. The touch-screen is terrible and inconsistent, and I frequently need to tap things multiple times in order to get a response.

Windows 8 might be okay if it weren't so completely locked down on the Surface RT. For instance, you cannot install any other browser; you're stuck with Internet Explorer, the worst browser available on any device, and cannot even install plugins to block spam ads and malware. The web browsing experience is truly terrible, and the design of the browser is sufficiently different from *every other browser* to make it as counter-intuitive as possible.

There is almost no software that will run on the device except what can be obtained through Microsoft's online store, which is a fresh hell that deserves it's own product review. At least with my Android devices I have broad compatibility and a wide variety of software available for just about every purpose.

The on-screen touch keyboard is clunky and poorly designed, and is at times incredibly difficult to use. For instance, trying to compile an email in GMail is pathologically difficult, since the keyboard takes up literally 75% of the screen, leaving almost no space to see what you're typing and making it incredibly difficult to scroll down to the "Send" button to actually send the email. There appears to be no support for swapping the built-in touch-screen keyboard with a better version like Swype, which is incredibly disappointing.

Attempting to connect USB devices is extremely hit or miss, and many I've tried simply do not work due to lack of "official" driver support. For instance, I purchased a "Belkin F4U047-RS USB 2.0 Ethernet Adapter" on the advice of several websites saying that they'd been able to use that specific adapter to add an Ethernet adapter to the Surface RT. Unfortunately, Microsoft has asked those websites to no longer distribute the drivers that made the device work, and have disabled the use of such drivers on the Surface RT since they are not Microsoft certified drivers, leaving me with no Ethernet and twenty dollars wasted.

I could go on for several more paragraphs, but I've wasted enough of my life on this piece of offal. If I didn't require this device to be physically present to test software builds on, I would have sent it back almost immediately.

title: Crystal Clear Film, Easy to Apply, No Loss of Sensitivity
text:
This crystal-clear screen protector film is very easy to apply. It's pre-cut to exactly fit the Kindle Fire touch screen, and it presses on without any need for additional adhesive. After the film is applied, there is no loss of sensitivity in the touch screen.

The application process is very simple: (1) clean the screen thoroughly, using the included microfiber cloth; (2) use the #1 tab to remove the plastic stiffener/shield from one side of the double-sided film; (3) position the uncovered side of the film on the Kindle Fire screen (holding the film by the #2 tab, starting at one corner, and allowing the film to fall gently onto the screen); (4) use the included smoothing card to get rid of bubbles; (5) use the #2 tab to remove the remaining plastic stiffener/shield; and (6) use the smoothing card again to get rid of any bubbles. The whole process took me less than 10 minutes.

Whenever I apply screen protector film, I usually have to try two or three times to get everything right. With this kit, the first application was successful, because the film adhered properly at the edges, and all but one tiny bubble smoothed out. Now, should I ever need to re-apply the film, I have the second shield in reserve.

It's probably worth noting that the Kindle Fire has a larger screen than an iPhone or iPod Touch or camera viewfinder, so that the risk of getting dust particles under the film during application to the Fire is higher. Also, it may not be necessary to install protective film on the Fire at all, because the touch screen is supposed to be made of particularly tough, scratch-resistant glass.

title: Dead spots are gone.
text:
This wireless range extender was fairly easy to install. The directions were straight forward, and the device was up and running in less than fifteen minutes. It comes with an CD, but we didn't have to use it. We did have to reset the IP address on the computer, but that may have a user issue and not related to the device itself.

It took a little while to find the best place to plug the device in based on our home's layout, but we found one that worked. In our house plan, the best place ended up being in the hallway at baseboard level. Fortunately, the device is small and plugs straight into the wall, eliminating any unsightly cords. It would have been nicer to have the device a little more out of the way. We were a little concerned about this thinking it might get kicked or knocked by the kids as they race around and play. That hasn't happened yet, but it is something to take into consideration if you have small children or pets around. We tried placing it in a less open area hoping to protect it a little more, but none of those areas produced a satisfactory result.

It's very easy to tell how much of a signal the device is receiving from the main router. Three bars is full signal, and one is low signal. The signal indicator light is easy to read and is quite bright. Since the device is in our hallway, it acts as a nice night light and would be rather distracting if it were in a bedroom.

The end result: the dead spots are gone. We can use all of our devices in the those areas without having to worry about losing a signal.

title: I'm really liking the Ulanzi brand
text:
When I purchased the [[ASIN:B08RRV6S6W Ulanzi battery handle]] to go with my DJI pocket, I was impressed with the quality of the product. When gathering together my camera gear for my vacation, I realized that I actually purchased a couple of other Ulanzi products previously. Since then, this brand has jumped out at me when looking for camera accessories.

This ULANZI MT-33 Camera Tripod had a convenience feature that I didn't realize it had when I ordered it. It is well thought out and has good build quality (with one minor caveat). It is a flexible tripod that is strong enough to hold my mirrorless Lumix camera and is equipped with a cold shoe socket as well as a 1/4" screw hole. The cold shoe can hold a microphone or small LED video light which the 1/4" screw hole can either mount another cold shoe or other camera accessories.

The convenience feature that I didn't know about is that the mounting head of this tripod can open up to become a phone holder. It's not a separate accessory that screws on to the quarter inch screw. The spring-loaded phone holder is actually part of the mounting head's design. What this means is that one can switch from taking pictures with a camera to filming with a cell phone without fumbling around with phone brackets.

In my pictures, you will see a screw with its tightening wheel. The screw is supposed to be securely seated in the wheel but it wasn't seated properly in the product I received and it came apart. It wasn't a big problem. Simply reassemble the screw and wheel back and then mount a camera to the tripod. By tightening the screw to the camera and keep turning. The tightening action will seat the screw back into the wheel and should not come out anymore.

I'm not a video blogger but it seems like I'm slowly collecting many accessories that make me think perhaps it's a shame for me not to be? I have the necessary tools for it... not everyone is made to be in front of the camera, I guess.

title: Not professional, but one of the better ones this price bracket
text:
[[VIDEOID:91ed971de75e2a1d366c0694560e3ad4]] Let's get this metric straight: Those who are saying a projector under $300 looks good, are probably comparing it to other cheap off-brand projectors. I've tried a few of these to use as throwaround backyard movie night things, when I don't want to get my expensive prosumer home theater ones dirty or burn out the bulb, and they all suffer from things like flat colors, lack of brightness (fudging the lumens numbers) and the worst: Inconsistent focus. Nothing makes me crazier than trying to nail the focus and finding the center focuses while the borders are out of focus, but adjusting for the edges makes the center out of focus. Usually this is because the lens is cheap and lacks proper rectilinear support, and it is MADDENING once you notice it. In short, sometimes you might find it looks better on a smaller TV than a bigger washed out and fuzzy projector.
But... usually, you should expect to pay somewhere towards DOUBLE this for a brand name projector that looks decent, so I'm trying to keep my expectations realistic for the price range. And I have to say, this is the first one that actually seems to have proper focus across the projected image! I mean, you do get some chromatic aberration in the corners (see image and video attached), but this is nothing compared to others in the sub-300 dollar range. I love that this also has built in features like miracast (which I tried and works great!) as well as an Office Suite so you can technically show a presentation without a laptop or casting device- just plug in a USB stick with your content and go!
These are not necessary in my opinion, I'd rather have better colors and sharpness than gimmicks, but honestly I think this might be the best of the lower end projectors I've tried yet! If you care about how your movies and presentations look, I'd still recommend a brand name like Viewsonic at the bare minimum. But this is fun for the kids, backyard movie nights, or impromptu presentations when a bigger and more expensive projector wouldn't be cost justifiable.

It is not an issue when you are not holding it: for example, using the tablet to watch movies and it is supported by the folded case on a flat surface (although this feels somewhat precarious/barely balanced). The issue is when you are holding the case in your hand and trying to read with your Kindle: the lip digs into your palm or fingers and after a few minutes becomes uncomfortable. You end up shifting the kindle to your other hand every couple of minutes. This is uncool, and makes what would otherwise be a great case almost unusable as a hand-held device. I thought about returning it, but given the hassle involved, I decided not to bother for a $12 unit.

I cannot recommend this case. If you plan on reading with this case (i,.e. holding it in your hand for any length of time), it will be uncomfortable (sure is for me anyway).

text:
This is my first GoPro and I'm underwhelmed.

Starting with the good: The camera inside is great for video. It can record at 5.3K resolution @ 60 FPS, 4K @ 120 FPS, or 2.7K @ 240 FPS. The video quality is really good. Crispy and clear. Love it.

Now the bad: first off, this thing CANNOT shoot still photos (??), which is absurd. If you want a photo, you'll have to record a video and take a screengrab. No idea why they didn't include a photo feature.

The second-worst thing is that there is no screen, front or back. While I obviously knew this going in, not having any preview display has been a bigger annoyance than expected. It feels like this is being marketed as a more rugged version of the Hero 11 Black, but I'd rather just throw a case on a Hero 11 vs. not having a screen.

A couple other missing features, it doesn't have any scheduled capture mode or GPS. Neither of those are important to me, but I figure I'd mention them.

There is a flip-out cover that has a USB-C port and an SD card slot. It does not support an external microphone (!) and does not have an HDMI out. It's possible it'll support the GoPro external mic in the future after a firmware update, but TBD.

The battery is not removable, which I think they did to save (physical) size on the device. The battery is billed to give 60 minutes of recording time at max resolution, which feels about right given my experience. Lower resolution or FPS will allow for longer battery life.

I'd pass on this. Too many missing features to justify a purchase.

title: I'm officially a hit with my sons! They love these headphones.
text:
I was looking for stocking stuffers for my two teenaged boys. Both had expressed an interest in the Beats by Dre. I don't know about you, but I was looking for a reasonable pair of headphones to accompany other high priced gifts (new Xbox, Laptop etc) they were getting for Christmas. BUT paying almost $200 for the Beats seemed unreasonable. So when these (V-Moda, Crossfade LP) were highlighted on Amazon on Black Friday, I seized the opportunity and purchased two pair (which was still cheaper than one pair of Beats), and hoped that I could rely on the reviews that I read. (Please note that I did read reviews for Beats, and found that the V-Moda pair received more positive reviews.) So with both sets of reviews under my belt, I begin to compare the features and was even more convinced that I had made a wise purchase. (Also note that later my sons were able to compare them with the Solo Beats by Dre and they still liked the Crossfades better.)

Features that my sons say make these a standout amongst most headsets:
* The overall sound quality is great and not too bass heavy.
*The over the ear covers (ear piece) have memory cushions. They are very comfortable and you can't hear outside noise (Of course I found this to be true when they could not hear me calling them. Of course, they may be ignoring me). I also can't hear the music that they are listening to.
* The volume or pause feature can be used from a control button on the cord. They even say that besides skipping songs, the rarely have to touch their devices when using these headphones.
* These earphones are versatile and can be used with multiple devices (i.e., the computer, Ipod, cell phones, etc). They are able to even use them in the car by connecting with the stereo.
* These headphones are stylish and attractive. I ordered one pair in Phantom Chrome and the other in Phantom Black.

And finally, what Mom likes about the headphones...well, the price. These headphones were reasonably priced and offered the same features as the Beats. And later when I compared them with the Beats, they appear to be better quality in terms of sound quality and workmanship (the Beats are plastic looking and don't seem to be as well constructed as the Crossfade, which seems sturdy).

title: Super basic dash cam; basic setup is relatively quick; memory card NOT included
text:
[[VIDEOID:8a05ea6494b6e1be751fa342867838c]] I purchased this to replace my wonderful DOD TECH LS460W dash cam that broke and which I absolutely loved. This package includes the camera, user manual, suction mount, and car power adapter. I had to supply my own memory card, so I used the 64GB ADATA microSD card from my previous dash cam. It can take up to a 256GB card per the manual.

I've used this four about a week so far (see video) without fully completing all the setup options. My plan is to eventually set this up fully in my house by using the 12-volt DC (direct current) receptacle of my [[ASIN:B00CMP3Z4E Clore JNC300XL 'Jump-N-Carry' 900 Peak Amp Ultraportable 12V Jump Starter with Light, CEC Compliant]] so that I don't have to sit in the car in the cold selecting the available options.

I was able to use this within about 15 minutes of receiving this by not changing any defaults. After unpacking everything, cleaning my windshield behind the rearview mirror, and running through the language, date, time, and formatting the SD card, I began recording. Note that this is supposed to turn on when the car turns on. It does not do that. In fact, sometimes I have to press the power button several ties before it will come on. I do not mind if I have to press it once but rarely does the camera come on the first time. The red recording light should come up automatically. If it does not, then the record button also has to be pressed.

Below are the PROS and CONS.

PROS
- Setup is relatively easy by following the manual's instructions.

- This one has a 1080p wide-angle video image as long as that is what is selected in the setup.

- The controls are user friendly.

- The camera is compact and has a relatively thin and tiny profile.

- The camera secures tightly in the dock. I did have to turn the knob on the mount because it was originally flopping around as a result of the mount socket being loose.

- No shaking is visible in the recorded picture which surprised me.

- The power cable is extra-long so it can be routed through the headliner of the car. I cannot do this since I have a convertible.

- The camera has a loop record feature so that it overwrites the previous recordings when the disk gets full.

-There's also a G sensor option that forces emergency recording on impact. Of course the only way to know if this works is to get into an accident.

- Date and time are recorded if set. I'm not sure how it remembers the date and time when the card is turned off because it does not have an internal battery and my 12V port is not powered by my car battery when my car is turned off.

- The camera has three modes - video recording, photo (to take a still photo), and video playback (to see what you recorded).

- The camera has a motion activated feature that's for use when not in motion. This only works as long as the car is running, is hooked to a battery pack such as the JNC 300XL, or a car whose cigarette lighter does not turn off when the car is turned off and it is set.

- The camera records sound in the cabin.

CONS
- There is no GPS stamp on this which means if one gets in an accident or captures an image, the GPS location will not be known.

- There is no speed recorded.

- There is no internal battery.

- The manual does not specify how many languages are supported.

- If the 12V connector in the car does not turn off when the car turns off, it is recommended that this dash cam be unplugged or it might drain the car battery.

- Exposure to extreme heat or extreme cold reduces the lifespan of the camera (as per manual warning). I believe this is to be expected.

In summary, I wanted a dash cam that was easy to set up and was relatively cheap. I do not need all the bells and whistles such as recording when parked, in cabin recording, an on-board battery, a rear camera, wifi, etc. This one fits my needs so far due to its simplicity. The only thing I miss is the GPS and speed stamps of my other dash cam. Those I feel should be mandatory on all dash cambs. I also miss the automatic start when the care turns on as this does not work that way on my car.

I will update this review if this dash cam fails prematurely. I expect to get at least 2 years of service out of this unit. I got my other dash cam in January 2015 and it lasted until November 2021, which is almost 6 years.

title: This 12.9" iPad Pro provides me with the great viewing experience I was looking for and is intuitive to use
text:
My boyfriend is an Apple lover and I prefer Android. I have a Google Nexus 7 that I love, but it's small. However, it was the iPad's 12.9" display that sold me on this version and the ease of setup and use that sold me on the iPad in general. Apple's reputation also sealed the deal.

When doing a side-by-side comparison, I seriously considered the 9.7" iPad Pro with its wide color and true tone display because that offers a richer viewing experience. Also, the 12-megapixel camera of the 9.7" produces more vibrant photos with better resolution than the 8-megapixel pictures taken with this 12.9" iPad Pro. Nevertheless, the large screen on this 12.9" is best for me. Portability was not an issue because I got this for home use to watch videos and to easily type on the larger virtual keyboard. I've had it for over one month now and love it. Set-up was a cinch. Battery power is also excellent and lasts for over 10 hours.

The one negative that I noticed is that Apple does everything in its power to control their users. For instance, I had to wipe out the "sent from iPad notice" when sending an email as I do not want to freely advertise for them. I also dislike how all my boyfriend's iPhone messages that use to go to my Gmail account, now landed only in iMessage on my iPad and none went to Gmail. At first I thought he was mistaken when he told me he was sending me messages and I no longer got them until I discovered them a day later on the iPad. This required I only use the iPad until we both figured out how to correct that. Nevertheless, I consider this a small annoying price to pay for what is a user friendly device that provides a rewarding viewing experience.

In addition to this iPad, I decided to purchase the [[ASIN:B008MOHLVC amPen hybrid stylus ]] instead of the [[ASIN:B016NY7784 Apple Pencil]] because I did not need the precision of the pencil. FEATURES

- This Bluetooth speaker pairs beautifully with my Nexus 7, my boyfriend's iPad 3 & iPhone 5, my BLU Life One 4G LTE SmartPhone that I use only as a portable tablet, and my HP OMEN. All I had to do was press the Bluetooth button on the speaker after I activated Bluetooth on the devices.

title: Netgear couldn't have made installation any simpler
text:
I wanted a wired connection in a far room out of reach of my router. This works perfectly for that by allowing me to use any power outlet in my condo as a way to extend my wired network.

I tested my upload and download speeds with a network cable plugged from my laptop directly into my router and compared it to a wired connection with the Netgear Powerline Outlet. There was no discernible difference either positive or negative. I even ran video under both scenarios and I detected no difference in performance.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the router, my ping was 12 ms, download was 17.08 Mbps, upload was 5.17 Mbps.

When my laptop was plugged directly into the Powerline using my electrical house wiring, my ping was 12 ms, download was 16.63 Mbps, upload was 5.20 Mbps.

Although these speeds are not great, that is the performance I usually get with the router and service provider I have. Based on my results, this works as designed. Below is a list of what comes in the package and the PROS and CONS.

The package includes two Netgear Powerline 1200 Outlets each with an extra outlet and one Gigabit Ethernet port, two 6.5 foot Ethernet cables, and a quick start guide. For the initial installation of these units, both outlets have to be used because one Powerline must be plugged into an outlet near the router so that the Ethernet cable from the Powerline can plug into the router. The other Powerline can be plugged into an outlet anywhere else in the home. The other Ethernet cable is then plugged into this unit on one end and an Ethernet-enabled device such as a laptop, SmartTV, etc. on the other. If additional Powerlines are purchased then both units can be used for two additional wired connections.

PROS
- The LEDs on the Powerline enable the user to diagnose if there's power, Ethernet connectivity, or the ability to "Pick A Plug" (a.k.a. electrical outlet) with the strongest performance.

- There's an extra outlet on each Powerline. This unit covers the second outlet if it's plugged into the top outlet of a two-outlet receptacle. However, I do not see that as a problem for two reasons. First, there's an extra outlet on the unit. Therefore, I am still getting the ability to plug in two items like I would have had I not been using the Powerline. (In this case the Powerline is one item and a light is another.) If I want to turn my outlet into a three outlet receptacle, then all I have to do is plug it into the lower outlet. This would allow me, for instance, to plug in a lamp in the top receptacle, the Powerline in the bottom receptacle, and another item into the extra outlet on the Powerline.

- According to the manual, the network can be secured by pressing the security button for two seconds and then pressing the security button on one of the other adapters in the existing network. If additional adapters are added throughout the house when security is already enabled, then ALL the adapters should be factory reset. To re-enable security, all that has to be done is press the security button for two seconds on one adapter and then select any ONE other adapter (it's not necessary to do all adapters) and press that security button for two seconds. Both security buttons have to be pressed within two minutes time.

- There's a 1 year warranty plus 90 days basic customer support.

CONS

- I see none at this time.

I will write Netgear to find out what is meant by security with these security buttons. Up to 16 adapters can be installed in a home. I know if I were to install another set of these, I would actually be able to use both Powerlines for extra wired connections, thereby increasing my wired connections to three from one. It's only for the first installation that the extra Powerline is lost because that is used to connect to the router.

In summary, I feel this Netgear works as designed with no discernible difference in speed over a wired connection whether I was plugged directly into the router or the Powerline. Installation was simple and turning any one of my electrical outlets into a wired connection was practically instantaneous.

UPDATE April 27, 2015 - I contacted Netgear for an explanation of why there's a security feature on these adapters and exactly what that means to me. Below is Oleg Fishel's (of customer support) response which I slightly paraphrased.

The security refers to encryption between each of the Powerline adapters on my network. A random key is generated and shared among the adapters when the security setup button is used. All traffic is then encrypted using the highly secure 128 bit AES encryption protocol that prevents any unauthorized person from accessing the communication on my network. The reason enabling this security is recommended is to prevent someone from coming into my home with another Powerline adapter and connecting directly into my network to get information or for free Internet access. Although this scenario might be rare, this may be a concern with apartment buildings and offices where electrical circuits might be shared and in the case of homes that have outdoor electrical sockets. In summary, it is best to enable security. It is especially important when the Powerline is on a shared electrical circuit where someone can come along and plug one of these adapters in and piggyback off the network.

In regard to another question I had regarding the use and installation of 16 adapters all at once, he said "The HomePlug standard (HPAV2) used by the PL1200 supports up to 16 adapters on the network working together simultaneously. So if you purchased 7 kits (14 units) in addition to the original kit, you could have a 16 node network."

title: Versatile for users with multiple USB devices
text:
I received this as a review sample and tested the claimed specifications on a few platforms. The following are my observations that, with Debbie Lee Wesselmann's excellent review, should give you a complete picture of this hub.

First, word about using this hub for charging devices. The specs on this product page at the time of this review claim that this hub will NOT charge devices. Actually, it charged my two phones and another device while I was doing other tasks. Perhaps the specs mean it is not intended to be a standalone charger. The only thing that I do NOT like is the wall wart type power supply that is approximately 3x2x2 inches. It can (and does) block adjacent plugs in my surge protector. However, I can live that that considering the functionality I get from this hub.

My favorite feature and the reason I awarded this hub five stars is the integrated electrical safeguards that protect against over voltage, over current, leakage and short circuits. This may not be a big deal for cheap peripherals like mice, but for an expensive hard drive or my Galaxy Note 3 it's a welcome feature.

If you have a computer and peripherals that are USB 3.0 compliant this hub will boost your transfer speeds significantly. For example, my new Samsung Note 3 will transfer at the 5gbps speed, but frankly I do most of my data transfers over WiFi. However, if you wanted to attach an external 3.0 hard drive to your laptop this hum will allow it to operate to it's full potential - which is lightning fast.

Set-up is easy. You literally connect the included power supply, plug it into your system's USB port and switch it on. All of platforms with which I tested it immediately recognized the hub and the things I plugged into it (which included a flash drive, mouse, two snart phones (Galaxy Note II and Note 3), and a speaker that is powered by USB.

This hub works with Windows 98 (I have an old Sony running it and this hub plugged in and worked with it), and above. I know it works with Win XP, Vista and 7 because I also tested the hub on those platforms. I do not have access to a Windows 8 system so am taking the manufacturer's word that it works on that too. If your experience is different please leave a comment.

One final feature that makes this a five star hub in my opinion is the fact that this will simultaneously support maximum data transfer of up to four high speed devices (three of which can be USB 3.0) plugged into it. Of course the host system needs to be USB 3.0 too, but the hub will sling data as fast as the host can accept it. Not all hubs will operate in this mode, and I suspect that the external power supply has something to do with that level of performance.

title: Decent price for name brand, but USB2 speed
text:
I love and trust Lexar products for my work jobs (professional grade memory cards and other solid state storage), so I had high expectations for this product. I love the build quality of this material, it's a solid feeling metallic body instead of cheap plastic, and it gives the impression of a product that will hold up to the test of time.
The price is also impressive for a name brand product with this kind of build quality. However, I had almost forgotten how slow USB2.0 can be. I'm so used to USB3 storage speeds of easily over 150MB/s, that the benchmarks on this one seem almost painfully slow at around the 20MB/s mark. But, that's par for the course with the older standard, so I can't really fault the product for it. This is a great value but you could easily get a much faster storage stick for a bit more money. I could see this being useful for someone who wants to distribute a hard-copy of something by hand and would like to order a bulk supply of durable and fast-enough but still affordable media. Otherwise, I think I'd recommend one that is USB 3 compatible at least since you can always be backwards compatible with 2.0 if necessary, but have the increased speed when available.
