title: Superb protection
text:
I received this as a free review sample. Although it's designed for notebooks, I am using it for my 10.1 inch tablet and for that it's perfect.

One of the main reasons why I rated this so highly is the protection that it affords. Part of the reason why it's so slim and light, yet protects so will is the interior has an arrangement of raised, circular shapes. They provide cushioning on both sides of the interior. They also greatly reduce shock in the event of a fall. I tested that by taking a functioning - but no longer used - Acer Aspire One notebook and dropping it from waist level inside this bag on a hard floor. There was no physical damage to the exterior of the Acer and it powered up and operated normally.

The exterior of the bag has a spongy feel that also diminished shock, so the protection is twofold. Other features I love are the heavy duty seams and zippers, and even the color scheme. On the latter, there is enough red to catch my eye when I am packing my gear and doing a visual scan to make sure I did not leave anything behind. I have 'forgotten' black cases in the past, but this one is hard to miss.

Do be aware that there is a slight chemical odor to this bag when you first unpack it. That will go away in a day or less, but it's there and you need to know about it before you make your final purchase decision. Also carefully read the part of the product description that states, ' If your laptop screen size is 14 inches, and the maximum thickness greater than 28mm (0.11"), please do not select this bag.' That will save you some frustration if your laptop is too large for this bag.

title: Sturdy and well made laptop stand/riser
text:
The EPN adjustable laptop stand is constructed of heavy-duty aluminum and feels sturdy. I tried it with both my 2017 15" Intel MB Pro and the redesigned 2020 16" MB Pro with a thicker bottom case.

I tend to lean my hands on the edge of my laptop, so I found the rise on the edge to be somewhat high when using it with my older computer, although I do appreciate having the extra fans for cooling on that model because Intel Mac Books Pro models tend to overheat.

This stand can handle the weight of both machines, with the latter coming in at over 4lbs, along with the weight of my hands leaning on it, and there was no indication of it wanting to sag or sink in any way. It will stay put at whatever angle or height you choose. At least it did for me.

I like having a slight angle when I type, and being able to raise my screen's camera to eye level so I am not looking down at it during Zoom meetings for that double chin effect. It's also convenient to have that little nook of space to tuck any cables and SSDs underneath, and out of the way.

There is about an inch to two inches of overhang on either side with larger computers, but it's not much, and both computers felt stable.

Overall, I would say it's a very good, and high-quality laptop stand. However, it is a bit smaller than I expected.

title: Truly Couldn't Be Happier {Updated 04-04-2017}
text:
I knew, due to my disability, that I was going to need to find a professional installer to install this Boss Audio Systems B9351WRC head unit and wireless reverse camera along with two replacement door speakers I decided needed replacement (and wow, they really needed replacing). The installation took approximately three hours or so. The only problem which may not be a problem but I'm a worrier. The bracket for the wireless reverse camera somewhat, but not entirely, covers the plate expiration stickers somewhat. Other than that the head unit fit as good if not better than the stock radio fit. in the dashboard.
This radio plays AM/FM stations though there's very few decent radio stations around here. The unit also plays from USB thumb drives which plugs into a port under a panel under the volume/pause/power button. I put 600+ songs on a USB 2.0 16 GB driver and it played everything as far as I could tell. There might be a couple VBR or odd format MP3 files it may not play but I haven't gotten to them yes. Nothing's refused to play and even a couple that had imbedded album artwork actually showed up but so small it was almost impossible to see and I had no idea how to make it better. The instructions in the manual were basically "Play with things and see what happens!" more than specific directions how different functions work.
What I went with, is a 32 gig micro-SD card that had the same 600+ songs the thumb drive has. But with the micro-SD card you can close the hatch under the volume and control knob which you couldn't with the thumb drive. There's also an AUX input jack for old style MP3 players and phones.
The six inch screen is sharp and crisp. The backup camera, even with a streetlight thirty feet away had more than enough light to back out of my garage. I even backed down the street a ways in almost complete darkness and could see just fine with just the reverse lights on the car. Now as long as no cops have a problem with it I'm golden.
I tried home burned CDs and while it took a few seconds longer to recognize it played them fine. I tried store bought CDs and they played right off the bat. OH! and it plays DVD discs jut fine in case my passenger wants to watch a movie as we drive. I promise I'm no dumb enough to watch a movie while I drive.
According to the installer I can leave the micro SD card in the unit all the time. So, 600+ songs anytime I want which I can shuffle or randomly pick and play songs anytime I want. I couldn't be happier. With the stock deck I'd sometimes get to my destination just as the deck decided to recognize the CD so this deck is a godsend when I really needed a new one. Now with as many songs as I can cram into a 32 gig drive. Right now I've got 687 songs and tons of free space. I may have to start buying more music and ripping some more albums from my collection to add to my micro-SD card.
So I can play hundreds, thousands of MP3 songs on a micro-SD card. I can play CDs both homemade and store bought. I can watch DVDs on a pretty sharp (all settings can be changed in the system) the dimmer is a bit bright until it goes off completely but it's not too bad or too bright. There's a user setting EQ option as well as several other preset settings to choose from. There are options to add sound effects such as large hall, church, cavern, etc. I avoided them entirely and set my own EQ settings with the loudness off. The new speakers sound great for high end and midrange. The stock back speakers add some needed bass.
All in all? This is an affordable head unit with all the features and functions one could ask for. It comes with a remote that I'm not sure I'm even going to keep anywhere in the car. Anything you need to do can be done on the deck and no one's sitting in the back seat of a '07 Hyundai Accent, seriously. So the remote is useless but amusing.
I love this unit, the backup cam is awesome, The many ways to play music. The fit and finish, it's close to perfect.
This a little long and meandering review but I really like this radio and I'm glad I replaced the door speakers and went with a professional installer who's basically given me a lifetime warranty on his labor. I couldn't be happier.

Update 04-04-2017: It's been nearly six months since I had this head unit and backup camera installed. Radio reception is still bad, I still despise listening to radio so that's no big deal. Have kept a micro SD card loaded with hundreds of songs installed. Turn the unit on it automatically defaults to that. Everything is still working fine. Professional installation was worth the money.

title: Not fantastic but OK
text:
If you expect things to look like daylight, you'll be disappointed. It is far better than an old Russian unit I have which was an early generation light amplification unit, (green glow type). What you have here is a lot like a B&W security camera with an IR illuminator built into a hand held portable unit.

As some of the other reviews indicate, in the beginning it will seem somewhat cumbersome and clunky getting used to the controls and finding the most pleasing contrast settings. Takes a while, but once you get used to it, it gets a lot easier to make it work like you want it too.

One problem is that if you are just moving around in very low light and want to take a better look at things, it takes time for your eyes to adjust from darkness to the brightness in the viewfinder and then going back. The best way to use it is looking through it for an extended time scanning the area of interest, keeping your eye on the eyepiece. Different types of scenes will take some adjustment to optimize the appearance. Some things reflect light better than others so the best scenario is watching a particular area for an extended period. Once your eyes adjust and you get the contrast dialed in, it works pretty well. The IR illuminators are surprisingly pretty powerful. At short distances the high powered one will "wash out" what you're looking at, but it does seem to reach out pretty good. The claimed 600 feet is a bit of a stretch except under the most ideal of conditions. If you have some ambient light, I think it is better without it. But in really dark country night where you can't see your hand in front of your face, it does a great job of lighting things up.

My feelings on it are mixed. The basic idea of a monocular fits that role of "occasional use" where you want a quick better look at something, but I think that is asking too much from such a device. Plan on spending some time to get a better look at things because your eyes need adjustment time. Once you get the unit dialed in for the scene your watching, it will work pretty well. It's not cheap by any means, but it does work and it's a nice compact package. If you want really high performance night optics, plan on spending a lot more. It will definitely allow you to see reasonable well in darkness, but you have to fiddle with it. A lot has to do with the application. The pros and cons have given me some ideas about building a special purpose device.

Overall, it's a big improvement on some of the early night vision technology. The more I use it, the more I like it and learn tricks about using it effectively. I am happy with it, but for the average person with little experience with night vision, your expectations may not be met and that's why I'm giving it 3 stars. You will need a little patience to go through the learning curve using it.

title: Charged my Lenovo right up!
text:
I have a discarded 7th generation Intel Lenovo I was given from an office to scrub and give to someone who's working from home during the coronavirus shutdown here in NY. Problem is, they gave it to me without the charger and I can't go back to the office and get it until they reopen the doors. Thankfully, it uses a standard USB-C shaped plug to charge. I have plenty of phones and tablets that use that, but apparently laptops need the more robust Power Delivery standard, and not the lower power of USB phone chargers.
Amazon to the rescue, with this excellent replacement PD adapter. I love that modern computers and devices are starting to embrace a standard like this going forward- Macbooks and PC laptops both use this now, and it's even backwards compatible with USB devices like phones and tablets (the reverse isn't true- I couldn't use my phone charger on this laptop, but this laptop's PD charger can charge my phone).
This device worked great for getting that Lenovo back up and running, very appreciative for a future full of standards!

title: Innovative design and works flawlessly with ipad 6th gen
text:
I'm relatively happy with this pencil. It is certainly better than many of the off-brands claiming to do the same thing. There are a few things I don't love, so I will get those out of the way first. The pencil in perfectly rounded and very slick, so it is a danger that it will roll away or fall from the desk or other surface you are using it at, unlike the Logitech Crayon. As a comparison, this pencil is much more comfortable to hold than the Crayon, but it feels more breakable.

I also don't love that the extra charging piece (converter) that you get is so tiny, as is the cap, since that makes me feel like I am always in danger of losing these small parts off of the counter where they charge. (If you have kids, then you know what I mean about things sprouting legs and disappearing.)

Otherwise, I love it. This pencil is highly responsive to the touchscreen of the ipad (I'm using the 6th gen) and it works great with note taking apps, beautifully with procreate, and also as a general scrolling tool or selection pointer. The battery lasts for a decent while and I am happy that there is now a way to charge it, without having to have the pencil sticking out the bottom of the ipad, as that just seemed like a recipe for disaster.

The pencil feels like it is made of good quality materials. it is heavy, but not obtrusively so, and the points are nice. The pencil feels sturdy to the grip ad like it isn't cheaply manufactured as some of the other pencils do. This is more than just your average stylus.

Although, I admit, when I first saw the price I thought it was a bit ridiculous, after owning this product for a while, I now see the difference between it and the competitors and I do believe it was worth the investment. Plus, you can order tips for it directly from amazon for a reasonable price, which, in my opinion makes it even more worth the money. I have had a hard time finding tips for the crayon without going to the logitech site or other outside sources. I prefer to do all my shopping at once, so this works for me.

I would definitely recommend this product to other ipad users, as it has changed the way I work for the positive and sped up my productivity. It was easy to connect, the packaging is beautiful as always, and the instructions were clear and helpful. I find myself becoming more and more attached to Apple products as time goes on.

title: If you are in the Samsung camp this is great
text:
There are more than enough helpful reviews, product specs and Q&A, so I am going to focus on this tablet for folks who are upgrading from another Android tablet, and especially another Samsung. I'll say up front that the biggest reason [for me, anyway] is the extra screen real estate and resolution.

I had a small surprise in that mine did not come with Amazon apps pre-installed like they did on my [[ASIN:B00D029NNA Samsung Galaxy Tab 3 (10.1-Inch, White) 2013 Model]] that it replaced. Locating the App Store application so I could install all of the applications that I have purchased was a bit of a hassle, but I finally got that resolved. Like my older Samsung tablet this one is a little less than spectacular when it comes to streaming music to a speaker via bluetooth. I do not know why Samsung cannot get it right on tablets because I have never experienced any issues streaming on my Note II and Note 3 phones.

Another issue of which you need to be aware is this tablet is thin and flexible. I knew that in advance and purchased a [[ASIN:B00KCDBD2E Samsung Galaxy Note Pro 12.2-inch Case Cover]], which in my opinion is one of the better cases for this tablet. The hard shell part of the case into which you insert the tablet provides a rigid casing that allows zero flex. No matter which case you ultimately select I strongly recommend that you get one.

You may have issues with some apps if you opt to install an SD card to expand your storage, or if you are moving an SD card from another tablet to this one. The KitKat version of the operating system will not write to SD cards under certain conditions. There is a free fix called SD KitKat Fixer by JRummy Apps that you can get from the Play Store. I highly recommend it. As a side note, I had no issues with this SD card: [[ASIN:B00N2ROG9O PNY Turbo Performance 64GB High Speed MicroSDXC Class 10 UHS-1]]. title: Excellent GPS Navigator
text:
I bought a Garmin Nuvi 1450LMT for my wife for Christmas, after researching the market and trying to find a unit with the best balance of features against the price. I have two Garmin hand-held GPS receivers that I use for geocaching so I am comfortable with Garmin's GPS products, so I settled on this unit feeling confident that it would meet my wife's needs in a GPS for the car. I was right.

This particular Nuvi has a large, bright display that is easily readable in direct sunlight, which was one area of concern for me. I have seen some electronic devices that are not readable in bright light such as direct sunlight and I was pleased to see that Garmin took care to ensure that the Nuvi would fare well in any lighting.

When we first put the Nuvi into service we were unsure how long it would take before it would acquire satellites and be ready to navigate. Pleasantly, even before leaving the garage the Nuvi found the satellites and was ready to navigate in a short time, usually less than a minute.

The Nuvi has a clear, understandable voice when she (?) speaks which is a big help. The maps are very easy to read and interpret, giving very clear indications of not just what roads to take but what lane to be in while navigating so as to be ready for turns, merges and more. It's very much like having someone give precise directions and pointing to a map right there in the car.

The display shows a lot of important and useful information, including time to next event (turn, exit, etc.), speed limit, travel speed and more. One of the most important is the traffic delay indicator, something that comes in handy when trying to deal with rush hour traffic or traveling around a major interstate exchange such as the DC Capitol Beltway system. It is nice, too, that is shows the speed limit and then marks the travel speed, turning said travel speed red when it is greater than the speed limit.

One of the few complaints I have about the Nuvi is that, when there is a long distance to go until the next turn or exit, the Nuvi is silent and says nothing at all until roughly one mile away from the next turn/exit. When this happens it is almost a shock to suddenly have a voice in the car. Given a choice, I personally would prefer that the Nuvi speak up every 10 minutes or so to avoid that surprise.

One very weak spot I have encountered with windshield-mounted devices is the actual suction cup used. All too frequently, the cup is either very difficult to get stick on to the windshield or it does not hold well enough, letting go very unexpectedly while driving. Garmin did a very good job with their mount, making it super easy to attach to the windshield and making it adhere very well. I have never had any suction-cup-attached device attach and adhere as easily and predictably as the Nuvi.

One reason I chose this specific Nuvi is for the lifetime map and traffic updates. To buy these as an after thought is very expensive though they are very important if you want the GPS receiver to remain useful.

Updating the Nuvi is easy (though, understandably, it is a time-consuming process). Connecting the Nuvi to a Windows 7 64-bit laptop the OS immediately recognized the device and installed drivers. A quick visit to Garmin's website resulted in a browser plug-in being installed and shortly after that I was downloading the updates for the Nuvi. The updates are large, of course, and this is the reason the updates take a while, but the process itself is practically painless.

Some reviewers complain of the Nuvi not charging and navigating at the same time. That has not been our experience. When plugged in ours has worked just fine.

Our experience with the Nuvi 1450LMT has been very good and we're delighted with it. It does an excellent job with navigation, it's easy to read and understand and the map updates are the icing on the cake.

title: Bluetooth 4.2 and no true ANC
text:
I am reviewing the ‘TruSound TruWireless Noise Cancelling Earbuds | True Wireless Earbuds with Charging Case for Buds and Phone | Comfortable, Secure Fit | Immersive Stereo Sound, Deep Bass | Easy Touch Control Operation’.
Based on my experience thus far I would like to share my thoughts.

Pros:
1- The sound is decent but compared to other Wireless Earbuds that I have tried, these are pretty average.
2- The case is rechargeable via the included 18650 battery. This allows you to have extra 18650 batteries on hand which is an interesting feature.
3- It comes with extra ear tips.
4- It comes with a mini USB cable and even a USB type A to Mini USB adapter.
5- Aesthetically the earbuds look nice, feel comfortable and don’t protrude much when wearing them.
6- They stay in place quite well and do not randomly fall out.
7- Earbuds are held in place magnetically when in the case charging.
8- They pair up real fast and very easy. I have had no issues at all with pairing.

Cons:
1- I ordered these based on the description stating “active noise reduction is also a standout feature of TruSound ear buds, ensuring a distraction-free audio experience”. I took this as they had ANC or Active Noise Control. This is not the case. These “isolate” the outside sounds via the ear tip inserted into the ear canal. If you get the right tip fit, they do “isolate” the outside sounds but just not as expected.
2- No USB type C. In my opinion all new devices should have USB C charging.
3- The case is a bit bulky due to the fact that it uses the 18650 battery.
4- The case is plastic and uses two plastic tabs to snap the lid closed. The design makes it really hard to open the case once it’s snapped shut. I am worried that I will break the plastic tabs at which point I would need to use a rubber band to keep the lid closed.
5- The Stand-By time is not the greatest. I fully charged the 18650 battery with my own charger when I first got the Earbuds. I used the Earbuds briefly while initially testing them and when I went back a couple of weeks later to try them again, the battery was already dead. I have other earbuds that have this same issue. I should be able to fully charge my earbuds, keep them in my backpack for a few weeks and have them ready to go when I want to use them.
6- No IPX rating? Pretty much all of the newer Earbuds these days have some kind of waterproof rating. It’s not advertised so I am not really sure if they are.
7- No Bluetooth 5.0? These have Bluetooth 4.2+EDR which isn’t bad, but there are sync issues when watching YouTube, Netflix ect. It’s not bad, but it’s noticeable and I could not use these to watch videos for too long.

Overall these TruSound Earbuds are average, and I feel that compared to the flooded market of True Wireless Earbuds these are a bit overpriced. With that said, I do like these but, I do feel there could be some improvements made that would ultimately increase the value.

The connector bases are reinforced at each end of the wire which really help hold all of the wires in place even if you have to bend and twist it to fit it within the plug. The plugs have a protective rubber boot guard that protects the clip on the plug - this becomes very important when snaking the cable through walls and tight spaces. Prior to doing this I wrap the boot and plug with a small piece of electrical tape to make sure I don’t unintentionally snag anything.

I love the white PVC shielding on this cable - not only is it durable and will help the cable withstand damage but it can be run along a wall and then painted to match the wall color.

I used this 100 foot cable to run between my router to a PoE switch that branches to several power and transmit data to and from one zone of my security cameras - a primary connection where speed and a reliable relay is critical - and I’ve been nothing but impressed by this product.

title: I like to move it, move it ....
text:
Logitech says that their products are designed to move you, and this mouse sure lives up to that promise. Seconds after opening the beautifully packaged box, I was up and running and you can do it too. The instructions tell you everything you need to know, from how to put in the batteries (2 x AAA, included), how to turn it on (power button on the bottom), and where to insert the Nano receiver (USB port). For more features, Windows users can install the software included, and Mac users can go get the download.

Installation takes quite a few minutes, but once that's over, your mouse gets super powers, and can scroll from side to side (perfect for those extra wide pages), help you search the internet with the push of a button, and also navigate backwards and forwards between internet pages. How cool is that?

Here's all the OTHER good stuff about the VX Nano:

1. It's cordless
2. It's compact and cute, and oh so ergonomic (at least for small hands)
3. The MicroGear Precision Scroll Wheel (fancy name for the wheel thing between the buttons that you scroll with) has two modes: Hyper-Fast, for when you need to scroll down long documents at warp speed, and Ratchet, for when you don't have a long, long way to run. You switch between them by simply pressing down on the wheel. (Tilting the same wheel left or right gives you the side by side scrolling once you've installed the software)
4. There's a LED light to tell you when your batteries need changing
5. There's a compartment at the bottom of the mouse to store the Nano-receiver securely. Alternately, you can just leave the little thing attached to your notebook USB port.
6. The package includes a nice Logitech zippered case to keep your mouse snug as a bug in a rug.
7. You can use it on your desktop machine too. It comes with an "extension cord" that you plug into the USB port of your CPU, and insert the Nano-receiver into the little gizmo at the other end, and you're all set. I didn't even have to evict the regular mouse that was already living on my mouse pad.

Believe me, after you've gone Nano you'll never want to go back to cords again.

text:
I got this set of headphones to go with our panasonic phone system in your house for our landline. Many times we get power failures so we still keep a landline. But when the power is not out, I like to use our landline for calls. Our system uses bluetooth for headsets so this is where these came in handy.

HOW ARE THESE?
These headphones are red. I love the color. they seem sturdier than expected, There is a slot in the headphones which you can insert a MicroSD card so you don't HAVE to use a player with the headphones (like phone or MP3, etc). These are bluetooth as well and have a volume button.

My family is a bunch of ear phone addicted fanatics. We have some of the best and some of the worst and everything in between. One of our kids, a daughter, grabbed the headphones to try them and loved them so much, she is getting a pair for her pottery studio to listen to her own music.

I did not think these were too loud. They were controlled easily through the volume control on the headphones.

ADJUSTABLE?

DO THEY BLOCK NOISE?
These do block outside noise well which is another great feature of these.

VOICE?
So far the voice works well with these when I use them on the phone.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a decent set of headphones that are comfortable, block outside noise well, and do well on the phone for both listening and voice as well as music, these are a great choice. I love the red color too.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. These are great, affordable and work well so far. I will update if anything changes.

title: Good, Inexpensive Magnification Lenses
text:
The primary lens I have on my camera is a good 18mm-55mm lens and it does great for capturing images that are a foot or more away. When I get much closer than that my camera is unable to focus properly and I end up with a crummy shot and I either have to give up or back up so that it can focus – not what I want most of the time. These magnifying lenses are a good solution, but there are somethings you have to keep in mind when using them.

I will start with a statement that should be obvious: make sure you have the correct lens size when you are purchasing add-on lenses like this set. This particular set can be used only with a lens where the thread size is 55mm. If you have a lens that has a different sized thread, you should consider looking for this kit in a different thread size. You can use a ring adapter, but getting the right size at the start is better.

There are four lenses in this kit, a 1x, 2x, 4x and 10x lens, each increasing in power as the numbers suggest. You can somewhat view these as magnifying glasses for your camera, but that metaphor is not completely accurate. They do magnify the image for you, but they allow a closer shot as well and you can get very close to your subject when you have one of these attached to your lens. Perhaps a better way to describe them is to realize that they make your camera very nearsighted and your camera can see close-up well and distance not at all when using these lenses.

The main thing to remember about them is that as they go up the scale in strength they introduce a lot more edge distortion. This is most obvious with the 10x lens. If you take this lens and hold it so that you can see things through it clearly in the center, you cannot help but notice a large area around the edge of the lens that is distorted. The effect is less then you get it close to something on which you wish to focus but it is something to keep in mind. If there is too much distortion, use a less powerful magnification lens.

These particular lenses have a little bit of heft to them but they are not what I would consider heavy. Because they are glass they are a bit more substantial than resin or plastic lenses.

Overall, these are nice lenses. I have been able to use them for taking very close shots that I otherwise would not be able to take with my camera, such as ridge detail on a penny or dot patterns on magazine print. These are not real-world examples but they definitely show off the capabilities of such lenses. If you are looking for good magnification lenses for your camera, this is a good set that works well. Just make sure you have the right thread size before you buy.

text:
TLDR; 5 stars for functionality and effectiveness. Gave it 3 stars because it died after 11 months of daily use.
Loved this cooling pad -- I used it under my gaming laptop on which I gamed and did data analysis/coding, and it kept my computer cool. Without it, my laptop would quickly reach over 82 C, with the cooling pad it was kept right around 70 C.
I bought it in January of 2021 and it lasted until December 2021, almost a year. I loved it so much I'm considering rebuying it, but I wish I knew why it crapped out on me. It's not expensive or anything, and I did use it for 8-10 hours a day (and a couple times I forgot to turn it off so it was on all night), but still... I wish it had lasted longer. title: Perfect replacements for my G930, some people must not know how to install them
text:
My old G930 ear pads were flaking like crazy after several years of daily, all-day use, and I was hesitant to buy these at first because several people said they were too small. But I figured it's only $5, so it's worth a shot.

They arrived this morning and all I can think of is that whoever thought these were too tight or too small wasn't putting them on correctly. Maybe they thought they were just push-on instead of realizing that they have a flap (just like the ones that come with the headset) that needs to be lifted to go over the plastic part of the earpiece. That's what actually holds these things in place, people - otherwise they'd just fall off! Or maybe people aren't actually matching up the shape correctly. Either way - if you install them CORRECTLY, they fit perfectly.

These things are the correct size and I took some photos to compare the old Logitech-made pads with these. I also measured separately and they are the exact same size. If you take the time to look at how the original ear pads come off, you'll know exactly how to put these replacements on, and it'll take you all of about 10-15 seconds per ear pad.

These are virtually indistinguishable from the originals. I put these on and at first they seemed a little firmer than the original ear pads. However, I actually have a total of three G930 headsets (different purposes), so I was able to compare the feel of these ear pads to the original ear pads on one of the lesser-used, newer headsets. Again, pretty much identical - I guess they just get softer with use. Still, they are very comfortable even in their brand-new state, and I'm happy not to finish the day with black flakes on the sides of my face again.

PHOTOS:
I have three photos, two that are just comparing the back and front of the old pad to the replacement pad (and showing where the flap is that some people are apparently missing). The third photo is just showing the headset with one pad replaced so you can actually see that it looks pretty much the same as the original when installed correctly on the headset.

text:
I've tried a similar box to this one, I'm familiar with the concept and I really REALLY wanted to like it. But sadly, it needs some more quality control.
I've always loved the idea of a Android powered head unit, I've seen aftermarket ones sold for popular car models, and I was hoping this would give me that functionality without having to replace my radio. But sadly, I can't use this.
For starters, it takes a long time to boot. That means you are first going to be greeted with your car's normal radio display, connected to my phone over bluetooth, and then once I've already pulled out of my driveway and started down the road, THEN it finally shows up on my display.
That is, if it displays at all. It seems to do this thing in which is boots up, checks for display info, then reboots in the proper resolution. The instructions even imply it does this. The problem is, most of the time my carplay radio will freeze up when it does this. Not only will it get stuck and not display anything, but my radio locks up and MY TIME RESETS. It's the strangest thing. After looking at reviews here, it seems at least one other reviewer said it make his car radio go crazy, so I don't really understand what this thing is doing that might cause that, but at least it isn't just me!
And even when it DOES work, it has a similar problem to other Android-powered adapters like this: it is a cold boot every time, with no idea what the time/date is. This is a major issue because if I don't supply an internet connection, the mini computer in this reverts to the wrong date/time on the display which is SUPER annoying. Ideally, they should design this to have a small battery to "sleep" like a phone, so it can retain time/date function and wake up faster than a complete boot. The way this is designed right now is really a subpar experience, assuming you can get it to boot up at all on your system.

title: Wow!  No more, "What'd they say?"
text:
Thank you to all you wonderful Amazon reviewers. I'd never purchased a Bose product before, with the exception of possibly headphones at some point in time. We know the Bose sound is legendary, but I never really needed a Bose radio or CD player. The Solo caught my eye because I love my flat screen TV, but the speakers are only so-so at best. Like many other reviewers, I have trouble understanding some dialogue on TV. It's fine as long as there is someone around to annoy endlessly by asking "what did they say," but watching TV alone, I miss big chunks of the story & plot. The doctor says it's just "one of the vestiges of old age." Oh. Another one of those. Thanks, doc.

So, I wondered if the Solo speaker might help, and thanks to all my hard-of-hearing contemporaries here (or should I say THANK YOU), I saw all the reviews promising that I wouldn't have to ask "what?" every 2 minutes any more. I could jump for joy after hooking up the speaker and giving it a listen, although my doctor would probably advise against it. On my TV, unlike some others mentioned here, the TV speakers work along with the Solo speaker, so it's easy to mute the Solo and hear the difference between it and the TV speakers. It's amazing. The sound is rich, and big, and crisp in a way that my surround-sound system isn't. Most importantly, in answer to my wildest hopes, I can understand every single word of dialogue, even Christian Bale mumbling behind his Batman mask. No kidding. The Bose speaker took 20 years off my age, and reduced my waist by four inches. Ok, I am kidding about that.

As if all that isn't reason enough to get one of these gems, it has to be the simplest piece of electronics to hook up, set up & operate. It's simply two cords, one to the power outlet, and the other to the TV. They include all the cables in the box: digital optical, HDMI & RCA. Plug, plug, power. That's all. The remote is four buttons: power, mute, up & down volume. It's hard to believe that such intricate, complex sound can come from such a simple device. Thank you, Mr. Bose, wherever you are. Not only would I highly recommend this to my friends, I think everyone with a flat-screen TV owes it to themselves to get one. Seriously. This is the audio-visual experience I thought I was already having with 5.1 surround system.

title: Excellent earbuds, with a few issues
text:
These are excellent earbuds. The sound is open, spacious, clear, and pleasant. I have listened to music for hours on these, and my ears don't get tired at all. Here's what I like and don't like.

The sound is open, with sparkling high frequencies and tight, precise lows. The highs sparkle so much that some listeners might think that the sound is too bright. I'm pretty happy with it. The midrange is clear, voices very easy to understand. The lows are not at all boomy, and not as powerful as earbuds that advertise things like "deep powerful bass." But the bass is solid, and for music that has lots of bass energy, these earbuds let it all come through. Overall I think the sound is very accurate, uncolored, and not at all leading to ear-fatigue. I'm very, very pleased with the sound. Pretty sweet.

The product packaging is pretty silly. It's completely overdesigned, with an outer box that separates to allow you to get to an inner tray. I puzzled over the package for about 3 minutes trying to figure out how to get into it, before I discovered a diagram on the side panel of the box. After I successfully extricated the earbuds ...

The plug has a novel oversized swivel that allows it to attach either straight or at right angles to your sound source. It's clever, but I prefer plugs that are visibly more protective of the cord. There's no bendy thing where the cord joins the oversized plug, so I'm concerned that over time the wire might break at the join. We'll see. Whether the swivel is straight or right angled, it's a large plug that I think might be uncomfortably large with some phones or MP3 players. I'm using it with a laptop computer, and it sometimes gets in the way a bit.

In the middle of the cable is a volume control barrel. Just like the plug, it's a classy-looking silvery metal color. But what it earns in form it loses in function, as the volume control slider is very difficult to operate. I have some earbuds that cost only 20% what these cost, and they have a volume control slider that very much easier to use than we have here. Nevertheless, the slider does a good job of controlling the volume when I can get my fingers to operate it.

The earbuds themselves are interesting because they have rather large metal pieces that support the part that fits in the ear. My first reaction was that they would be uncomfortably heavy, or that they might fall out of the ear, but they work remarkably well. I've listened for hours, and had to reposition the earbuds only occasionally.

The cable is typical plastic-coated cable that's heavier than some other earbuds have. It feels rugged, and it doesn't tangle easily. A cloth-wrapped cable would be much nicer still.

The earbuds come with a case that stores the earbuds and the included airplane adaptor. It's a rather large case -- it doesn't fit well into your pocket (for traveling), but does protect the earbuds very well. There's also a second very small drawstring bag, which I assume is for traveling, but it's just a bit too small and stiff to do that job well.

Pros. Feels light compared to the Ottobox Defender on my Air 2. A very nice feel to it. Yes it makes it bulky, but not heavy. That was a big surprise. I didn't weigh the two, and the specs indicate the Defender and Lifeproof weigh about the same, but it just feels better in my hands than the Defender. The Defender does have a stand though.
Very easy to install and uninstall. Lifeproof provides a plastic key to open the case easily. Simple but wonderful.
Reasonable protection. I have the Apple Smartcover and Smartcase on my 12.9 IPad Pro. I like it. It's very light, has a stand, but does
not offer much in the way of protection. It's also very expensive, for what it is.

Cons. I was shocked that it does not have a screen protector. On the plus side, not having a screen protector maximizes enjoyment of the screen. Nothing to peel off either. If you add a screen protector, you increase the risk of leakage. If water isn't a concern, then add a screen protector. A stand feature would have been nice.

Other: The directions say to perform a water test before the first use, every 3 months, and before an expected water inflow, such as boating. A you tube video was very helpful. Otherwise, I would have thought I was missing a screen protector. There are some good amateur videos demonstrating an IPad Air installation. Same process.

Pair the headphones to your phone and hold the middle button down for 5 seconds to power down. All you gotta do then is hold the middle button down to turn on until the lady says "power on", let go of the button when she says this -- and boom -- "head phones connected". Very very easy.

Only complaint is VERY VERY rarely you won't hear anything when you hold down the middle button and you have to plug the charger in and press the middle button 9 times and repeat this process until you hear "power on". Usually takes a few tries but this has rarely ever happened so I still give 5 stars for these headphones.

Don't listen to these reviews and go out and try it for yourself. They really are the GOAT and I have tried a lot of headphones.

title: Best Wear OS for true Android users, but not perfect
text:
I will avoid the facts that this watch is outdated at launch by its hardware (processor). That, coupled with retail and even discounted price also are out of step with the competition. These two big gripes aside. The watch is good and likely the best choice going into 2023 for pure Android Wear OS users (not looking at Apple or Tizen overlay users.)

Its not perfect and Pixel users will benefit the most when paired to this watch. Its lost most of the lag recent watches from other Wear OS brands. Has all the sensors the majority of buyers could want based on watch tech right now. It swipes, it plays well with the apps made for it. It gives you the info you ask of it. There are even a few nice 3rd part accessories now to avoid Google Gouging for proprietary bands. And there are few quirks I hope they iron out soon. Mainly, when the phone is in Bedtime Mode. Make the watch do it too, or add that Zen Mode feature to the watch also. It sucks to have animals tripping the security cameras outside dinging on my wrist and killing my sleep score. The snooze/do not disturb button on watch fails too easily and you have turn it on/off manually everytime.

As many claim, the battery sucks. Sort of. I can go up to 36+ hours on a slow day, and many others can too. It will depend on too many factors to list. But basically your popularity with notifications and thinking you need the screen always on are the biggest battery hurdles. Most can get use to touch to wake. And maybe only having text, phone, front door doorbell and one email be allowed to bother your watch with notifications. Do you really need to know what cousin Billy had at Dairy Queen when he posts the same pic/vid on Facebook, Instagram, Tic Toc and YouTube, etc. Find a nice balance of wrist information along with what sensors you need checking if you are still alive. You can start the day and track everything till the next morning when you charge it again while you shower and get the next day started. It charges quickly. And most other Wear OS watches have the same daily charge requirements. Nobody on Wear OS is winning on battery. Or Turn every setting all the way up and have a spare charger puck ready for a mid day juice. If you go that route. I suggest a quick release band to ease the removal of the watch.

So, its not up to the level or price of the Ultra Apple Watch. And if you don't care for Samsung. Your love for stock Android will eventually lead you back to this watch. Unless you forgo ECG sensors. The price will drop soon. Cases are minimizing the fragility of an ALL glass jelly bean design. But when comes to keeping your phone pocketed and yet still have info relayed in a useful way. Pixel Watch is the best current albeit not perfect solution for now.

Let me be honest here. My post is very subjective, but I'm going to post it as honestly as possible for the benefit of those like-minded people.

The unit itself is really great. Ultimately I returned it because I was not working out for me. It's as simple as that.

The more complex nature of my unhappiness may come from the fact that I am a long-time Apple product user who really, really tried to go beyond the Apple brand. The Kindle Fire is a GREAT device - but when replacing an iPad it really didn't compare for me. Things sync'd seamlessly with my Apple products, but not the Kindle (I didn't expect it to, but I did miss that). It took a bit of relearning how to navigate the Kindle, but that was fine (and very easy to do). The image was crisp, the response quick, the actual unit solid. It felt nice to hold in my hand, and the Origami case was a nice touch. But when push came to shove I ended up returning a perfectly good device because I just wasn't in love with it. I missed many of the features and uses that came naturally from my iPad. I may need to spend a bit more to get it, but if it is what truly works well for me without any sacrifice (other than about 200 dollars more)... then perhaps I should just save up and get the iPad.

It's embarrassing to admit all this, but it's true. I thought switching would be easy. The reviews are great - and the unit itself is truly great. But it just wasn't the right match for me and for my purposes. I'm heading back to the iPad.

title: They Look Better Than They Sound
text:
I have had several pairs of Panasonic headphones and I regard them as a budget-grade phone that is better than generic but leaves room for improvement. I was hopeful that these phones would be better and would distinguish themselves as better than average. Unfortunately they do not and they suffer from the same issues I have had with other Panasonic phones in the past. They're certainly not bad, but there is some room for improvement.

First off, these look great, though I would stop short of calling them "retro" in appearance. They're styled to be retro-looking, but they betray their youth in the plastic details. That said, they have the cool factor that they are going for and the will stand out over most run-of-the-miss headphones than you'll find most people using.

One of the problems I have with these is strictly a personal preference. When I use over-the-ear phones like these, I want a phone that clamps down tight over my ear and applies some pressure. This does two things for me - it cuts down on the chances that they'll slip off when I look down, and it cuts sound leakage when I am listening to something. These are a more relaxed, loose fit, and this is not to my tastes. There's a good number of users that will be very happy with the way these fit, and as I said this is a preference, so I cannot say this is a fault. It's something to keep in mind, though. Aside from the tightness (or lack thereof), the pads and band are soft and these can be worn for a long while without issue.

These are Bluetooth phones, so I used them to connect to my Android tablet. They connected very quickly and without any real issues. I have no complaints there. They stay connected once paired and the range is good to at least 20-30 feet from the source which is good.

Where these headphones fail, though, is in the most important area - the sound profile. The highs are slightly muddy though not unacceptably so. The bass is present and not overdriven which to me is a very good thing. But, the midrange is not right at all, and as a result the music sounds like it is coming out of a tunnel when I am listening. Yes, I could fix this with an equalizer, but many people will not think to do that or do not have access to one. This is a familiar issue I have had with Panasonic phones, and unfortunately these do not correct the issue.

For speech, these sound just fine.

These are interesting phones and they look good. For those liking a loose fit, they're going to be very comfortable. However, there is an issue in the sound profile that anyone serious about their music will not be able to help but notice, and at the price point it's a more serious issue than if these were inexpensive (budget) headphones.

title: A big improvement over the Smokin' Buds
text:
When my iPod buds finally died on me, I decided I wanted in-ear 'phones. However, I was short on cash, so I decided against the Shures, Etymotics, and the like. I saw the Smokin' Buds in a store for $[...], and gave them a shot.

First off, the sound wasn't terrible. It was at least on par with the Apple buds. I had problems with the fact that the sleeves wouldn't stay put in my ears for any reason, slipping out almost as soon as I'd inserted them. In addition, the cord was rather thin, and anytime it rubbed against my clothing, or heaven forfend, my jacket's zipper, it would create enough noise to drown out my music. The nail in the coffin was the small chrome ring on the left bud. I had foolishly thought it was structural, but when it popped loose it turned out to be merely ornamental.

I took them back for a refund, and sent off a letter to the company expressing my dissatisfaction with their product. Much to my surprise, I was invited to try another pair, with the promise that improvements had been made and I was sure to find them more to my liking.

The buds that arrived in the mail were the Full Metal Jackets. The difference in construction is night and day. Where the bulk of the Smokin' Buds is plastic, these are aluminum. The sleeves never slip from my ears. The cord is far more durable, and thicker as well.

The sound was quite boomy when I first tried them, but I let them run at high volume for 24 hours on static to loosen them up. This helped quite a bit, and the sound continues to improve. It's still bottom-heavy, but turning off the EQ function on my nano helped balance it out. I really like that I can run my nano at half volume and still hear everything clearly. In fact, I would caution against running them at full volume while they're in, as I'm certain one would suffer hearing damage. My battery life has improved tremendously. I'm very happy with the sound and the comfort of these buds. I can't think of a better set of earphones for the price... and the warranty is first-rate.

9 February 2008: I sent my FMJ's back for a warranty repair, which turned out to be a warranty replacement. The jack on my 9mm FMJ's had developed a short, and was causing the left 'bud to cut in and out.

I received an RMA number within moments of contacting them at their website, [...], and while I paid for shipping the 'buds back, they replaced them immediately, free of charge. Not only did they replace them with a new set, they sent the 11mm FMJ's. The jack is a bit longer, in order to provide better strain relief, I suppose. Otherwise, the build quality is identical. More importantly, the sound is far better balanced top to bottom, and while the bass is still great, it no longer dominates the sound spectrum as it did on my 9mm's.

In short, the 9's are really good, and you can't get anything better (in my opinion) at the price, but the 11's are worth the extra money. All the things that made my experience such a positive one with the 9's is improved with the 11's. Definitely a 5-star rating.

title: Beefy, portable power that works with my Pinecil soldering iron
text:
This portable power bank is quite beefy and has some real heft. It weighs 2.5 pounds without the case but with this heft, you get some real power.

It sports two Type-A ports at 18w max, a type-c port at 45W max, and a 110V AC output at 120W max. The type-a ports are fairly standard and isn't anything out of the ordinary. The AC output should be enough to power most laptops but you would still need your laptop's power adapter.

The type-c port was why I wanted this device. It can be used to charge this power pack at 45w, which means you can fully charge this thing fairly quickly (sorry, I haven't timed it). The 45w output of the port allows me to run my pinecil soldering iron at full wattage, which means that my soldering iron can go to 300 degrees within 10 seconds.

Another use I had for this thing was that I had a skunk that was breaking into the crawl space under my house and I needed a camera to keep an eye on the movements of the skunk. Rather than purchasing a motion sensing camera, I was able to take one of my WIFI cameras and power it with this thing. The battery not only lasted the entire night, it only went down by one light (out of 4 lights total).

Two things I wish this power supply had: An adjustable DC output with a barrel connector. This would allow charging of laptops without having to plug in the laptop's adapter. I would also have liked the type-c port to support 100w because many laptops that charge by Type-C require at least 60w output. Those laptops will trickle charge from this power bank but will complain about it being under-powered.

title: Another top notch product from Sony
text:
I'll admit, I'm a fan of Sony. I've owned all sorts of things from the brand, from the aftermarket stereo in my car to my professional camera equipment I use at work. They just make reliably good products. However I've mostly owned Samsung television sets just because it's what I had access to on a more regular basis.
I was therefore excited to try out this TV and see how it compared. To be honest, I really REALLY like Sony's color science. It's part of why I prefer their camera equipment, and it shows on this display. The contrast ratio and dynamic range are everything I wanted it to be and more. The skin tones as well, however the average consumer probably wouldn't notice or care about these things. Where the big differences lie in major TV brands these days is going to be features. The latest crop of Smart TVs have so many bells and whistles, you practically don't need anything other than an internet connection anymore. Unlike Samsung's UI which has embraces Amazon's Fire Stick style UI, Sony has gone the Google TV route. There are pros and cons to both approaches, although I think perhaps arguably there isn't as much free included content as Samsung (Samsung actually includes free live TV channels via "Samsung TV", which Sony does not have). But for all the content I actually WANT to see, Netflix, Prime, Disney+ etc, it works perfectly!

So why only 4 stars? This isn't the fault of Sony's TV, but I really wish they'd make it easier to spot and turn off... I really REALLY hate the default motion smoothing (aka "soap opera effect") that all the big brands use these days. As a content creator, I shoot videos in a particular frame rate on purpose. The motion blur or lack thereof helps tell the story in some kinds of scenes. But most TVs want to show off their high refresh rate and therefore use realtime smoothing algorithms to create fake overly-dramatic effects to pump out extra in between frames. The motion looks too smooth to the point it seems CGI (because it sort of is). It just looks off once you notice it, and Sony is no exception. You have to dig around and figure out what they call it on every TV just to make it look normal again, on this set it is called Motionflow and it can be confusing to turn it off. I wish manufacturers would make it a simple and easy to understand toggle switch... maybe even present it as an option to the viewer upon setting it up so they can understand what they are enabling and decide if they want it or not (I strongly recommend not!).
But again, that's true of all modern Television sets, on its own right this is a solid TV and I would recommend it.

title: Two sets of RCA inputs make it perfect for me
text:
Up front I will say that these fill a niche for me that was made possible because of the two sets of RCA inputs in the back of the main speaker. I cannot speak to the value for general purpose use or compare it to similar or competing products.

I use my speakers to connect both a bluetooth receiver (a [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]]) for streaming music from my smart phone, and a netbook to my TV. Please see my customer-supplied images at the top of this page for photos that depict how.

The bluetooth receiver allows me to stream music from my Droid X smart phone to the speakers. This is an important feature for me because I have most of my music collection on that device.

Using the second set of RCA inputs, and a [[ASIN:B00004Z5CP Belkin Audio Y Cable Splitter 1-Mini Plug/2-RCA Plugs (6 Feet)]] I am able to transmit my netbook's audio to the speakers, while a [[ASIN:B0002AHT0M Standard 15-Pin VGA Male to VGA Male Cable]] connects the netbook to my TV.

Regarding the sound: these speakers pump out clear sound that allows me to easily enjoy the full richness of my music up to 25 feet away. It favorably compares to my larger, power hungry surround sound system in quality, clarity and volume.

A nice feature that I personally don't use is the headphone jack in the front of the master speaker. For folks who are connecting these speakers to a desktop or laptop system to extend their sound capabilities, this is a plus because at night or in an office it gives the privacy you may need.

My only complaint is the power supply, which is more like a brick. Because of its size it takes up three outlets on my surge protector - one for the power and the size blocking two more. Please see my third customer-supplied image at the top of this page to see in detail what I mean.

As you can see, my use is somewhat unique. If you are looking for a set of speakers for your laptop or desktop, plus a smart phone audio or MP3 player and do not need bluetooth streaming, then you can dispense with my configuration that uses the [[ASIN:B0047T79VS Belkin F8Z492TTP Bluetooth Music Receiver]] and replace that device with a simple [[ASIN:B00004Z5CP Belkin Audio Y Cable Splitter 1-Mini Plug/2-RCA Plugs (6 Feet)]] that will connect to the audio out jack on most smart phones.

title: Good sound - good price
text:
I'm somewhat particular about my music and my headphones and have specific things I look for. I'll try to touch on those items in this review.

Sound Quality: obviously most important. I look for solid bass (not boomy or hyped). And clear trebles (not sizzling or hyped). These headphones performed okay on both counts although it did seem the bass was a little hyped. I have some expensive headphones that these did not compare favorably to. I also look for general clarity in vocals... here, they did good... nothing nasally or buried in the mix. The exception came when turning on the noise reduction circuit. More on that later.

Comfort: okay, I have a big head (size xxl hat). So comfort is important to me. These headphones are adequate in that regard. I had to extend them fully, but at full extension they fit me properly and comfortably, sealing off around the ear. They did not completely surround my ears as some studio monitors do, but they did cover my ears. The padding is decent and I was able to listen for a reasonable amount of time before they became uncomfortable pressing on the perimeter of my ear. If your head/ears are smaller, my guess is they'd be plenty comfortable.

Noise reduction: I'm not used to using this feature and wasn't sure how to test it, so I simply sat down next to an air cleaner I have in my home and tried turning noise reduction on and off to see what happened. There was definitely a reduction in the noise... mainly in the lower frequencies. It didnt completely eliminate the sound of the blowing air, but what was left was a thinned out version of the original noise. It was definitely an improvement in the level of noise. The only thing I didnt care for was that there seemed to be an impact on the sound of the music also. Again, the noise reduction thinned the music and left it a little nasally.

Controls: straight forward controls. Theres a slider to turn noise reduction on and off and an adjacent button to activate the phone function. Since the phone button was just below the slider, I kept accidentally turning on the phone when trying to activate the noise reduction. Better button placement would have helped.

Overall, I was reasonably impressed with these headphones. Especially considering the price, they seem to do well. They come with a nice, soft sided carry case and needed cables. I expect I'll get some good use from these.

title: Great lens and sensor, bad shutter lag, audio and switches
text:
The wide angle lens is wonderful. The field of view and the speed (light gathering ability) of the lens can only be rivaled by high end camera and lens combinations costing six to ten times as much (admittedly those are superior in many other ways as well). Still, the point is that no other compact point and shoot camera can rival the field of view and speed of this one. Nevertheless, some things come up short of fair on the LX3.

The shutter lag is terrible. I am a very instinctive shooter that is quite capable in photojournalist style candids but I am almost always defeated by this camera.

I am not a photophile or electronic gadget spec sheet bench racer. I've done wonderful 8x10 prints with a 6MP camera and 10MP is enough to get prints after substantial cropping. I have huge film scans when I need them but I cannot realistically show dozens of megapixels on screen or in print for more than a handful of images. I also shoot in .jpg and it's great. I can't imagine the agony of terabytes of raw data jamming my PC.

I love the LX3 video quality for movies. It's ideal for Youtube and even Youtube HD. I do not like the Quicktime .MOV format or the weak compression algorithm. I wish it had H.264 and wrote an .MPG type format. It still beats the data format from a DVD camcorder though.

The audio quality for movies is terrible. Again, I'm not talking audiophile critique here. For comparison, my Sony DSC T9 (ultra compact point and shoot) has far better sound.

I hate the manual aspect ratio slider. If I shoot movies I want 16:9 but for stills I want 3:2 (of course). The LX3 requires that I remember to both turn the dial and slide the switch or I will end up shooting 16:9 stills.

Overall, it's a great camera. I hope they get the rest sorted out by the time I expect to buy another one in about 3 or 4 years.

I have not had this issue with my older docks with the wider connection, although I guess I've never had such thick cases as we have now.

Pros
+ Good Sound
+ Completely Plug and Play (although you can add an app if you want)

Cons
- Connector not long enough to work with iPod or iPhone Cases on.
- App for the dock is just OK, there is room for improvement.

All in all, it is a decent dock for the price. My son is very happy with it, other than the fact the connector does not work with our cases.

title: Solid, Steady Connection but Not Great Speed
text:
In terms of convenience, this is an outstanding product. It literally is plug and play. Just plug the transmitter in near you router and plug the Ethernet cable into an open port. Plug the receiver where you need the signal press the button on each device and setup is about complete. I had zero issues in terms of connection.

The farther the distance you span and the more walls and obstacles between, the slower the resultant signal will be. I tested the unit in a multitude of locations and I always received a signal, although it dropped the farther away I moved.

The point of this device is to use in locations where it is not possible, or where it would be difficult to run an Ethernet cable. If you are in a position where you need to get a signal to a TV to stream programming this would be a great choice. I tested it with Hulu, Prime and Netflix and it worked great. Depending on distance spanned and the strength of your original signal it probably would be adequate for internet use. However I can not recommend this as a viable option for gaming.

This set will definitely fulfill many people’s needs. It is just important to consider your use in relation to the WiFi product you install. For my family this worked fairly well.

title: Really solid for the money, good value compared to Sony WH-1000
text:
There's a lot that I like about these Philips headphones. All the classic features you'd expect from a higher-end over-the-ear style wireless headset are there, including support for an optional 3.5mm jack with included cable in the box, and they even threw in an airplane adapter and carrying case.
It's got soft ear cups and padded head bar, and a pretty awesome NC system. Here's the thing: I own a pair of Sony WH-1000 headphones so I was expecting to be somewhat spoiled and biased about the sound quality and build. And I am. The Sonys are still some of the best and the standard by which I judge other headphones in this style. BUT... at the time of this review, the price of this Philips product is less than half of what I paid for my Sony. Are the Sonys better? A little. Are they twice the price better? NO WAY. This is far better quality in sound and build than the cheapo bluetooth headphones, and if I didn't try them side by side with my Sony, it'd be hard to tell them apart. The feature set are similar, including the app control which actually made the phone really easy to pair as well.
One thing I actually really like about these is that there are more buttons than the Sony alternative. A dedicated button for mute, a dedicated button for noise cancellation, and of course power/pairing. But there are also touch sensitive controls on the ear cups, which I did not realize at first. I have mixed feelings about touch controls, I feel like they are easy to accidentally trigger, but so far it's actually been pretty good.
I think for the current asking price of around 150, the pros are solid enough to be worth recommending.

It is very simple to set up AND has the ability to give you a full surround sound experience. It is capable of running up to a total of seven speakers along with a subwoofer. It comes with seven HDMI inputs which can accommodate multiple devices. The Bluetooth wireless connection gives you the ability to connect the device to a smartphone, tablet or computer. All you have to do is download the free Yamaha Musiccast app from Google Pay Store or iTunes.  You can play music through most of the popular sound apps (i.e., Spodify, Pandora, Apple Music, etc). The Sound quality is great and gives you the ability to choose different surround sound options (i.e., sports, action games, music video, standard, adventure, drama, mono, etc). The system also has the multi-room capability and the ability to make adjustments on your television screen. Power is not a problem and gives you 100 watts of power per channel. Overall this is a great receiver (for the amateur music enthusiast) and gets 4 stars.

title: Before you buy please keep in mind of few things
text:
Please keep in mind the service is friendly. They will take back item, but there is a 20% restocking fee. The price of sending it back and the fee does not make it worth it. You lose money either way if you wind up thinking that you will get a hard, clear, LCD screen protector and find out the only hard cover is the one that acts as a shade to the screen. Once you close that part, you don't see your LCD screen.

It's not so much the service afterwards. It's the service of not being more clear on the words and the picture before hand. I had 2 options. Either buy from another site that actually has a hard, clear, LCD screen or from this one which I've thought was that and then some. Instead the screen cover is just the flimsy sticker that everyone sells for a few bucks. Those don't stick on very well without bubbles showing up. The few tries didn't go as smoothly as one would like so it makes the screen look worse.

If you want to buy the black cover/hood, the flimsy sticker for the LCD screen and the lens cleaner all in one then this is the set for you. If you're wanting a clear, hard, LCD screen protector to protect your LCD screen and camera better, this is not the one.

The idea is to invest in something that would protect the camera better.

Yes, the items did come within estimated time. But I've found it odd that it had a sticker on there stating it's time sensitive. It took 9 days to be delivered from CA when it usually takes 4-7 days for things to get to my state.

4 stars for the courteous reply in trying to resolve the matter, but the restocking fee isn't good.
1 star in not being clear about wording and pictures that is misleading.
3 stars for the items being alright.

In no way that I'm saying this is a bad seller. Just wish some things were more clear. I want future buyers to know what they're getting unless they want to be disappointed. For those who want a clear, hard, LCD screen cover for the Sony HX200, go to that well known auction site. But it's not sold as an auction which is good.

title: These are NOT bone conduction headphones
text:
The only thing these headphones have going for it is a respectable battery life. Everything else is just a disappointment, unfortunately.

I've been trying to find a good but affordable pair bone conduction headphones because I keep a headphone on my head almost all day while I work and write my code but I end up shutting the rest of the family out and miss half of the conversations going on in the house. When I discovered open ear bone conduction, it seemed to be the perfect solution.

So far, I have not found a good one. The specific problems of this pair of headphones is that it is not bone conduction. It is a simple pair of speakers set next to your ear. There is no bone shaking going on. With bone conduction, you can put in earplugs and still hear the audio fairly clearly, with these, the sound is clearly muffled and hard to make out.

In addition, there is a half-second delay on these headphones meaning they are no good for watching videos. I have not experienced bluetooth delay in quite a few years so I wasn't expecting it. Further, there is no charging light, meaning there is no way to tell if they are charged or not.

title: Incredible range!  I recommend using high quality wifi router connected to their LAN port.
text:
**update - no more drop issues - in my review below I was having internet drop-outs, but I found out it was an issue with my source wifi connection. The CC Vector device is amazing and I'm super happy with it. The best way to sum it up, is that it's not a super "smart" device - so you'll need to connect to a strong source wifi signal - if you get ANY kind of drop out issues with the source wifi, you'll have issues. But if you have a WIFI source that is strong and consistent, this will allow you to connect to it from very far distances. I'm very happy with it!

**original review below**

We needed to get a wifi signal across a property to another building about 600 feet away, a property with scattered trees between the 2 locations. Nothing seemed to work, and I was hesitant to spend $300 for a solution, and I didn't want to pay for another internet line to the other building. I tried a few cheaper $100-$150 solutions, but they simply didn't work. The CCrane kit worked right away. It did take about an hour or so to assemble and setup, and it was by far the easiest long-range wifi solution in terms of the technical setup - it's no different than setting up a basic wifi range extender/repeater.

We connected the CCrane repeater to a 200Mb/s wifi connect connection, and with a 60% signal we were getting only about 10Mb/s download rate - it was slow, but usable. We generally range from 45-75% signal performance with where we setup the receiver antenna. I would HIGHLY recommend putting it as high as you can - we got about double performance when we put the antenna 15 feet high vs. 6 feet high (6 feet high gave us 10MB/s performance, 15 feet up we got about 18MB/s performance)

After a few months of on and off performance, I started to get tired of the slow and unreliable WIFI signal. It worked...good enough for browsing, but not good enough for taking business calls, Zoom meetings, etc. Wifi calling would constantly be unclear. We also ran into dead internet issues: a few times a week the wifi signal seemed fine, but would not allow for any internet activity and I'd have to turn off and turn on the wifi rebroadcaster to make it work again.

I almost gave up, but I decided to try to use the ethernet ports on the back of the unit. There is one wifi antenna and 2 ethernet ports on the CCrane unit. I simply stopped using the CCrane wifi, and I plugged an Asus AC1200 wifi router into the back of the CCrane unit. BOOM - we went from 10Mb/s performance up to 60Mb/s performance. NOW everything feels right. This number would be accurate - CCrane does say you get about 1/2 the performance of the base internet because it's a repeater and that's what they do.

Unfortunately I still get random internet drops - the CC Vector repeater will say it's connected to the internet, signals are strong, but the internet will not work. This happens about once a day and we have to reboot for it to work again. I'm currently working with their support to see if this can be resolved. (review update - this was because of an issue with the source wifi signal - I ended up connecting a Wavlink Ariel HD2 bridge to the source WIFI router, and now we're getting very strong and consistent speeds without any dropouts).

So all-in-all - I'm happy with it. The included CCrane wifi could use some technology improvements and updates, but I think they make these things for random couples who RV around the country and don't need blazing internet.

Once you bypass the CCrane wifi and use the ethernet in the back with your own high performance WIFI router, you'll notice much improved performance.

I hope they update the built in WIFI - it would have been nice to just use one router with a $300 setup!

text:
After retiring my well used and beat up Welt tripod after 35 years of field use and began looking for a new tripod I was shocked when I saw the prices of medium to light weight tripods for 35 mm camera use. $200-$300 -- are you kidding me? I like quality and long term durability (as was my Welt, but...no longer made) and am usually willing to pay for it. However, I decided to give this relatively inexpensive Benro a try and couldn't be happier. I've had it in the field 8 times already, setting it up in water, on muddy slopes, in freezing temperatures and it performs very well for me. The legs extend easily. It is firm. It is light, and with the attachment of a shoulder strap is comfortably carried. I also purchased the Benro BR268 Ball Head for it and it too is of high quality and excellent functionality. This is a great value.

----
Update March 2012. This may be moot, as Benro no longer makes this model. It has been updated to the A0580F as far as I can tell. Anyway, this inexpensive aluminum tripod has performed great in the field. I've done my best to beat it up everywhere from a hike to the bottom of the Grand Canyon to sloughing through the Everglades. It works fine. The Benro Ballhead BR268 is another story. The quick attachment/release spring loaded button/pin now longer works and the entire mechanism has too much play in it. I only paid $38 for it. So I upgraded to a Manfrotto 496RC2 which works wonderfully, smooth and tight. As I was researching ballheads I checked out tripods. Nothing comes close to the value, portability, and toughness of this cheap Benro. There isn't anything out there with the stability and light weight of this Benro. At 2.4 lbs it is lighter than all Carbon Fiber tripods of the same relative size costing $250 and up.

Note to reviewer who complained that Amazon.com should have better details on the size and weight. He is right, but I think most people do the research and find that information elsewhere, then come back to Amazon.com to buy. Benrousa.com is easy to find and has all the data you could want.

title: The Speaker Itself Is Good But Bluetooth...
text:
Bottom Line - The speaker itself is excellent but Bluetooth can be an irritating technology.

The speaker is lightweight and even has an attached carrying strap. Unlike a lot of lightweight products though, it doesn't feel flimsy or fragile at all. Instead it has a nice, solid, durable feel to it. While I am not an audiophile, the speaker has a deep, rich sound that I really like. It does well with audiobooks, music, and videos.

The problems seem to be with Bluetooth. One major issue is that the sound stutters while using Bluetooth. It's very noticeable when playing music and very irritating when listening to audiobooks. That's happened with every Bluetooth speaker I've ever tried. A google search indicates that it's a common problem related to the amount of information the computer is trying to pump out to the speaker. There's a checklist of possible issues to go through to try to fix the problem but the stuttering seems all too common with this technology.

Another issue involves changing modes on a Bluetooth speaker. To sidestep the stuttering I plugged this speaker into my computer with a standard jack. It worked fine and the sound was good. When I unplugged it to bring the speaker into another room with me, I had to redo my audio settings. When I plugged it back in with the jack, an audiobook played just fine but there was no sound while playing videos. Again, I had to go into the audio settings and fiddle with them to be able to watch a movie. I've had similar issues with other Bluetooth speakers.

If you are a techie you may be able to resolve such things quickly and easily. The less tech adept you are, the more hassle they will be though. Myself, I'm just going to leave the speaker connected to my pc via a good old fashioned jack because I like its sound. Bluetooth? Bah, I haven't got time to bother with it.
