title: Comes with EVERYTHING! But the average cell phone has better IQ
text:
Ok, to be fair I work with cameras for a living. I wasn't expecting this to compete with my cinema cameras or even popular DSLRs for video, but I was expecting it to at least hold up to the standards people are expecting from cell phone cameras these days. It doesn't. Aside from filling a 4K frame, there aren't a lot of positives to say about the video quality.
To be fair, this has a LOT of advantages over using a cell phone. Recording for long lengths of time onto an SD card is a big plus, not the mention the ability to mount it to a standard tripod and have accessories like a mic and light attached to the body (which are all included!). It comes with a wide angle lens (that is oddly called "macro", but no- it's not for macro shots, its for going wider) which screws on to the front, as well as a handle mounting bracket, an LED light and a microphone. It even comes with a 64GB card, a spare battery, and not one but TWO useful carrying cases (a large one for everything, and a smaller one for just the camera solo). But that's about all the positives I can say about it. If you are outside with a lot of light, you can get decent shots, but this isn't a zoom lens, the zoom is digital only. You can go wide with the external lens or just stay at a fixed medium without it. So no closeup shots for soccer moms. The dynamic range when using it indoors was pretty bad, worse than your average mid-range cell phone. Forget about low light. But that's ok, because the ergonomics of a camera make it better than a cell phone, right?
Well, sorta. Holding it with the strap and the flip out screen is nice. But the UI is confusing, it's hard to go back and watch clips you took because everything is kind of sluggish and not intuitive- once we went past the first page of recorded clips, it was really difficult to move to the next page without accidentally clicking and opening a clip for playback. It just feels really laggy to navigate. Then there's the mic input... it's actually a proprietary plug that goes into the charging/USB plug, and gives you a pigtail for USB on one side and a mic input jack on the other. Odd, considering it COMES with a mic, you'd think it would have an input directly on the body. But no, just this weird mess of wires. Everything about this feels like jumping through a hoop to make it do what you want, and at the end of the day you have to wonder if you couldn't just be better off getting a mic adapter for the cellphone you already own and putting it in one of those holster cages.
Speaking of cell phones, this does have an app which supposedly lets you remotely control and perhaps even copy files from it, but I didn't get that far. I tried to install the app but then gave up when I decided I didn't want to grant this all the permissions it wanted from my personal phone. And I didn't think the video quality was worth it either.
Oddly enough, I kind of like the accessories it comes with. The LED light is pretty nice, the mic isn't terrible either. But for the money, I feel like I would have rather skipped those accessories and just gotten a better camera for a little bit more. It feels almost like they realized this camera was a hard sell so they beefed it up with lots of a accessories for the price.
In conclusion, you DO get a lot of accessories for the money. It's not the worst camera I've ever used, and you can't really get a set with everything you need for any less so I'd say it's worth at least 3 stars for being a functional kit. But I can't really imagine a scenario that I would recommend it.

title: Lowepro SlingShot 202 AW
text:
The fit and finish of this bag are top notch. I've been camping and backpacking for decades and I have to say the quality of this bag and the workmanship are among the best I've seen. The nylon material is heavy duty and durable. The bag and shoulder strap are well padded for comfort and protection of your gear. The pack includes a built in micro-fiber cloth and two memory card slots in the main compartment. There's even a tuck-away all-weather cover in the bottom of the bag for inclement weather situations. The dividers in the main compartment are infinitely adjustable and all can be removed/repositioned. The pack includes a pull-out tripod holder/foot pocket and strapping system on the side of the bag. There's also a separate compartment at the top of the pack for personal items large enough for wallet, keys, an emergency poncho, etc. Also included are two smaller pockets on the back of the pack suitable for lens pens, notepad, pens, what have you.

This bag is huge. Easily as big as most hiking day-packs. There's room for everything and the kitchen sink. Currently I have my old Canon AE-1 with 80-200 mm lens attached. My 55 mm auxiliary lens. A half dozen assorted filters. Cable release. 1:1 reverse adapter AND my Kodak Z-650 point and shoot all in the main compartment.

Ease of use is incredible. The shoulder strap and waist belt are widely adjustable for people of almost all sizes. The zippers work flawlessly and fast never catching or hanging. The velcro throughout the pack is quite heavy duty and looks like it will hold up to years of abuse. All you need do is slide the pack from your back to the front of your body and the camera access section is right there. You never have to take the bag off to get at your rig.

Those are the pros.

Here are just a couple cons:
The micro-fiber cloth is not removable. I'm not sure what you could do if it became soiled or stained and needed cleaning. The strap for the tripod is not fixed to the pack and could easily be lost. The all-weather cover fits very tight to the bag (in and of itself this is a good thing, but...) it won't fit over any but the smallest mono-pod or tripod. My [[ASIN:B00005T3TI Ambico 54 Inch Tripod with Quick Release (V-0555)]] just barely fits on the pack.

I have no doubt this bag would last years for anyone from amateur to most demanding professional.

title: Looks better than it sounds. 2.5-3
text:
My first thought when I initially saw the Motorola Sphere 2-in-1Bluetooth Speaker with Over-Ear Headphones was, wow. It is extremely attractive and would definitely appeal to the young folks. Ironically, our house is full of loud, music playing teenagers who have very clear ideas about what sounds good and which products they prefer to use. They like speakers and headphones that offer clear sound quality with bass. We have a Bose Soundlink speaker, and VModa or Sennheiser earphones. So unfortunately when I reviewed these, I was comparing them with others that I have used. While this product might look good (definitely a 5), it needs to sound good. And this is where I am disappointed – in the sound quality.
In a nutshell:

Attractiveness – The Motorola Sphere is attractive. It is black and looks like a head with headphones.The system looks nice on a bookshelf, desk or dresser in a dorm room, bedroom, etc.. I do love the look.

Set up – The directions for setting up the device are easy to follow. Once you pair the headphones and the sphere (separately) to your phone (via Bluetooth), it is pretty easy to use. There is sometimes a lag when you disconnect or switch between the sphere and the headphones. You might have to press the button on the headphones to make the sound switch between the two devices.

Headphones – They are adjustable and the sound quality is good via the headphones.

Sound Quality – The sound quality is not good thru the speaker. I’d give it 2.5 at the most. To me the frequency response seemed a little high, which is why the sound thru the speaker is hollow or missing something, no matter the genre (i.e., classic, jazz, rap, rock) played. But a plus is that the quality of the sound thru the headphones is better, it is more balanced and therefore rates 3.5-4 (although the bass is still not heavy).

In conclusion, while I love the look and concept (2 in 1 – speaker and headphones) of the Motorola, I wouldn’t recommend it. I would instead suggest investing a little more money and getting a better more quality speaker.

title: Pleasantly Surprised by this Router
text:
After my Netgear router decided to degrade to the point of uselessness I set out to replace it and researched several different routers. After looking at a number of reviews online and looking for any information I could find on mid-range wireless N routers I decided to try the MediaLink router. The number of good reviews on this router led to this decision, and so far all of these positive reviews have been justified from my perspective.

Without reading the directions and without running the setup software I had this router online and working with my network in only a few minutes. I did things a little out of order though - I allowed each of my devices to connect to the router first, then I connected the router to the cable modem after which everything worked without any issues.

Tapping into the router's configuration settings is simple, especially since instructions to do so are included. Once in the user is presented with a very simple and self-explanatory menu system that is easy to navigate. In no time at all I had my DHCP reservations set for each device (useful when connecting printers to the wireless network), I had my security key set and had my SSID set for the network.

So far, the router has been stable and fast. In addition to having good network speeds, booting up the router takes very little time - 10-15 seconds, maybe? This is far and away faster than my previous routers.

I have found only a couple of minor drawbacks with this router, neither of which are really problematic but are just things I have noticed. First, I have observed that the signal strength is a little weaker than my previous routers. The router is on the top floor of the house and the main computers I use are in the basement, with one floor in between. While the systems can see the router and connect to it with no issue, the reported signal is not as strong as other routers I have used in the past. Second, and this is a nitpick, I have a dual-boot box that has Windows 7 and Linux on it. When connecting with Windows, the router recognizes the box by its name, but when I connect with Linux it has no name at all - even when I reboot from Windows into Linux immediately.

The MediaLink wireless N router is a decent router that seems to live up to the numerous good reviews it is getting. It seems to be fast and stable and so far I have had no troubles with it at all. The price is very reasonable. If you need a decent and affordable wireless router and you're willing to try a less-familiar name, consider giving this router a try.

title: I Wish It Was Just A Half Inch Bigger But Still Handy
text:
I got this for my daughter who is involved in a business situation where a camera, laptop, and tripod (plus accessories) are required for product photos, posting, and keeping track of inventory. She is always misplacing things. I wanted this to be in one place for her. Let's take a look.

WHAT IS THIS LIKE?
This is true to the photos with the listing. The case is padded, has a velcro flap on it which has a zipper in the front flap for flat things like our flat flash which we keep in a padded box, or cords, etc. The case itself has plenty of padding in it and non-abrasive soft fabrics.

CAMERA CASE
The camera storage has two adjustable velcro type walls in it so that you can make it bigger or smaller. The other two compartments are for storing lenses etc, and one of them has a flap, but the flap is not something you can fasten down. The camera that goes in here is a Fuji Finepix S1. The front lens sticks out quite a bit but it is stored on its back and is plenty protected by all of the padding.

ZIPPER ACCESS
There is a top zipper access so that if you have the flap down but need a quick access, you can quickly zip open the top and remove the camera.

LAPTOP POCKET
We have a laptop that I was sure would fit in there, but it is just about a 1/4 inch too long for the pocket. I thought it was a 14 inch, but it turned out to be 15 inch instead. A 14 inch laptop or tablet will fit in here perfectly. A 15 will not.

STRAPS
The straps on the bottom are adjustable to hold a tripod which is great to help keep all of this in order. When I want to make it easier to store, I remove the tripod and stand it next to this bag until it is time to use again.

SIDE MESH POCKET
This has a side pocket appropriate for a water bottle or can of coconut water, etc.

HANDLES
There is a single carry handle and a shoulder strap. The carry handle makes this a bit awkward, so we tend to use the shoulder strap except when we need to move the bag quickly.

THE BOTTOM LINE
Even though I wish this were slightly bigger to fit the laptop, it is my error, not the bag company, so I have to say other than that, this bag is well designed and does the job. It is a great way to keep all of the camera gear handy for the jewelry business it is needed for.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. It is not fair to remove a star for the misunderstood measurement, but this is not as handy for my needs as I had hoped. I am leaving this at five stars, because it is still handy to keep everything together for taking photos for the business it is intended for.

The other reason is the connector has loosened up a little which I've noticed in both my tablet and Kindle but it still works so it's a good backup cable to have around. The new cable end are very tight fitting which I'm happy with, the old one was getting a little too easy to pop loose but it got a LOT of usage so I really can't complain seeing as how much longer the six foot cable lasted. If this ten footer lasts that long I'll be quite happy.

Update 01/23/2018 - I bought this 10' cable based on the longevity of the company's 6' cable of the same style. My 6' cable lasted nearly a year of numerous daily times plugging and unplugging my tablet. With no discernable change in usage or handling the 10' cable is now disconnecting from the tablet at the lightest touch after less than three months. Very disappointed.

Update: 02/08/2018 - I contacted Anker about warranty support for this cable. They were very quick to respond, friendly, concerned and quickly sent me a braided upgrade cable to make up for this cable failing. title: FANTASTIC SOUND BAR with a remote that is an absolute disaster.  Fix the remote and 5-STARS no question.
text:
The sound from this bar is clean, clear, crisp and LOUD! A very decent amount of BASS, with a sub woofer output should you want to connect one. I found out I ordered a longer bar than is recommended. How did I find out? The packaging for this bar states that it is for a 42" or larger TV. I purchased it for a 32" TV. The concern, I believe, is that if the speakers are too far from the TV's center it will not seem as though the audio is coming from the actors. My brain is making the leap and tricking me so all is well. I use my TV for music for the most part anyway (Comcast Music Choice and Fire TV Music).
It is disappointing that Fire TV Music has such poor audio quality since it is there that I can make personal music choices unlike Comcast. Fire TV just sounds plain bad. It did on the TV speakers and now on the bar; it is just un-listenable. Safe to call it "LOW FIDELITY"
As far as connecting an input to this bar from your TV you have many options and most all the cables you may need are included. I really liked that they included the cord to to connect the bar to a sub. This cord is over and above what is required to connect the bar to the TV...very nice touch VIZIO. Now I need to go to my storage and try to find my sub :-)
My TV only offers 2 audio outputs, head phone and optical. Included with the bar were a headphone-to-2 RCA connector cord, and a fiber optic patch cord, among others. That allowed me what would be considered the worst quality connection and the best quality connection possibilities. If you don't have OPTICAL OUT on your TV do not despair...the worst possible option (headphone-to-RCA patch cord) sounds FANTASTIC! I can detect no loss of fidelity between the two. You will not be missing out.
Now to the reason I gave it 3 stars rather than 5. The back of the remote just keeps sliding off. It is not broken in any way. Just poorly designed. I often use the sound bar in dark or nearly dark conditions. It is taking time to train myself to not go where I normally would to use the any of the buttons. So how about the POWER button? It is not the top left button on the remote as you will see and are used to on any other remote in your home. For some strange reason instead of the power button being in the far upper left of the remote they felt this was a good place to position the INPUT button. Power is upper right. Volume UP/DOWN is traditionally placed on the left side of the remote with a paddle switch or separate buttons. Located in the standard volume UP/DOWN positions are the TruVolume and the TruSurround HD. The volume UP/DOWN are located on a FLAT 1-3/8" (34.9mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) multi-function EVER SO SLIGHTLY RAISED square. To be honest I can't even tell that it IS raised at all most of the time. If you go for the volume in low light you may operate any of 3 other function controls. Lastly, if you were hoping the VOLUME controls are the 2 well raised buttons on the right (traditional location) you would be wrong. Those are your BASS/TREBLE controls.
I am not sure I would buy this bar again knowing what I do now about the remote. As I said I often use the remote in low or no light. The problems I mention here may just be my own...but I doubt it. All of these tiny buttons and controls are all scrunched into a small 2-3/8" (60.3mm) x 1-3/8" (34.9mm) upper 40% of this little remote and they are not raised enough and not far apart enough to be used just by touch. I well believe that just 3 functions on the remote will account for 90% of it's use. POWER (that CAN be felt but it is in the wrong place...you'll get used to that) and the VOLUME UP/DOWN that exist on a square, fully smooth (NO tactile feedback...I'd hate to see a blind person trying to operate), 4-function piece of plastic that is raised about 1/32" (0.8mm). On the bright side for me, I found out fairly quickly that my cable box remote controls the basic functions of the sound bar. I hope you get so lucky.
Knowing what I know now I should have purchased a bar in the 28"-32" (71mm-81mm) class looking for features such as the control panel on the bar being mildly illuminated and a proper remote perhaps with illumination itself. My roommate may buy mine from me for a location that is always well lit and has a 42" TV. I'll lose $20 on the deal but I can get the absolute right bar for me.. I don't return items that are not what I would like due to my own failure in researching. So, for better or worse, the bar is mine. There is one thing you cannot fault; THIS THING SOUNDS AMAZING!

title: Small but capable music player
text:
The Philips GoGear Raga is the first exposure I have had to Philips' line of mp3 players and I was unsure of what I should expect of it. The price is comparable to other mp3 players of similar capacity so I expected it to be in the ballpark with them. For the most part I was correct, though there are a few things about which one should be aware when using this particular offering. It's a good product, but it has its quirks.

Setting up the Raga is easy. In the package is a USB cable that allows one to connect to a PC (packaging does not indicate if MacOS supports the Raga), and upon connecting Philips Songbird downloads and installs automatically. The installation is painless and does not take long, and a few clicks of the mouse along the way and the software loads up.

The first thing I tried to do was load music into the Raga, and once I got the music into Songbird the Raga disappeared from the available devices list. I am not sure what happened. I unplugged it and shut down Songbird, plugged the Raga back in and everything was as it should be, so I dragged 67 songs to the Raga for transfer. I saw two problems. First, the user has to know to drag and drop - there is no "transfer to..." option that I could find in any of the menus. The bigger problem, though, is that the transfer speed is abysmal and it took close to 2 minutes to transfer 67 songs that average 5MB in size. With my old iPod and with my ZuneHD, transfer speeds are appreciably faster. This doesn't make the Raga a piece of junk, of course, as the problem may be Songbird itself, but the transfer speed is something of which to be aware, especially if transferring large amounts of music.

Navigating to the newly transferred music is simple. For that matter, navigating the Raga is simple, period. Anyone with even slight familiarity with music players will have no problem finding and playing music on the Raga.

For comparison, I matched the Raga against my ZuneHD for playback. Of course, the Zune HD produced a more natural and clear sound, but only slightly. For the difference in price, I would have expected the ZuneHD to REALLY outperform the Raga, but this was not the case. In fact, when playing with the built in equalizers in both, I was able to get the Raga to get very close to the ZuneHD for sound quality. The difference was more pronounced with higher end ANC headphones, but this is unlikely to matter to the large majority of users.

The Raga has a tiny screen (the package says it's 1" diagonally) so this is not the kind of player one would want if frequently messing with settings and searching through. That said, the Raga is designed as a player to be worn with the included arm band, suitable for using at the gym. The ear buds that come with it have over-the-ear hooks to help keep them in place.

Considering the price and size, Philips has put together a very nice music player that will suit active users very well. It has some idiosyncrasies, in particular the transfer speeds, but it really is a capable player.

title: Astounding Sound AND Noise Cancellation
text:
I decided to buy a pair of noise canceling headphones after moving to a different location at work where I am in closer proximity to a rack of computers that runs constantly. After a short while the whirr of the fans in the computers and the rack in which they are mounted gets very tiring and annoys the ears. After doing some research, I finally decided on the Bose QuietComfort 15, and almost immediately I have seen that I made the right choice.

I was fortunate enough to get my hands on one of these before I committed my money so I could test the quality. I was very pleased when I put on the headphones, turned them on and all of the ambient noise around me simply vanished. The sound of the air conditioning, the murmuring of people chatting around me, even traffic outside was reduced to such a degree that I felt like I was in a bubble. I bought them on the spot.

I put these headphones through two major tests outside of work.

First, I plugged them into my iPod and turned them on. All I could hear when the music played was the music. Talking around me was overcome by the noise cancellation and the music, which was not set to a particularly high volume. As many have commented, the bass is very rich with these headphones but that's fine with me, as I really appreciate good bass response. Treble and mid-range are also good, though not quite as bright as the bass.

The really big surprise was when I plugged them into the mixing board where I was doing live recording. I was shocked at how effectively I could hear every sound coming through the microphones but practically nothing else. The sound was clear, crisp and not muddied in any way I could ascertain, which gave me a much better idea of what was recording onto the CD. I had used a lesser headset for this purpose, but no longer.

Some noises do get through, such as loud talking and even the typing on my keyboard, but those sounds are muffled quite a bit. The idea is to eliminate droning, obnoxious noise such as engine noise (there are several mentions in the documentation about wearing these on planes), while still allowing certain things to get through. These are certainly not perfect in that regard but they do come close.

In the past I have bought headphones only from either Sony or Sennheiser, with a very strong bias for the latter. This is my first set of Bose headphones and they are definitely the best pair I have ever used (let alone owned). I regard these as very much worth the price and gladly recommend them for anyone wanting to hear nothing but the music without blasting out the ears. These are high quality earphones and will please the enthusiast looking for good sound as well as the traveler looking for a quiet ride.

title: Good build quality and good picture quality.
text:
This Wireless WiFi Outdoor Security Camera Solar Battery Powered is a good camera. Taking it out of the box, I was able to tell that it is well-built and well thought out. The solar panel is of good quality and can be mounted on the camera or separately. The necessary USB extension cable and extra mounting arm is included in this camera kit if you decide to mount the panel separately from the camera. Mounting is easy. Just two screws into the eaves and you're done. No wires to pull and no batteries to change. Compare this with systems like Arlo where you would need to break out your ladder to switch out batteries every month or spend extra to purchase a solar panel for each camera.

This camera has all of the standard functions of live feed, motion detection, and night vision but of course it also has the pan and tilt function which helps to get a clearer picture of what you're trying to see. Local SD card storage means that a subscription service isn't necessary to review past events. It's all quite nice. I did find that there is a significant lag in the camera. It can take a full second for any pan and tilt commands to actually go through.

This camera works with the Tuya app (also works with Smart Life) so it's up to you to decide how much you can trust those apps, but otherwise the camera is a solid purchase.
